articles.title: The private creative world of Rabindranath Tagore, the man Yeats called ‘greater than any of us’
articles.summary: A previously unseen family archive offers a glimpse into the Indian Nobel prize winner’s artistic process and personal relationships in his final…

blocks.text: It’s easy to run out of words to describe Rabindranath Tagore. The first non-European to win the Nobel prize in literature, Tagore was a Bengali poet, musician, novelist, philosopher, songwriter, painter, humanist and educator.
Born in 1861, Tagore left an indelible mark on the subcontinent’s literature, music, education and art. Among his enduring legacies are the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.

As Nobel laureate economist Amartya Sen once wrote, Tagore was “a towering figure in the millennium-old literature of Bengal”, whose songs resonate across eastern India and Bangladesh, while his ideas on education, nationalism and freedom of the mind remain relevant today.

Yet his work also made a deep impression on the literary world far beyond the shores of India. WB Yeats is said to have described Tagore as “greater than any of us”. Gitanjali, the collection of poems that won Tagore the Nobel prize that same year, was praised by the committee for its “profoundly sensitive, fresh and beautiful verse”. Tagore’s English translation was published in London that March and reprinted 10 times by the time the prize was announced in November.

Tagore’s life and works have, of course, been well documented, but a collection of material preserved in a private family archive is now being brought into public view for the first time at an exhibition by Christie’s, opening in Mumbai this month. The archive draws from Tagore’s visits to the family home of his protege, Maitreyi Devi, in the bucolic village of Mungpoo in Darjeeling between 1938 and 1940. He died in 1941.

blocks.caption: An intimate glimpse … one of Tagore’s unseen artwork on display. Photograph: Christie’s Images Ltd 2026

blocks.text: The collection on display – artworks, manuscripts, letters, photographs and personal effects – offers an intimate glimpse into Tagore’s creative process and personal world in his final years.
I spoke to the exhibition curator, Nishad Avari, head of south Asian modern and contemporary art at Christie’s, about the stories behind the archive.

One instructive document Avari points to is a manuscript from 1940. It appears to be a draft of Tagore’s memoir Chelebela or My Boyhood Days, in which he reflects on his life – from growing up in a large family in Calcutta (modern-day Kolkata) to the rapidly changing world ushered in by electricity and the motorcar.

For Avari, what stood out was how the ideas in the document echoed the educational philosophy Tagore put into practice in Santiniketan (or Abode of Peace), the experimental school he set up about 100 miles from the state capital.
“He speaks about how education is like being in prison and that it should be open and free … about the idea of wonder and even fear as inspiring creativity,” Avari told me.

“That’s a direct relationship to Santiniketan and the open model of the school where people sat under trees with their gurus and learned in the open. Education didn’t feel like a restriction, prison or imposition,” he added.

blocks.caption: Window to a master’s practice … A manuscript by Rabindranath Tagore, on display at Christie’s. Photograph: Christie’s Images Ltd 2026

blocks.text: Avari points to another detail that makes this particular document valuable. Of the 10 complete manuscripts in the exhibition, it is the only one dictated to Devi, whose father was a close friend of Tagore’s. For Avari, this speaks to their close relationship and the trust he placed in her.

“If you look at the collection as a whole, she has copies of almost every single one of his publications signed to her by him,” he says. The collection includes hundreds of letters, too: first between Tagore and her father, and later between Tagore and Devi herself.

There are doodles among corrections, Avari explains, which show how his literary practice fed into his artistic practice. Alongside the manuscripts and correspondence are vintage photographs and personal effects, including a kurta and a lungi that Tagore left behind at the family home.

Among the artworks in the collection is a portrait of Devi, particularly notable because Tagore’s figure studies were not generally attributed to specific individuals in the way that portraits by his nephews, Abanindranath and Gaganendranath, often were, Avari said. There is also a landscape depicting the forests of Mungpoo, which Tagore embraced as a retreat.
On the international art market, Tagore’s paintings command significant prices. This year, Sotheby’s sold one of his watercolours for £1.02m (Rs 12.97 crore), nearly four times its low estimate.
Institutions such as Visva-Bharati in Santiniketan and the National Gallery of Modern Art hold much of Tagore’s archival materials, making the discovery of a private archive particularly rare.

He hopes that making these materials public will offer historians, scholars and admirers alike additional perspectives on Tagore. “We hope to add to the understanding of the artist, their career, and in this case, of course, our understanding of the man beyond his art as well.”
Rabindranath Tagore and Mungpoo runs between 10 November and 18 December at Christie’s space in south Mumbai.

blocks.caption: A voyage through another time … Malvika Singh’s Cooking for my Firefly. Photograph: Handout

blocks.text: Freddy Birdy, a copywriter whose delightful words have earned him a devoted Instagram following, recommends writer and historian Malvika Singh’s cookbook, Cooking for My Firefly.

“This book isn’t about recipes, though it does include them. It is a voyage through another time and place, tracing the social fabric of India of the 60s, 70s and 80s, trickling down to today. Told in Malvika’s beautiful prose, it takes us to a time when people entertained in homes, not in restaurants; when dishes were cooked in-house and there were no caterers or party planners. An era long before Instagram posts, WhatsApp invitations, celebrity chefs and food delivery apps, when the point of having a party was simply to have fun. It is an archive of photographs, food, culture, gossip, movie stars, politicians, royalty, set against the spectacular backdrop of Malvika’s dining tables through the decades. I like to dip into it every now and then, much as one might do standing in a dark kitchen with the light of the refrigerator enticing you to midnight goodies.”

Vibe check

blocks.caption: ‘We’ll find a way to sing’ … Dopeher Blues by Aamir Aziz. Photograph: Youtube

blocks.text: At a time when public anger has spilled into the streets, artist Aamir Aziz’s new track, Dopeher Blues (Afternoon Blues), captures the frustration and angst of a generation that has lived through many crises.

Aziz describes the song as an expression of a period of deep suffocation. Issues such as farmer suicides, unemployment and conflicts in Palestine and Kashmir, he told me, are things he has grown up with even as public attention shifts with the news cycle. It is also a warning, in part, against internet culture, where injustices risk becoming normalised.

Aziz, 35, works in acting, music and writing, and became an internet sensation with his defiant poem Sab Yaad Rakha Jayega (Everything Will Be Remembered) during the citizenship protests. At the heart of his new track is a note of defiance and hope: “We’ll find a way to sing,” he says, as he calls on everyone “to keep speaking up even in a climate of fear, misinformation and oppression.”

articles.title: Americans head to polls in midterm elections seen as referendum on Trump
articles.summary: Control of the Senate and House of Representatives, both currently held by the Republicans, is at stake
articles.byline: Robert Tait in Yarmouth, Maine, Joseph Gedeon in Detroit, Michigan, and Rachel Leingang in Waverly, Iowa

blocks.text: Americans are heading to the polls today in US midterm elections widely seen as a referendum on Donald Trump’s second presidency and a chance for opponents to rein in his untrammeled power.

Democrats and Republicans have scrambled in recent days to deliver their final pitches to voters, with control of the US Senate and House of Representatives – both currently held by the Republicans – at stake. Also on the ballot are 36 governor’s races, as well as control of state legislatures, sheriffs races and ballot measures.

The campaign has been overshadowed by Trump, who has staged several dozen rallies across the country while urging his make America great again (Maga) base to vote for Republican candidates and pretend his name was on the ballot.

The party holding the White House typically loses congressional seats at midterm elections, and Democrats are hoping Trump’s nose-diving popularity can be exploited to generate a “blue wave” groundswell of popular opposition that will win them the Senate and the House.

They are seeking to wrest control over both chambers of Congress to put a brake on Trump’s presidential power, which has gone largely unchecked as he launched a fierce immigration crackdown involving mass arrests and deportations, waged war on Iran, imposed tariffs on foreign imports and embarked on vainglorious building projects, including a White House ballroom.

Opinion surveys have suggested the Democrats are well positioned to win the House. The party faces a tougher task to regain control of the Senate, although it has targeted several Republican-held seats including Ohio, Texas and Maine.

“There has to be a better way for everyday people to be able to live their lives out here,” said Maine’s Democratic senate candidate Troy Jackson in final pitch to voters on Monday. “And if we quit wasting money on foreign wars, if we quit giving money to billionaires, if we quit doing these dumbass tariffs and things like that, we can make people’s lives better by prioritizing what we want to do in this country to help regular, everyday people, and that’s what this race is about. I’m tired of watching elected officials cater to people like Elon Musk.”

blocks.caption: Volunteers hand out signs for the Democratic candidate James Talarico at his final campaign rally in Austin, Texas, on Monday. Photograph: Mike Segar/Reuters

blocks.text: A final set of polls from the New York Times and Siena University, published on Sunday, put Democratic candidates ahead in five of seven key battleground contests – including Texas and Kansas, where voters have not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1988 and 1932 respectively.

The final stretch of the campaign was not without drama for the Democrats, however. In Michigan – widely seen as a crucial pillar to either party’s ambitions of control in the Senate – the Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost her party’s senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed his Republican rival, Mike Rogers, on Sunday.

Stevens was widely condemned by fellow Democrats over the move, which followed a feud with the El-Sayed campaign over an outside group’s campaign ad that blamed the high cost of living on US support for Israel. Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, described her endorsement of Rogers as “a despicable betrayal”.
“Whatever they’re trying to distract you, it’s because they’re picking your pocket,” El-Sayed told hundreds of supporters in Royal Oak, Michigan on Monday.

The extraordinary rupture took places days after the party faced damaging headlines in Alaska, where it was reported that the Democratic senate candidate’s campaign was behind an effort to recruit a challenger with almost the same name as her rival, the Republican senator Dan Sullivan. (The Democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, has denied any knowledge of such a scheme on the part of her campaign.)

Before the report of the Peltola campaign’s involvement, the Department of Justice (DoJ) filed a lawsuit to block the certification of Alaska’s Senate results in the event of a Republican defeat, citing potential “voter confusion” over the presence of two Dan Sullivans on the ballot. The lawsuit has since been dismissed by a judge.

Trump has put himself center stage by crisscrossing the country to deliver a succession of speeches for Republican candidate, despite opinion polls showing his approval ratings falling to record lows of between 33 and 37%.

In his final public campaign appearance on Monday, Trump spent most of the time in a rambling talk about his problem-plagued renovation of Washington’s reflecting Pool. “This is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime,” he said, 26 minutes into the speech, before quickly returning to talking about renovations. Schumer called it a “pathetic closing message”.

blocks.caption: These midterms are widely seen as a referendum on Donald Trump’s second presidency. Photograph: Ümit Bektaş/Reuters

blocks.text: Democrats have sought to reinforce the message that the election is about Trump while trying to highlight the perceived corruption of the US president and his family, along with affordability issues and the impact of the conflict with Iran, which is seen as having exacerbated the cost of living.

Opinion surveys have shown that voters have become increasingly concerned about corruption in government. A recent Harris poll for the Guardian found that 76% think elected officials care more about enriching themselves than improving the economy for ordinary people.
Disclosures to the US office of government ethics show that Trump has made about $2.2bn since returning to the White House, including royalties from his own name-branded meme coin.
As the president has grown wealthier, voters have chafed under rising living costs, which Trump vowed to reduce during his 2024 presidential campaign.

The war with Iran – which Trump launched in February in tandem with Israel – has stoked inflation by increasing global oil prices, which has led to higher prices at the pump for American motorists and raised the cost of diesel, a vital fuel for supply chains and farmers.

“We need to focus that anger and point it at where it ought to be pointed, which is at a broken two-choice political system that is too easily abused to allow elected officials to be corrupt and to be lazy and still hold power,” Rob Sand, Iowa’s Democratic candidate for governor, said on Monday.
The US elections also take place under a shadow of uncertainty about whether Trump will accept the results if they do not go the Republicans’ way.

Alaska is just one of the cases being pursued by the justice department – under the control of Trump’s close ally, Todd Blanche, the attorney general – that opponents say are designed to cast doubt on the election’s integrity, including through baseless claims of mass voting by non-US citizens.
The department plans to deploy a record 1,000 election monitors to polling stations across the US. Critics have denounced the move as voter intimidation.

articles.title: Why South Africa's local elections matter
articles.summary: South Africans head to the polls on Wednesday amid water shortages, frustration with local services and questions over whether the ANC's support will keep falling.

image.caption: Water shortages ‌and unreliable electricity ⁠supplies ⁠have become symbols of municipal failures that have angered votersImage: Themba Hadebe/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "We've decided not to vote. At all," said Vatiswa Zoya, two days before voters in South Africa cast their ballots for new municipal government leaders. "What is the point? We will still sleep hungry."
These very same frustrations are what will lead 22-year-old Lindokuhle Mbandazayo to the polls, although she has yet to decide where to place her cross.

"When we vote for councilors, we ask them to fix the area," Mbandazayo told DW. "The electricity goes off regularly here. There is also sewage in the streets and we have to jump over this. There are a lot of things that need to be fixed here."

Both women live in Tembisa, a township in Ekurhuleni, a municipality on the outskirts of Johannesburg, South Africa's largest city. Both express an "embedded frustration" over their living conditions.

blocks.caption: Many voters will be asking whether they'll have water to shower on election day, as shortages persistImage: Siphiwe Sibeko/REUTERS

blocks.text: Sanusha Naidu, an analyst at the Institute for Global Dialogue, noted that it is this "embedded frustration" that prompts people to vote.
"Your vote actually puts some of these political parties' feet to the fire, but I think that frustration is also inherently coming from the fact that it's not going to happen overnight," Naidu said.

On Wednesday, South Africans will vote in local government elections that will determine control of the country's largest cities and test whether the African National Congress (ANC), the leading party in a national government coalition, continues its electoral decline.
Here are five things to know about the November 4 election.
1. Water as a key voter issue
Many voters will be motivated by whether they can shower or not on voting day, as many parts of the country experience water supply issues.
In Johannesburg, several neighborhoods have faced water cuts and rationing for weeks as old infrastructure struggles to keep up with supply.

"Every province has an issue. So if we take for example drinking water quality, half of the drinking water systems in South Africa are not fit for drinking," said Ferrial Adam, executive director of water rights NGO WaterCAN.

"Almost 70% of our wastewater treatment works are in a critical state and spewing sewage into rivers and streams across the country," she told DW during a protest over water cuts in Johannesburg, adding that "it is a definite water crisis across South Africa."
In Tshwane, a metropolitan area that includes South Africa's administrative capital, Pretoria, a recent water treatment failure left more than 400 residents sick.

Sanusha Naidu, an analyst at the Institute for Global Dialogue, says that despite widespread worries about water quality and supply, many of those campaigning have not provided adequate details on their solutions.

"I think their promises have been very transactional. Their promises are always, you know, we're going to bring water to your community. We're going to make sure the taps are flowing. We're going to ensure that we're going to deal with the old infrastructure around water, etc. But I don't think they've dug deeper in terms of understanding what the budgets say about water access," she said.
2. ANC in decline
Many voters place blame for the state of municipalities on the African National Congress, which has historically held an outright majority in most municipalities.

In 2016 the ANC secured 53.91% of the overall vote and had an outright majority in 161 of 213 councils. In 2021, that decreased to 45.59% of the overall vote with a majority in 122 of 213 municipalities.
Global marketing research firm Ipsos predicts that the party's support could fall as low as 30% in this election, resulting in an increase in coalition-run municipalities.
South Africa sees nationwide protests over migrants
Naidu notes that the party has struggled to keep up with the expectations of evolving voters, particularly millennial and Gen Zvoters who now make up the bulk of voters.
"You have an electorate that wants to see who are these people that you're putting out there to say you're going to make things work for us," she said.
Mbandazayo is one such voter, who is casting her ballot in her second election and says she is looking for a new voice in politics.
"We need change. I am considering voting for another party because the current party is not doing well for us because we've been voting for them for a long time," she told DW.
3. Migration a big talking point
South Africa has seen a wave of protests around migration for several months, ramping up in October with opposition to the country's asylum process.
Murmur Intelligence, a digital analysis firm, says parties including Action SA, the MK Party and the Patriotic Alliance have used immigration as a campaign issue.
"The party that might claim the most benefit from that sentiment … is Action SA, noted Murmur Intelligence co-founder Aldu Cornelissen.

"They would make a clear argument that we need to get rid of illegal immigrants. We need to improve immigration. We need to protect our borders, which are all legitimate concerns, right? So, if any of the parties could capitalize on this sentiment, it would be them."
"But for what percentage? I would wager between 6% and 8%, roughly," Cornelissen added.
Those margins may seem low, but in an increasingly fractured political landscape parties are fighting for every vote.

The Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) has said 136,760 candidates are contesting across the country, with 75 parties contesting in Johannesburg, 70 in Tshwane and 69 in eThekwini (Durban and surrounding areas).
4. Election misinformation

Fake news and false AI-generated content have become a feature in this election, with the IEC investigating over 700 complaints of disinformation. One of the prominent claims has been an accusation that the ANC plans to mobilize asylum seekers to vote for them.
Asylum seekers, refugees and permanent residents can't legally vote in South African elections regardless of how long they've been in the country.
South Africa election hit by disinformation surge

William Bird, director of media monitoring agency Moxii Africa, says misinformation and disinformation "are now kind of part and parcel of your standard build-up to any electoral environment, wherever you are in the world."

"What we see with disinformation is that it always picks up on whatever the hot button news issues are, as well as the standard kind of tropes about elections, he said, adding that there's always going to be "some bunch of clowns" saying the elections are rigged.

"And in South Africa's case, there's no evidence to support that at all. The IEC [Electoral Commission of South Africa] is one of the best electoral management bodies in the world. So of course, you then see people that are either wanting to destabilize, or they're wanting to just shake things up and make people scared or angry, and so they use those kinds of narratives. And that, unfortunately, is becoming an increasingly common trait," Bird told DW.
Bird added that social media platforms often "incentivize and deliberately encourage people" to attack others online.
5. Will people make it to the polls?

Local government election turnout has historically been lower than turnout in national elections. In 2016, turnout was at 57.95% and dropped to 45.87%. In 2024, in the most recent national elections, turnout was at 58.64%.
Naidu says this election will ultimately depend less on online discussions or campaign slogans and more on how many people make it to the polls.
Voters will mark two ballots — one for a direct local representative and a second for a political party under a proportional representation (PR) system.
Seats allocated through the PR vote account for half of all council seats, making them as important as the direct votes for councilors and this is where voter turnout becomes a key element.

"That is why political parties are saying to people, go out and vote, go out and vote, because if you don't go out and vote, it has an impact on the calculation of what you win as a PR vote in the council and the seats that you get," she said. In turn, this affects the make-up of each municipality and whether new coalition governments will form.
Could you still afford to live in Cape Town today?
Additional reporting by Ahmed Kajee and Sofia Christensen

articles.title: Justice department funds research into gender dysphoria and violent crime in latest anti-trans effort
articles.summary:
Experts say ‘very dangerous’ move diverts attention from violence driven by far-right extremist ideologies

The US Department of Justice is funding research aimed at…

blocks.text: The US Department of Justice is funding research aimed at exploring whether there is a link between gender dysphoria and violent crime.

Last month, the National Institute of Justice (NIJ), the research arm of the justice department, said it would grant up to $1m for studies into the frequency and type of violence committed by people who have been diagnosed and treated for gender dysphoria.

The notice comes as the Trump administration has aggressively sought to curtail the rights of transgender people in the US, limiting their access to healthcare and identification documents with their correct gender identity on them. It also comes more than a year after the administration has cut funding to research into hate-fueled and extremist violence.

The Trump administration has repeatedly sought to falsely portray transgender people as more likely to commit extremist violence, said Wendy Via, the co-founder and CEO of the Global Project Against Hate and Extremism (GPAHE). By doing this, the administration diverts attention from violence driven by far-right extremist ideologies such as the “great replacement” theory, which several high-profile shooters have cited in their manifestos, she added.
“What the administration is doing is very dangerous,” Via said.

Experts and LGBTQ+ advocates call these attempts to link trans people and violence “pseudoscience”, because they depart from a growing body of academic literature showing that it is impossible to link a single characteristic, such as race, political affiliation or gender, as the prime reason for violence. Instead, researchers say the most common thread between most high-profile attackers is not their identity, but their views, which often include racism, homophobia, misogyny and nihilism.
That has not stopped public speculation around the role gender identity plays in violence.

After conservative activist Charlie Kirk was shot and killed in September 2025, rightwing influencers argued that the suspected shooter was motivated in part by what they call “transgender ideology”, a term often used by those on the right to falsely suggest that being trans is a political ideology, not an identity.

The idea that being trans or that being an ally to trans people represents a dangerous political ideology was included in a White House counter-terrorism report this year. Part of its counter-terrorism approach is to address leftwing violence and “transgender ideologies”.

The vast majority of mass shootings in the US have been carried out by cisgender people, although transgender and non-binary people have committed some mass shootings, including ones at Annunciation Catholic school in Minneapolis, Club Q in Colorado Springs, and Tumbler Ridge elementary school in British Columbia in Canada. In these cases, transgender shooters shared characteristics of modern high-profile mass shooters, such as idolizing other killers and online radicalization.

“We don’t know exactly why a person decides to commit mass violence, because they’ve all had things in their lives that have led them to it,” Via said. “Being trans or being straight likely doesn’t have anything to do with it.”

The NIJ’s new funding priorities will shift attention away from the dangers posed by far-right extremists and toward trans people, said Zane McNeill, a staff attorney with Lawyers for Good Government.

“I see it as a part of this larger apparatus to distract from who’s propagating the violence,” McNeill said. “It’s also about weaponizing funding decisions. They’ve been undermining projects while diverting taxpayer dollars for far-right pseudoscience.”

The NIJ is not the only part of the government trying to find links between transgender people and violence. The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) recently published the report, Where the Clinic Meets the Movement: Does Gender Ideology Arm Left-Wing Authoritarian Psychology?

The report was commissioned by HHS and authored by researchers from Rutgers University, the Manhattan Institute and the Network Contagion Research Institute. It’s based on a survey of about 1,200 adults in the US and suggests that people who receive or support gender-affirming care are more likely to support political violence.

Last month, McNeill sent a letter to HHS requesting several corrections to the report, and argued that it violated the agency’s own guidelines. McNeill and other researchers are trying to obtain access to the survey data so they can offer their own analysis.
“This research is so flawed that it should not be published,” McNeill said. “It’s obvious that it’s extremely biased.”
The NIJ and the institutions affiliated with the HHS report did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.
In a statement to the Guardian, HHS press secretary Grace Davis Jamison said that the department’s report will help the government better understand how “political radicalization develops”.

“The findings should be evaluated based on the evidence, and under the Trump administration, HHS will not shy away from asking important questions to protect the health and safety of the American people,” she said.

articles.title: Libya's top religious authority rules against wearing Nike clothes
articles.summary: The US company was named after the Greek goddess of victory, so the Dar al-Ifta said displaying its logo was unIslamic.

blocks.text: Libya's highest religious authority, the Dar al-Ifta, has issued a ruling banning Muslims from buying, selling or wearing clothing bearing the Nike logo.
The ruling, issued by the Tripoli-based institution, states that the US sportswear giant was named after the Greek goddess of victory and that its famous swoosh logo was inspired by her wings.
It argued that wearing clothing displaying the logo amounted to promoting symbols associated "with polytheism," or the worship of more than one god.
Libya is home to the ancient Greek city of Cyrene, where archaeological remains include a statue of the Greek goddess of the same name.
The religious committee also accused Nike of supporting Israel and called for a boycott of companies that back the country.

It referred to a statement issued by its Council for Research and Sharia Studies on 5 November 2023, urging Muslims to boycott Western companies it considers supportive of Israel during the war in Gaza.
The ruling, known as a fatwa, is a religious opinion on a matter of Islamic law. It was approved by Libya's Grand Mufti, Sadiq al-Gharyani.
The BBC has contacted Nike for comment.

The Dar al-Ifta is an influential religious institution based in Tripoli, in western Libya. The country is politically divided, with rival authorities and institutions operating in the east and west after years of conflict following the toppling of long-time leader Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.
Although its religious rulings can carry considerable social influence, they are not necessarily government orders or legally enforceable.

Last year it ruled against wearing jewellery and watches bearing the logo of French luxury jewellery house Van Cleef & Arpels, arguing that its four-leaf clover design was associated with Christian beliefs and the pursuit of good luck, which it said contradicted Islamic teachings.
The latest fatwa does not announce a state ban on Nike products or specify penalties for people who continue to buy or wear them.
Social media reactions were mixed, with some users welcoming the ruling, while others questioned its significance, describing it as ironic or a distraction from more pressing issues.
The ruling comes amid wider debates over the rise of religious conservatism in public life in Libya.
In 2025, authorities in eastern Libya announced restrictions on rap music, theatre and dance performances, citing concerns that some lyrics and performances violated public morals and Islamic values.
The measures were subsequently extended to western Libya.
The Dar al-Ifta has also previously issued religious rulings against music, although there is no clear evidence that it was directly involved in the restrictions on performances.
Nike does not operate an official store in Libya, however Nike-branded products are available through local sportswear retailers.
Sportswear brands such as Nike and Adidas are popular across North Africa.
In Libya, as in other countries in the region, counterfeit versions of popular sportswear brands are also sold in local markets.

articles.title: ‘Well-known individual’ fails in bid for injunction against Guardian and ITN
articles.summary:
Person’s anonymity remains in place subject to any appeal against high court decision

A “well-known individual” has failed in his bid to stop two media organisations from publishing…

blocks.text: A “well-known individual” has failed in his bid to stop two media organisations from publishing allegations of inappropriate sexual activities, the high court has ruled.

The legal team for the anonymous individual, known in court only as PPT, claimed he was “highly likely” to attempt suicide if the allegations were published by the Guardian and ITN. PPT denies the allegations.

The claimant is seeking to block publication of the allegations by citing article two of the European convention on human rights, which relates to the right to life, article three, relating to “inhuman or degrading treatment”, and article eight, which protects the right to respect for private and family life.

Mr Justice Nicklin said: “A decision permitting publication, the anticipation of publication and publication itself would each materially and very substantially increase the claimant’s risk of suicide.”

However, he ruled that there were not conditions for the court to block publication of the allegations under those articles. He found that it fell to the state’s health services to protect the claimant from harm.
“In the present case, the state has assumed responsibility for the claimant’s immediate safety through the psychiatric hospital and mental health services,” his ruling states.

“The claimant is detained under the Mental Health Act 1983. The hospital exercises direct control over his care, observation, treatment, access to means of self-harm, leave and eventual discharge. It has assumed responsibility for the very risk with which article 2 is concerned.
“The evidence establishes that the hospital can provide significant protection. Inpatient treatment cannot eliminate the risk, but it materially reduces the likelihood of suicide.”
The anonymity of the claimant remains in place because the judge granted him permission to appeal against the ruling.

articles.title: What's behind new India-China border tensions?
articles.summary: Indian authorities have confirmed a new border "face-off" between Indian and Chinese troops in Arunachal Pradesh, raising questions about the still fragile thaw in relations between New Delhi and…

image.caption: The de facto border between India and China runs through a remote mountainous areaImage: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) Director General Shatrujeet Kapur sounded alarm bells across India by saying Indian and Chinese troops confronted each other at several locations along the de facto border in Arunachal Pradesh state, in India's northeast.
"In the past few days, a situation arose where a face-off happened (with Chinese troops) at various locations in Arunachal and it still continues," he told reporters last month.
"It may be difficult to counter China by conventional means because their PLA and BDR (Border Defense Regiment) have gone way ahead with investment and modernization," he warned.
The disputed Chinese-Indian border runs through a remote mountainous region.
Throughout the decades, clashes along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto border, have repeatedly triggered security crises between the world's two most populous nations.
The ties between Beijing and New Delhi are still affected by the deadly violence in 2020, when both countries accused each other of trying to seize territory.

In June that year, a clash in the Galwan River valley in eastern Ladakh killed 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese troops, according to Indian sources. China later confirmed four of its soldiers died.
Arunachal Pradesh leader Pema Khandu says situation normal

Kapur's remarks have brought renewed attention to the Himalayan frontier. Arunachal Pradesh Chief Minister Pema Khandu has also acknowledged border transgressions, while also saying such incidents were not new and the situation along the border was normal.
Khandu pointed out the border was not properly demarcated and that China did not recognize the McMahon Line, drawn by the British Empire in 1914, which separates Arunachal Pradesh from Tibet.
Tracking the tense relationship between India and China
It was also not clear if the latest confrontations between the Chinese and Indian troops involved physical violence.
China rejects wrongdoing

The opposition Congress party criticized Khandu's remarks, and accused the ruling BJP, led by India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi, of "rationalizing" Chinese actions instead of asserting India's position.

"On this there has been a deafening silence from the PM and his establishment," Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh said in a post on X, referring to the face-offs confirmed by the border police chief.
Meanwhile, External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal attributed the incidents to Chinese forces changing up their patrol routes.
"As we have noted in the past, the situation in the India-China border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns," he said.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun rejected the allegations, saying Chinese troops were conducting "normal patrols" and strictly abiding by bilateral agreements.
Why do face-offs keep happening?
The LAC largely separates Indian- and Chinese-controlled territory. However, as forces from both nations patrol territory they regard as their own, they sometimes venture into disputed areas.
"There is a very simple reason — because there is no agreed line between the two," Gautam Bambawale, a former Indian ambassador to China, told DW.

The de-facto border stretches for 3,488 kilometres (2,167 miles) according to India, but China claims it is shorter. The two countries have held 25 rounds of talks between their Special Representatives since 2003, but have yet to reach a boundary settlement.
Finding home in exile: Tibetans in India resist China
The dispute is particularly sensitive in Arunachal Pradesh, which China claims as part of southern Tibet.
China building a hydropower dam in Tibet
Aravind Yelery, a China expert at Jawaharlal Nehru University, says the region has become more strategically important to Beijing.
"Both sides patrol a contested LAC, so friction is built into the arrangement," Yelery told DW.

"What is new is China's intensified focus on the eastern sector. Since announcing the 60,000-megawatt Medog hydropower project in Tibet, Beijing has poured infrastructure, troops, engineers and machinery into the area."
South Asia projects boost China's presence in India's sphere

He describes the LAC as "not a thin line but a deep zone of overlapping claims where patrols inevitably meet." Face-offs will continue, he argues, until diplomacy produces concrete arrangements on the ground.
According to Yelery, the diplomatic pledges made by Indian and Chinese leaders will take time to implement.
"A wide gap separates the leaders' promises from the measures that would prevent a repeat of 2020, namely disengagement and mutual restraint," he added.
What is different about the latest developments?
For India, the immediate concern is whether the recent encounters reflect familiar patrol disputes or a more significant change in Chinese activity along the frontier.
Ashok Kantha, another former Indian ambassador to China, said Chinese transgressions in the eastern sector were not new, but that their location and extent mattered.
"If the Chinese have now made deeper intrusions on our side of the LAC, or established a presence in new areas, or expanded their existing presence, that would be a serious development," he added.
He also pointed to agreements signed by the two countries to maintain peace along the border.

"Any such transgression would be in complete violation of several border-related agreements India and China have signed (1993, 1996, 2005, 2012 and 2013). In these, both sides committed to respect and strictly observe the LAC, and not to alter the status quo."
The Indian government has not publicly provided details of the locations or circumstances of the latest face-offs, making it unclear whether they have changed the situation on the ground.
A fragile diplomatic thaw

The renewed encounters come as India and China try to stabilize relations and move past the 2020 clashes. Both Beijing and New Delhi made reconciliatory moves, including restoring some direct flights and easing restrictions on travel and economic exchanges.

The diplomatic reset gathered pace after Narendra Modi and Xi Jinping met at the BRICS summit in Kazan, Russia, in October 2024. They met again at the SCO summit in Tianjin in August 2025 and at the BRICS summit in New Delhi this year.
The boundary dispute, however, remains unresolved.
India builds tunnel in Himalayas to counter China threat
Alka Acharya, director of the Institute of Chinese Studies in New Delhi, cautions against drawing conclusions about the latest encounters without more information.
The government has described the incidents as face-offs, she says, but has not indicated that Chinese troops have taken control of Indian territory.

"The question is what is the nature of the so-called 'clashes' … not why the clashes are happening again? Any opinion on this latest kerfuffle would at best be conjecture without any definitive evidence," Acharya told DW.

She points out that border incidents have occurred regularly over the past decade and a half, despite political and diplomatic negotiations. The unresolved dispute, she says, will continue to sustain distrust and constrain the broader relationship.
Whether the latest encounters signal a more serious escalation will depend on details that New Delhi has yet to make public.

articles.title: Trump claims U.S. will halt $4B funding to Israel at end of 2026
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump said Tuesday he made a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that Washington would stop $4 billion US in funding to Israel after the end of this year.

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump shakes hands with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu after a meeting in Palm Beach, Fla., in this Dec. 29, 2025, file photo. Speaking to Fox News's Fox and Friends on Tuesday, Trump said he made a deal with Netanyahu that Washington would stop $4 billion US in fund

blocks.text: World·New
U.S. President Donald Trump said Tuesday he made a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that Washington would stop $4 billion US in funding to Israel after the end of this year.
No immediate comment from Netanyahu's office on U.S. president's remarks
U.S. President Donald Trump on Tuesday said he made a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that Washington would stop $4 billion US in funding to Israel after the end of this year.

Speaking to Fox News's Fox and Friends, Trump said Israel no longer needed the funding and that some Democrats and left-wing politicians were using the U.S. financial support to Israel as a talking point to criticize Republicans.
"Now, as far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping," Trump said.
"We've already agreed that by the end of this year, we won't be paying Israel. Now we'll help Israel if they need it."
There was no immediate comment from Netanyahu's office on Trump's remarks.

items: A new progressive wave is exposing the Democratic rift over Israel — just the way Republicans want it
Lack of big-name Democratic candidates at pro-Israel conference confirms for some voters the party has changed

blocks.text: It was not immediately clear which exact funding Trump was referring to. A memorandum of understanding that provides $3.8 billion annually in U.S. military aid to Israel is approaching its expiration date in 2028, and conversations have been under way on how Washington's assistance to Israel would evolve beyond that date.
"They can buy whatever they want. They can buy whatever they want. So can Europe. We make the greatest weapons in the world," Trump added in his comments Tuesday.

Netanyahu said in a May interview with CBS that he hoped to wean Israel off U.S. military support within a decade. In a June letter to a U.S. ​congressman, he wrote that the time had come for Israel "to move from aid recipient to partner."

U.S. public support for Israel has fallen since the Gaza war began in 2023, particularly among Democrats. A June Quinnipiac University poll found 48 per cent of voters and 66 per cent of Democrats believe the United States is too supportive of Israel, up from 16 per cent and 20 per cent when the question was first asked in 2017.

Support for Israel among Democratic voters has plummeted, candidates critical of Israel are winning Democratic primaries and even moderate lawmakers are increasingly willing to challenge decades of U.S. support for Israel.
"The left uses the $4-billion payment that everybody knows about — well, it's no secret — as a signal of unfairness, and we can't allow that to happen," Trump said.
"We were giving them $4 billion, we are. But it gets cut off at the end of the year," he said. "Why? Because they don't need it."

articles.title: How Berlin's Arab queers are building their community
articles.summary: As the co-founder of the ADIRA Drag Festival, Lebanese performance artist, drag performer, DJ and cultural organizer Hassandra has become an essential part of Berlin's queer artistic landscape.

image.caption: Hassandra performing at the ADIRA Drag FestivalImage: Gönna Ketels/DW

blocks.text: "Adira" is an Arabic slang term used in Levantine queer culture to describe someone with a strong presence — someone powerful and accomplished.

It is also the name of a Berlin-based collective that curates events and club nights celebrating the diversity of queer Arab* culture. The asterisk signals the inclusion of non-Arab ethnic minorities and people with diverse identities and roots in Southwest Asia and North Africa.
Among the collective's events is the ADIRA Drag Festival, which celebrated its third edition in Berlin in late October.

This year's theme, "Who's Your Diva?!," brought together drag performers paying tribute to legendary figures from across the Eastern Mediterranean who have become queer icons — from Egyptian music legend Umm Kulthum to Turkish star Bülent Ersoy and Lebanese pop icon Haifa Wehbe.
Hassandra, co-founder of ADIRA and the ADIRA Drag Festival, was among the performers, taking on the persona of Lebanese pop star Elissa.
Inspired by 'imperfect' divas

"It is very important for me to bring my Lebanese Arab identity and culture into what I do, because I think it's a very beautiful culture. And there's a lot of campy, glamorous, beautiful divas," Hassandra said.

Elissa's "whole discography is very romantic, raw, soft, kind of like very Adele vibes," Hassandra told DW ahead of the October 30 show. "However, her personality is known to be the extreme opposite. She's very feisty. Very blunt, very unfiltered. Not soft at all as a person." The star is also known for speaking out on political issues in Lebanon. She has publicly voiced support for LGBTQ+ communities in the Middle East, while also frequently sparking controversy across the Arab world with her outspoken positions on other political issues.
Hassandra's ADIRA Drag Festival performance addresses this complexity, ultimately "tapping into her sort of controversial political opinions," the drag artist explained.

This reflects one of the ideas Hassandra hopes to promote with the theme of this year's festival. "As queer people, we tend to idealize a lot of pop divas. But these pop divas are very imperfect in their nature," Hassandra said. The show provides an opportunity to critically revisit these divas' legacy through a more critical lens. "And this sort of critical lens can be taken into the outside world, as in: never follow anyone in life blindly. No one should follow any politician, any political party, any pop diva, any activist blindly."

blocks.caption: Hassandra out of drag: They are also a DJ and cultural organizerImage: Gönna Ketels/DW

blocks.text: Building community through drag

Born in Beirut in 1994, Hassandra studied theater and stage acting at the Lebanese University before moving to Berlin in 2017. "I would say it was it was just a very sort of impulsive decision at the age of 22. I mean, there's no doubt that the economic situation was really bad in Lebanon and continued to become even worse," the artist said.
In Berlin, Hassandra became increasingly involved in the city's independent art scene and queer nightlife. Drag emerged as another form of self-expression for the actor.
Through performances that combine theatrical intensity, political humor, grotesque aesthetics and moments of tenderness, Hassandra challenges conventional understandings of gender and identity.

Their work explores themes of home, nostalgia, displacement and queer Arab culture. These ideas are also central to ADIRA, which Hassandra founded in 2023 with Syrian-German DJ and cultural producer Zuher Jazmati, also known as xanax_attax.
Through panel discussions, performances and music events, ADIRA fosters collective participation and community-building.
As Islamophobia and homophobia rise alongside the far right, spaces like ADIRA offer a sense of belonging and support for Arab queer communities.
That sense of community has become even more important following the deadly Islamist terrorist attack during Berlin's Christopher Street Day pride parade in July.
What does the Berlin Pride attack mean for city's identity?
In the aftermath, Hassandra felt caught between their different identities. As an Arab queer person, "you fall in this position where then you start receiving a lot of racism," they said.

"And I think this is why it's important, for us queer Arabs, to say we are sad over what happened, but that we also reject any of the racism that comes from that," Hassandra said. "I think we [the Arab community] are being used in a lot of ways as a punching bag for a lot of things that are happening."
Rather than allowing the attack to fuel hatred and racism, Hassandra said, "we should make Germany a safer place for everyone to live in."
"There's place for everyone. It's a huge country," they added.
The interview with Hassandra was conducted by Gönna Ketels.

George Madgwick of Hampshire county council has been charged with a total of 35 offences

A Reform UK councillor has been charged with 12 counts of rape, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS)…

blocks.text: A Reform UK councillor has been charged with 12 counts of rape, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) has said.

George Madgwick, the leader of the party on Hampshire county council, has been charged with a total of 35 offences, including two counts of sexual assault, two counts of assault by penetration, two counts of making and one count of distributing indecent images of a child.
The 37-year-old will appear at Portsmouth magistrates court on 25 November. A Reform spokesperson said he had been suspended from the party with immediate effect.

A CPS spokesperson said: “The Crown Prosecution Service has decided to prosecute George Madgwick for serious sexual offences, including multiple counts of rape. He has also been charged with making a threat to kill, false imprisonment and stalking.

“Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence and that it is in the public interest to bring the case to court. We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are now active and that he has the right to a fair trial. There should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information which could in any way prejudice these proceedings.”
Hampshire police said they launched their investigation on 24 July last year after receiving a report of a sexual offence. Officers then arrested a man in Wandsworth, south-west London, on 6 January.
The force said the allegations related to four victims, who were aged 16 and 17 at the time and are alleged to have taken place between 2008 and 2021 in Portsmouth and Wales.

articles.title: True crime novel about 1949 murder of Paris life model wins France’s biggest literary prize
articles.summary:
Philippe Jaenada wins Prix Goncourt with novel that seeks to solve 77-year-old case and rehabilitates reputation of its victim

A literary true-crime investigation that tries to solve a…

blocks.text: A literary true-crime investigation that tries to solve a 77-year-old cold case and ends up rehabilitating the reputation of its life model victim has won France’s most prestigious literary prize.

The author Philippe Jaenada was announced on Tuesday afternoon as the winner of the Prix Goncourt, for his book L’Inconnue du quai de Javel (The Unknown Woman of the Quai de Javel), a recreation of the murder of a 29-year-old Breton woman named Louise Cansot.

Known as “the woman with a hundred portraits” because she was so sought-after as a model for artists in Montparnasse, Cansot was found dead on 7 September 1949, but police never managed to establish the identity of her murderer.

blocks.caption: Philippe Jaenada. Photograph: Isa Harsin/SIPA/Shutterstock

blocks.text: This year’s edition of the Prix Goncourt has been overshadowed by the allegation that one of the other longlisted books, the Canadian-Haitian author Thélyson Orélien’s C’était ça ou mourir (It Was That or Die), was “almost entirely” written by artificial intelligence.

The Académie Goncourt, a Paris-based literary organisation, withdrew Orélien’s book from its longlist, and his Canadian publisher Boréal severed ties with the writer after an investigation. Orélien has denied using AI to write his novel.
Having been previously shortlisted for the Goncourt four times, Jaenada has finally triumphed with the 13th novel of his career.

The writer, born in Île-de-France, has made investigations into old news stories his trademark style since 2013’s Sulak, the story of a notorious and charismatic robber and escape artist who targeted jewellery stores in the 1980s.

blocks.caption: L’Inconnue du quai de Javel by Philippe Jaenada. Photograph: Syspeo/SIPA/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The subject of L’Inconnue du quai de Javel, Louise Cansot, left Brittany at 16 to work as a maid but then started to sit as a life model for painter Jean-Louis Boussingault, who introduced her to other Parisian painters and sculptors.
The original 300-page police report into Cansot’s murder concluded that she was a woman of “ill repute”, and newspaper reports at the time speculated that she was a sex worker or drug addict.

Jaenada’s 530-page book goes to some length to right the wrongs of the original investigation, not just by suggesting the name of the murderer, but also in its empathetic portrayal of the victim. “He spares no effort in trying to understand his heroine,” wrote the newspaper Le Monde, while also praising the book’s humour and “touch of grumpy tenderness”.

The author drew inspiration for his book by reading and re-reading 74 out of the 75 novels in George Simenon’s Inspector Maigret series, about the chief inspector of a criminal brigade in 1940s Paris.

articles.title: UK meat processing firms’ fridges heat up after cyber-attacks in Europe
articles.summary:
Cybersecurity experts say incidents had minimal effect but may represent the ‘foothills’ of a wider threat

Meat processing firms in the UK have been hit by cyber-attacks after hackers raised…

blocks.text: Meat suppliers in the UK have been hit by cyber-attacks after hackers raised the temperatures of supermarket freezers across Europe.
The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) said it was working with the affected companies but that the national impact was minimal.

Speaking at the launch of the NCSC annual review on Tuesday, the centre’s director of operations, Paul Chichester, said: “We’re aware of those incidents in the UK, and obviously we’re working with the affected organisations. We’ll keep monitoring that.
“At the moment, the impact is minimal.”

Cybersecurity experts meanwhile reported that attacks on “dummy” fridge controls – deliberately placed online to lure would-be hackers – displayed characteristics similar to previous malicious operations linked to Russia.

Retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems on Monday – with some rising to as high as 50C (122F) – and several companies confirmed they had been hacked. It follows similar incidents in France last month. It has emerged that the cyber-attack on French supermarket fridges involved legacy technology connected to internet with default passwords.
No UK grocery chain has been directly affected so far.
Chichester said the NCSC, part of the GCHQ spy agency, was working with organisations to identify similar loopholes in their technology and close them before hackers exploit them.
He said the NCSC was not able to comment on who might have carried out the attacks, but that they were not AI-enabled and had used vulnerabilities that had been “out there for a long period of time”.
after newsletter promotion

The NCSC’s chief executive, Richard Horne, said the fridge attacks represented the “foothills” of an enlarged cyberthreat that companies and the public face as AI systems highlight flaws in IT networks that owners were not aware of or neglected to patch.
“There are so many vulnerabilities out there that … you could say are waiting to be exploited,” he said.

The agency’s chief technology officer, Ollie Whitehouse, said everyday domestic devices connected to the internet would be susceptible to hackers in certain situations. He said manufacturers needed to be encouraged to make their technology safer, and consumers needed to accept paying more for safer equipment.

The British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (Aims) told the BBC some of its more than 300 members had been affected, with one company’s cold units heating to up to 100C and another two reporting their units had started to defrost. Aims said the affected units were empty at the time and no produce was lost.
Cybersecurity researchers said attacks on dummy Danfoss fridge controls – which were targeted by the hackers in mainland Europe – were similar to recent operations linked to Russia.

Xavier Bellekens, the chief executive of the cyberdefence firm Lupovis, said it had recorded 256 attempted attacks from 91 different sources between 20 October and 30 October after setting up online “honeypot” traps that are indistinguishable to attackers from real Danfoss fridge controllers.

The attackers attempting to gain control of the dummy controls remained anonymous, but most of the authentication attempts used the manufacturer’s publicly documented factory-default username and password credentials.

They also used what Bellekens called “bulletproof” hosting, which means using internet service providers that are particularly tolerant of malicious activity, often ignore abuse complaints or make it difficult for authorities to disrupt their customers’ operations.

“What caught our attention was the overlap between infrastructure involved in the recent probing activity and infrastructure we have previously associated with Russian-linked malicious operations,” he said.

“While we are not able to pinpoint a group yet, the number of actors that fit this bill is relatively small and the bulletproof hosting we have seen being used by these actors for probing was also being used by Russian groups some time ago.”

articles.title: Cyprus: From ties with Russia to a strategic alignment with the US
articles.summary: The Republic of Cyprus long balanced ties between Russia and the West. Now, it is phasing out Russian weapons, expanding defense cooperation with the United States and redefining its place in the…

image.caption: US Ambassador to Cyprus John Breslow said in October that 'the United States will protect Cyprus in the future'Image: Brandon Williams-Church/Planet Pix/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: In an interview with the Cyprus News Agency on October 4, the new US ambassador to Cyprus, John Breslow, outlined plans to upgrade the Andreas Papandreou Air Base in Paphos to accommodate large US military transport aircraft.
He also announced plans for more frequent visits by US warships to Cypriot ports and an expansion of joint military activities.
But one statement carried particular political weight: his assurance that "the United States will protect Cyprus in the future."
Although the remark does not constitute a formal US security guarantee, it reflects the growing cooperation between the two countries.

For a country that for decades maintained close ties with Moscow, viewed US foreign policy with suspicion and is not a member of NATO, the prospect of an expanded American military presence marks a significant geopolitical shift.

blocks.caption: The ambassador also announced plans for more frequent visits by US warships to Cypriot ports. Pictured here: US amphibious assault ship USS Wasp docked at the port in Limassol in 2024Image: Iakovos Hatzistavrou/AFP

blocks.text: It is perhaps the clearest indication yet of Cyprus's gradual loosening of ties with Russia and its increasingly close strategic alignment with the United States.
The nonalignment years
The shift is particularly striking given Cyprus's political history.
In the years after it gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1960, the Republic of Cyprus sought to balance its relations between East and West.

Under the leadership of Archbishop Makarios III, the first president of independent Cyprus, the country became a founding member in 1961 of the Non-Aligned Movement, a forum of nations that did not align with either of the two superpowers of the day: the United States and the Soviet Union.

blocks.caption: Under the leadership of Archbishop Makarios III (left), Cyprus became a founding member of the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961Image: Nicholas Tsikourias/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: This approach allowed Nicosia to maintain close ties with the Soviet Union without severing its connections to the West.
EU membership
Even after joining the European Union in 2004, Cyprus maintained strong political, economic and military ties with Moscow.
Relations with the United States, by contrast, remained overshadowed by the Turkish invasion of the island in 1974 and the US's failure to take decisive action against Ankara.
The United States prioritized maintaining its strategic relationship with Turkey, a key NATO ally, over taking a tougher stance against the invasion.

The US position fueled widespread anti-American sentiment in Cyprus, culminating in a violent demonstration outside the embassy in Nicosia on August 19, 1974, during which US Ambassador Roger Davies was shot dead.

Mistrust deepened further in 1987, when the United States imposed an arms embargo on the Republic of Cyprus, officially intended to prevent an arms race on the island and avoid undermining efforts to resolve the Cyprus conflict.
Close relations with Moscow

The US arms embargo contributed to the reliance of the Cypriot National Guard (the armed forces of the Republic of Cyprus) on Russia-made weapons systems, strengthening the Kremlin's position as a major military partner.
The response by Cyprus to Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014 illustrated the strength of these ties.

The Cypriot government expressed serious reservations about imposing tougher EU sanctions on Russia. Then-Foreign Minister Ioannis Kasoulides warned that such measures could have devastating consequences for the Cypriot economy.

blocks.caption: Even after joining the EU in 2004, Cyprus maintained close ties with Moscow. Pictured here: Nicos Anastasiades (left), president of the Republic of Cyprus, and Russian President Vladimir Putin after signing agreements in Russia in 2015Image: Nikita Shvetsov/Anadolu/IMAGO

blocks.text: Relations with Moscow deepened further in February 2015, when President Nicos Anastasiades visited the Russian capital and signed a series of agreements with President Vladimir Putin.

These included a naval cooperation memorandum facilitating visits by Russian warships to Cypriot ports. Moscow also agreed to more favorable repayment terms for its €2.5 billion loan to Cyprus in 2011.

Cooperation remained close as recently as October 2021, when then Foreign Minister and current President Nikos Christodoulides signed a Strategic Cooperation Framework for 2022–2024 in Moscow alongside his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov.
Turning point in 2022
The decisive turning point came just four months later, in February 2022, with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Konstantinos Adamides, an associate professor of international relations at the University of Nicosia, told DW that the invasion accelerated a geopolitical shift toward the West that had already begun.
"For the first time, the Republic of Cyprus openly and unequivocally chose to side with the West, despite the economic and political costs of breaking with Moscow," Adamides said.
Nicosia aligned itself with EU sanctions against Russia, despite the Cypriot economy's strong links to Moscow, particularly in services, investment and tourism.
The decision marked a significant departure from Cyprus's traditional foreign policy approach of maintaining a balance between Russia and the West.
Adamides said the government's position on Russia paved the way for closer relations with the United States, particularly in the field of security.

blocks.caption: Cyprus is seeking to gradually reduce its dependence on Russian military equipment. Pictured here: Russian-made T-80 tanks in a 2021 military parade in Nicosia Image: Philippos Christou/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Cyprus, he said, succeeded in convincing Washington that it could serve as a reliable partner in the Eastern Mediterranean.
What form does the rapprochement take?
The rapprochement had already gained an institutional foundation before the war, with a bilateral statement of intent on security cooperation signed in 2018.

Further initiatives followed, including the Cyprus Center for Land, Open-seas and Port Security (CYCLOPS), a US-funded training facility inaugurated in Larnaca in April 2022. The center provides training for security personnel from Cyprus and other countries in the region in areas such as port security, counterterrorism and preventing the trafficking of hazardous materials.
An even more significant development for the Cypriot National Guard came in September 2022, when Washington announced the full suspension of the arms embargo imposed in 1987.

The decision allowed for the export of lethal military equipment to Cyprus, subject to the necessary US approvals. The suspension, which was not permanent and remains subject to periodic renewal, has been renewed until September 30, 2027.
Cyprus and NATO
The strategic security reorientation is also significant because Cyprus is not a member of NATO.
The crash landing of an Iranian done on the British military base at Akrotiri in March reignited a debate in Cyprus about whether the country should join NATO.

blocks.caption: Earlier this year President Nikos Christodoulides said that Cyprus would apply to join NATO 'even tomorrow if it were possible'Image: Nicolas Tucat/AFP

blocks.text: At the time, Christodoulides said Cyprus was preparing for potential membership at the military, operational and administrative level and would apply to join NATO "even tomorrow if it were possible."
Christodoulides said, however, that joining the alliance was not possible because "the political conditions are not there, taking into account the well-known position of Turkey."
Phasing out Russian weapons
The country's changing strategic orientation is also reflected in the modernization of its armed forces.
After decades of relying heavily on Russian military equipment, Cyprus is seeking to gradually reduce its dependence on Russian-made T-80 tanks and Tor-M1 and Buk air defense systems.
The process accelerated following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, as sanctions against Moscow made it increasingly difficult to secure spare parts and ammunition for Russian weapons systems.

Another important step came in January 2025, when then President Joe Biden authorized Cyprus to participate in US defense procurement programs, including Foreign Military Sales (FMS) and Excess Defense Articles (EDA).
The decision gave Nicosia access to additional mechanisms for acquiring US military equipment, further strengthening defense cooperation between Cyprus and the United States.

articles.title: What US midterm elections mean for Ukraine, Iran and elsewhere
articles.summary: Donald Trump's Republicans control the US Congress, but that could change after the midterm elections. The outcome of the ballot will not only impact domestic policy but also conflicts in Europe and…

image.caption: The US midterms might not select a new president but they will affect US policy both at home and abroadImage: Jacquelyn Martin/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The outcome of the midterm elections will shape US policy for years — and have repercussions around the globe. Decisions made in Washington affect both US adversaries such as Iran and countries such as Ukraine, which is seeking more support from the United States.

President Donald Trump does not have the final say when it comes to deciding where the United States goes to war or which countries get financial or military aid. While the president wields more power in the US than in parliamentary democracies such as Germany, he does not govern alone — even in the land of opportunity.

The House of Representatives and the Senate, the two chambers of Congress whose composition voters will decide this Tuesday, wield considerable influence. They decide on legislation and government spending and also serve as a check on the president and the intelligence agencies.

The president can veto legislation passed by Congress. Congress can override that veto with a two-thirds majority in both chambers. The legislature also handles impeachment proceedings. In addition, the president can only appoint Cabinet members, US ambassadors and federal judges from a list of nominees the Senate approves.

Trump’s Republicans currently hold majorities in both chambers of Congress, making it easier for the president to govern. But recent polls suggest the Democrats could take control of at least the House of Representatives and possibly even the Senate. This could shift the direction of major foreign policy issues.
Battle for US midterm elections heats up
Support for Ukraine

Joe Biden, a Democrat, was in the White House when Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine. Alongside Europe, the US stood out as a reliable partner, supporting Ukraine with financial aid, military expertise and, above all, large-scale weapons deliveries.

The situation changed abruptly under Trump. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy famously received a notably frosty welcome during his 2025 visit to the White House. Trump now openly admits that he gets along better with Russian President Vladimir Putin than with Zelenskyy.

The US has suspended sanctions against Russia and reduced financial and military aid to Ukraine. If Democrats win majorities in both chambers of Congress, they could put increased support for Ukraine on the agenda.

"Democrats criticize the Trump administration for not doing enough for Ukraine," Brandon Conradis, a former DW journalist and now an editor at Bloomberg Government, told DW. "They can push legislation that would provide more aid to Ukraine."
If Trump vetoed such legislation, the outcome would depend on the balance of power in Congress. But a two-thirds majority could override his veto with support from some Republicans.
Is Trump trying to end the war in Ukraine, or helping Putin win it?
Iran War

Trump launched the war against Iran alongside Israel on February 28 without consulting Congress. Under the US Constitution, Congress must approve a formal declaration of war against another country. Democrats have repeatedly voted against the war and even passed a resolution, together with some Republicans, calling for an end to the hostilities. The Trump administration has ignored it.

"I don't think Congress will have huge powers here," said Michael O'Hanlon, director of research for foreign policy at the US think tank Brookings Institution, told DW, but added that Congress could perhaps prevent a major escalation by refusing to fund it.
How USAID cuts could result in higher HIV transmission
How the midterms could impact development aid

US support for aid projects around the world that help fight Ebola, AIDS and hunger was sharply cut back by President Trump shortly after he began his second term. Among other measures, he shut down USAID, the US agency responsible for foreign development assistance.

Whether a Democratic-controlled Congress could "reactivate" the agency against the president's wishes is questionable. But Congress could push for increased aid spending and investigate the controversial closure of USAID.

"Democrats would have oversight power and use it to scrutinize the closing of USAID," Conradis said. "There will be hearings, and they will drag officials they view as responsible in front of Congress."

Ultimately, the US remains a country with a Republican president. There will be no complete reversal of course. "It's not like if Democrats win control of Congress, everything is going to change. But some things will change because the power dynamics will be different."
This article was originally published in German.
