articles.title: Four planes flying across Europe targeted by bomb threats
articles.summary: Flights from London, Manchester, Copenhagen and Israel affected but no explosives found after touchdown

blocks.text: Four planes have landed safely after bomb threats were made across Europe, including for two flights that departed from the UK, according to reports.
Polish officials said they received bomb threats on Tuesday involving two Warsaw-bound flights, but the planes landed safely and no explosives were found.
The bomb warnings targeted a Scandinavian Airlines flight from Copenhagen and a plane from London Heathrow operated by the Polish airline LOT.

Elsewhere, the BBC reported that a Ryanair plane from Manchester made an emergency landing at Murcia in southern Spain after another threat and a fourth flight from Israel was forced to land in Sofia, Bulgaria.
Francisco Lucas, the Spanish government’s delegate in the region, said on X that no explosives were found on the flight that landed in Murcia.
The separate incidents came the day after a Wizz Air service from London Luton made an emergency landing in Budapest, escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet.
The plane, which was due to depart from Luton at 8.15am on Monday for Sofia, was diverted after a bomb threat was received “during the flight”, Wizz Air said.

blocks.caption: A Wizz Air plane in Budapest on Monday night after being diverted because of a bomb threat on its way from London Luton to Sofia.  Photograph: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The Scandinavian Airlines plane landed at Warsaw’s Chopin airport, where it had a security inspection that did not turn up any explosive devices.
The airport closed a landing strip but was able to continue operating, a spokesperson said.

The LOT flight, which had also been scheduled to arrive at Chopin, was diverted to the Polish capital’s other airport, Modlin. Authorities closed that airport after the alert and the Boeing 737 MAX landed without incident.
“The passengers were evacuated and the plane underwent security checks. Nothing was found,” spokesperson Adam Szablowski told AFP. “The airport has been reopened and is operating normally.”

articles.title: Multiple flights to European airports targeted by bomb threats
articles.summary: The bomb threats involved two passenger planes bound for Warsaw, a Ryanair flight from London to Spain, and a fourth flight traveling from Israel to the Bulgarian capital, Sofia. No explosives were…

image.caption: One of the targeted flights from Copenhagen landed at Warsaw's Chopin airport to undergo checks [FILE: Jul 24, 2026]Image: Marek Antoni Iwanczuk/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Polish authorities said they carried out inspections of two passenger planes targeted by bomb threats on Tuesday but did not find any explosives, in a string of bomb threats that hit several European airports.
A bomb alert forced a LOT flight from London's Heathrow to make an unscheduled landing at Warsaw-Modlin airport, prompting the airport to shut down. Operations resumed around midday.

"The passengers were evacuated and the plane underwent security checks. Nothing was found," airport spokesman Adam Szablowski told the French AFP news agency. "The airport has been reopened and is operating normally."
A SAS Scandinavian Airlines flight from Copenhagen also received a bomb threat before landing safely at Warsaw's central Chopin airport, where it underwent a security inspection.
No explosives were found on either plane. It was not immediately clear whether the threats were linked.
Flights bound for Spain, Bulgaria also targeted
Also on Tuesday, a Ryanair flight from Manchester, UK, to Murcia, Spain, was hit by a bomb threat. It landed safely and underwent checks after all the passengers had disembarked.
The Spanish government's delegate in the region of Murcia, Francisco Lucas, confirmed on X that police "ruled out the presence of explosives on the plane."
"The International Airport of the Region of Murcia resumes its activity normally. Thanks to the emergency teams that have participated in the operation," he said.

And in the fourth such incident, the Reuters news agency reported that another flight traveling from Israel landed in the Bulgarian capital, Sofia, on Tuesday after a bomb threat was received via email. Counter-terrorism units were checking the plane for possible explosive devices, ​BTA news agency ⁠quoted Interior Minister Secretary General Lyubomir Nikolov as saying.

Later, two more bomb threats also targeted Ryanair flights from Lisbon and Dublin to Rome’s Fiumicino airport, according to Italian media. Air Force jets were deployed as a result. Both threats turned out to be false alarms.
The six threats on Tuesday come after a WizzAir flight from London to Sofia was redirected to the Hungarian capital, Budapest, on Monday after it received a bomb threat mid-air.
Similar such incidents have been reported across different European airports in recent weeks, with alerts later turning out to be false.

articles.title: Yemen: Houthi clashes near Taiz leave residents in a 'state of panic'
articles.summary: Fighting between Iran-backed Houthi rebels and Yemeni government forces has intensified around the city of Taiz. Residents face growing shortages of food, water and medical supplies as thousands flee…

image.caption: Shifting frontlines in Yemen's war are currently concentrated in Taiz governorate, where the Houthis have laid siege to the strategic city Image: Marzouq Al Jabri/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Four months into the fighting in Yemen between the Iran-backed Houthi movement and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, clashes are concentrated around Taiz in the country's southwest. Yemeni authorities have warned civilians of sniper fire from surrounding hillsides. Houthi forces have also largely blocked the delivery of goods to Taiz, which is under the control of government forces.

Taiz is Yemen's third-largest city, with a population of around 1 million people. However, fighting has displaced around 134,000 people in the Taiz governorate region, accordingto the International Organization for Migration. The governorate accounts for almost half of the more than 319,000 people displaced across western Yemen, the organization said on November 1, 2026.

"The Houthis have blocked fuel, water and medical supplies, basically all things required for hospitals to function properly," Niku Jafarnia, Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch, told DW. "Even those who can reach hospitals may not be receiving the care they need," she said, adding that it has had a devastating impact on people's health, particularly those with chronic illnesses.

blocks.caption: As the Houthis have blocked fuel, water and medical supplies into Taiz, even patients who reach a hospital, don't receive the care they need, HRW warnsImage: Anees Mahyoub/REUTERS

blocks.text: Taiz residents scared but steadfast
Ammar, a 45-year-old photographer in Taiz, told DW on Monday that he sees people in a "state of panic" and yet he feels that "the determination not to submit to the Houthis is very strong."

Afnan, the mother of a schoolchild in Taiz, told DW that "neighbors share the little food they have and help each other and many people in Taiz refuse to flee." She and the other residents who spoke to DW asked that their full names not be published, fearing reprisals.

Hanan, a 30-year-old mother of three, said that prices have skyrocketed while there is almost no petrol, cooking gas or drinking water left in the city. "This increases the mental load on people who are already scared by hearing the clashes of the fighting day and night," she said. Despite this, she numbers among those who have decided to stay.

Meanwhile, Nabil Shamsan, the governor of Taiz, told DW that negotiations are underway to bring food, fuel and water back to the city. While it remains to be seen when and under what conditions this might happen, international aid organizations remain extremely concerned.

"Fighting and insecurity around Taiz is making it unsafe for civilians to move freely and also for our staff to deliver aid," said Alison Bottomley, an advocacy adviser with the Norwegian Refugee Council in Yemen. "This is preventing us from reaching the 7,000 people we are supporting with emergency tents, blankets and educational activities for displaced children," she told DW, calling on both factions to allow "civilians and humanitarian workers to move safely."
Why is Taiz under siege again?

During the previous Yemen conflict, which began in 2014 and largely ended with a UN-brokered truce in 2022, Ansar Allah, the formal name of the Houthi group, had already laid siege to Taiz in 2015 and 2016. That siege brought the population close to famine and caused a humanitarian crisis, but the Houthis never captured the city.

In turn, Taiz, as a bastion of resistance, represents something the Houthis have struggled to subdue for more than a decade, Hisham Al-Omeisy, a senior Yemeni adviser with UK-based advisory firm Coral Core Consultants, told DW. "The city symbolizes a deeply rooted tradition of political pluralism, civic resistance and rejection of the Houthi model of rule," he said, adding that the city's continued resistance is both a military obstacle and a political challenge to the Houthis' claim that their authority across Yemen is inevitable.

blocks.caption: The Houthis have laid siege to Taiz before in 2015 and 2016 but never gained control over the strategically important city that connects the country's north and southImage: Anees Mahyoub/REUTERS

blocks.text: Following the truce in 2022, the Houthis controlled the capital Sanaa, most of northern Yemen and parts of the center, while the internationally recognized government controlled much of the west and the south including the city of Aden. However, fighting reignited in late July and the clashes intensified in September, as the Houthis seized territory from forces loyal to the internationally recognized government.

Control of the strategically important Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, is contested. The precise territorial situation remains unclear, while the Houthis retain the capacity to threaten maritime traffic. The conflict continues to escalate, alongside an exchange of missile and drone attacks between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia.

Data on the number of people injured or killed in Yemen varies because of the ongoing fighting and separate statistics given by the Houthi movement and the government's health authorities. According to the latest WHO Health Cluster situation report, at least 1,677 people had been killed and 7,395 injured as of October 25, 2026.

blocks.caption: The majority of people in Taiz decided to stay despite the Houthi siege, shelling and clashes around the clockImage: Anees Mahyoub/REUTERS

blocks.text: A key battleground in Yemen's war

Meanwhile, seizing Taiz is highlighted as a key strategic step by analysts. "Taiz would give the Houthis a major advantage in consolidating their hold over northern Yemen while opening the way for further expansion toward the south and the Red Sea coast," Al-Omeisy said, adding that controlling Taiz would give them stronger cards in any future negotiations.
"Taiz is far more than simply another military front for the Houthis," he noted.

"However, the Houthis may not actually need to capture Taiz to achieve many of their objectives," Hisham Al-Omeisy said. "If they can isolate the city, sever its remaining supply lines and neutralize it as a military threat, they could consolidate their positions along the western coast while tying down significant government forces," he added.

"My greater concern is that the Houthis could use gains around Taiz to progressively weaken and fragment the anti-Houthi camp, rather than immediately launch a full-scale offensive against Aden," Al-Omeisy told DW, adding that the Houthis have repeatedly demonstrated an ability to exploit divisions among their opponents, and those divisions remain one of the government's greatest vulnerabilities.

articles.title: US supreme court to hear arguments in Catholic preschools’ LGBTQ+ exclusion case
articles.summary:
A decision could reshape the relationship between religious freedom and nondiscrimination laws in the US

The US supreme court will hear arguments on Tuesday over a challenge brought by two…

blocks.text: The US supreme court will hear arguments on Tuesday over a challenge brought by two Catholic preschools in Colorado, arguing that they should be admitted to the state’s free education system despite their rejection of children with LGBTQ+ parents.
A decision in the case, St Mary Catholic Parish v Roy, could reshape the relationship between religious freedom and nondiscrimination laws in the US.

The Catholic preschools claim that they been shut out of a 2023 state funding program that provides 15 hours per week of state-funded preschool and want the same benefits extended to them. Colorado says that the schools “remain welcome to participate in” the program but only if they agree to the same equal-opportunity requirements that apply to all other publicly funded preschools–public and private, secular and religious”.

But to join the program, Colorado says, the schools must consent to “provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability”.
The plaintiffs argue that making funding contingent on accepting that agreement amounts to unlawful religious discrimination under the first amendment guaranteeing religious freedoms.

The case – in essence a clash between religious freedom and non-discrimination laws – has been making its way up the court system. A lower appeals court ruled for the state but acknowledged that the highest court has previously held that states “cannot categorically withhold those funds from religious institutions”.

In the lower court’s view, the rulings do not apply to the current case because Colorado “did not exclude” religious preschools from its funding program and had “welcomed and actively solicited their participation”.

The archdiocese claims that the state allows participating preschools “to discriminate in favor of LGBTQ families and other groups”, such as “gender-nonconforming children”, “children of color”, or members of “the LGBTQ community”.

Nicholas Reaves, counsel at the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, a firm that litigates religious liberty cases, told the National Catholic Reporter that Colorado had “denied families … the ability to use that funding at Catholic preschools, simply because those preschools have religious beliefs the state doesn’t like”.
In an amicus brief submitted to the court, the US Conference of Catholic Bishops argues that Colorado had disqualified the preschools “solely because of their adherence to Catholic doctrine”.

The lower court’s decision, the conference said, “will embolden other states and municipalities to discriminate against religious adherents’ rights by enacting ostensibly neutral statutes that discriminate in fact”.
If allowed to stand, it added, “the resulting harm to the nation’s social support infrastructure would be immense.”

A day after climbing to a career-high world No. 17 ranking, Alex Eala holds off replacement foe Emerson Jones of Australia to kick off her Hong Kong Open campaign
MANILA, Philippines – Alex Eala kicked off her Prudential Hong Kong Tennis Open campaign on a high.
Apart from entering the tournament at a career-high world No. 17 in the latest WTA rankings, the Filipina tennis star also cruised past Australia’s Emerson Jones, 6-4, 6-3, on Tuesday, November 3.
Eala rose to world No. 17 just a few months after her previous career-high ranking of No. 18 in August.

The 21-year-old Filipina, the second seed in the WTA 250 tournament, was originally supposed to go head to head with Alycia Parks. The American player, however, was forced to withdraw from the competition at the last minute due to a shoulder injury.
“It was a really good match. Emerson is such a sweetheart off the court and such a great player on the court, so I’m looking forward to many more matches together,” Eala said of world No. 132 Jones.
She will face Czechia’s Tereza Valentová on Thursday, November 5, in the round of 16.
The Hong Kong Open is Eala’s last tournament for the year.
Eala will then mark her homecoming with “Alex Eala Live: Game. Set. Celebrate” on December 8 at the Philippine Arena in Bulacan, where she is set to face Indonesia’s Janice Tjen. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Public service union refuses to back Labor at Victorian election, condemning job cuts and $1.2bn consultant spend
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Community and Public Sector Union denounces ‘privatisation by stealth’, joining growing number of unions turning on Carroll government

  • Get our

blocks.text: Victoria’s public servants union says it will not support Labor at this month’s state election, condemning the government for cutting public service jobs while spending $1.2bn on consultants.

The Community and Public Sector Union (CPSU) will announce the decision on Wednesday, joining several other unions that have refused to back Labor or are actively campaigning against the government ahead of the 28 November poll.

Although the CPSU’s Victorian branch is not formally affiliated with Labor, it has worked closely with the party in the past. But its secretary, Jiselle Hanna, told Guardian Australia it can no longer support the government.
“If Ben Carroll’s government won’t commit to no job cuts in the public service, then our union cannot support him,” Hanna said.

The Labor government has made successive cuts to the Victorian public service (VPS), a smaller subset of the public sector that is largely administrative, as it seeks to rein in employee expenses – the state’s largest area of expenditure.

This included cutting about 1,000 VPS roles including more than 300 executive positions, and merging several government entities following an independent review, led by Helen Silver, last year. The government has said the changes delivered $4bn in savings, while frontline roles weren’t affected.
As of June 2025, there were some 58,000 employed in the VPS – compared with the almost 400,000 in the total public sector.
Hanna said since the Silver review, there had been more than 200 further restructures, many of which had resulted in “redundancies, job losses and pay cuts”.
“The public service used to be a reliable and secure place to build a career – that job security doesn’t exist any more, it’s been replaced with precarious employment,” she said.

Meanwhile, the Coalition has committed to implementing an indefinite hiring freeze across all back-office public service roles if it wins government, saving $22bn over a decade. The opposition has said the hiring freeze would remain in place until VPS staffing levels returned to the population-adjusted equivalent of 2014–15 – when it was last in government.

Hanna said both Labor and the Coalition’s distinction between frontline public sector roles and back-office VPS roles overlooked work performed by public servants including directing firefighters during bushfires; analysing DNA, fingerprints and ballistics; developing school curricula and investigating childcare centres.

She said while the union accepts “budget savings need to come from somewhere”, cuts to the public service would only lead to increased use of consultants, which she described as “privatisation by stealth”.
after newsletter promotion

Analysis released by the union, based on Victorian government annual reports since the 2017-18 financial year, showed Labor has spent $1.2bn on consultants across 10 departments. The Department of Treasury and Finance had the highest spend of about $222m since 2017, while the Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action had the highest annual spend of about $86m in the 2024-25 financial year.

The CPSU has launched a campaign urging Victorians to sign a pledge supporting the public service and committing not to vote for candidates who propose cutting jobs. While the campaign does not endorse any political party, it highlights that both the Greens and the Victorian Socialists oppose public service job cuts and the privatisation of public assets.

Last week, Guardian Australia reported the Electrical Trades Union (ETU) state council resolved not to run a statewide campaign for Labor, despite spending more than $1.6m supporting the party at the last election.
On the same day, the United Firefighters Union – which has been embroiled in a wages dispute with government since 2021 – launched its ad campaign urging Victorians to “put Labor last”.

The Australian Services Union is also running ads calling the premier a liar, as part of its long-term campaign to lift the 1.5% rate cap on councils, which restricts pay rises for workers below inflation.

Members of the Australian Education Union, which is not formally affiliated with the Labor party, have also said they won’t be campaigning for the party. The Health and Community Services Union, meanwhile, has eight members running this election – though none for the Labor party it is affiliated with.

But Guardian Australia can reveal chief executive, Dennis Barnes, who has a base salary of $1,845,126, opted not to accept the extra cash.
The company’s chief financial officer, Kim Josling, who has a pay packet worth $828,839, received a $215,440 bonus, according to the company’s annual report for the 2025-2026 financial year.

Its chief operating officer, Maia Schweizer, received a base salary of $1,050,503, and pocketed a $255,570 bonus, while chief commercial officer, Gordon Wymer, who has a base salary of $1,142,268, took home a $280,915 bonus.
The company’s long-delayed renewable energy project, Snowy Hydro 2.0, will not be completed until the end of the decade and is expected to cost taxpayers as much as $25bn.
It was first put forward in 2017 by the Turnbull government and came with an original price tag of $2bn, but the project in the Kosciuszko national park has climbed in cost.
The project was revised to almost $13bn in 2023, and construction was expected to completed by the end of 2028.
Snowy 2.0 now won’t be completed and fully commissioned until 2029.
A Snowy Hydro spokesperson said “short term incentives are based on a range of performance outcomes across these parts of Snowy Hydro’s business”.
“Mr Barnes recommended to Snowy Hydro’s Board that he receive no short term incentive payment for FY26,” the statement reads.
At Australia’s national science agency, the CSIRO, its chief executive, Doug Hilton, received a bonus of $198,517 on top of his $789,391 base salary, according to its 2025-2026 annual report.
He was the only one of the organisation’s senior executives to receive a bonus classed as a “salary at risk” payment.
The cash was awarded the same year the agency made a number of painful cuts, shrinking its workforce by several hundred people.
after newsletter promotion
More than 1,100 jobs have been cut from CSIRO in the last two years, according to the Community and Public Sector Union.
Separation and redundancy payments cost the agency more than $27m.
A CSIRO spokesperson said the agency’s board determined the annual value of the “at risk payment” which was assessed on key performance indicators.
Bonus payments to other senior executives were removed in the 2021-2022 financial year to align the agency with the public service, where such payments were also being removed.
“The size of CSIRO’s workforce is now expected to remain stable, supported by additional funding from the Australian Government in this year’s federal budget,” the spokesperson said.
“CSIRO acknowledges that change can create uncertainty for affected staff, and we do not underestimate the impact of that.”

articles.title: Car finance: Barclays becomes first big lender to offer payouts for mis-selling of loans
articles.summary: Bank to make ‘early settlement’ offers before outcome of legal battle, with those who accept likely to get money before Christmas

blocks.text: Barclays will this month start offering compensation to tens of thousands of people who claim they were mis-sold car loans, with some of those who accept likely to see the money land in their account before Christmas.

Amid an ongoing legal battle over an industry-wide compensation scheme for victims of the UK’s car finance scandal, Barclays has become the first big UK lender to break cover and begin offering payouts to some customers who have complained.

Under the rules, “early settlement” offers of this kind must at least match what people would receive under the multibillion-pound scheme that is being challenged – which may help to address fears that banks might try to make “lowball” offers.
But consumers face a tricky decision as, depending on the outcome of the legal battle, they could end up with more money, less money or nothing at all if they decide to decline the offer and wait.
In March this year, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) announced a £9.1bn compensation scheme for the millions of victims of the scandal.
But legal challenges forced the regulator to partly suspend the scheme, and a hearing to decide what happens is due to go ahead in February next year.

The FCA had expected to start paying out £829 on average this year to those affected by the scandal, in which drivers were overcharged for loans as a result of commission payments between lenders and car dealers between 2007 and 2024.
Millions of people were treated unfairly when they took out motor finance to buy a new or secondhand car, motorbike or van, and ended up paying more than they should have done.
Until the legal challenge is concluded, lenders do not need to pay compensation to people owed money under the scheme.
However, Barclays Partner Finance – part of the banking group – has decided to offer payments now to some of those who would be due compensation under the scheme.
That has prompted speculation that other companies on the hook for payouts will follow suit.
It is understood that over the next couple of weeks, tens of thousands of Barclays customers who have already complained will be contacted directly and offered “an early full and final settlement”.

Barclays is using the FCA model to calculate the compensation offers. It said: “Acceptance is optional, and customers will receive clear information on how their offer has been calculated and what accepting it would mean.”

They will have a month to accept or reject the offer, and if they say yes, the bank will pay the money into their designated account. It is thought the first payments for those who accept the offer will arrive before Christmas – which may feed into some people’s decision-making.
after newsletter promotion
But those who accept cannot then later seek additional compensation or pursue further complaints or legal claims relating to the commission on that agreement.

Alternatively, people can reject the offer and wait to see what happens. The FCA said that if it saw off the legal challenge and its scheme was upheld, payments could begin in 2027, but if the judgment was appealed or the scheme was partially or wholly overturned, any compensation owed could be delayed until 2028 or later.

Ultimately, depending on the outcome, those who decline the early offers could end up being entitled to “more, less, or no compensation”, the regulator said. It added that it supported lenders making settlement offers, “as long as customers are offered no less than they would receive through the scheme”.
Barclays Partner Finance said it would not ask people who accept now to repay any of their compensation if the final outcome meant they would have been entitled to less cash.

Barclays has set aside £430m in connection with alleged motor finance mis-selling, and it is not clear how many people could be affected in total, or what proportion will receive early settlement offers.
Under the FCA scheme as it currently stands, compensation payments depend on the details of the case.
By far the biggest category is deals that allowed the dealer or broker to increase the interest rate the customer would pay, to get a higher commission.

blocks.text: World·New

Warsaw-Modlin Airport reopened around midday Tuesday after a bomb threat forced a passenger plane from London to make an unscheduled landing there, while another plane from Copenhagen was checked at Warsaw-Chopin airport for the same reason.
Separate bomb threat affected flight from Israel, which landed at Bulgaria's Sofia Airport

An airport in Warsaw reopened around midday Tuesday after a bomb threat forced a passenger plane from London to make an unscheduled landing there, while another plane from Copenhagen was checked at another airport in Warsaw for the same reason.
"We would like to inform you that air operations at Warsaw Modlin Airport have been resumed," the airport said in a statement.

"The aircraft, which was the subject of a report of a possible bomb threat, is currently being checked by the relevant services. Passengers and crew members remain in the arrivals hall to wait for further decisions."
A spokesperson for Polish airline LOT confirmed earlier that the flight that landed at Modlin was one of their flights.

A bomb threat was also reported on an SAS flight from Copenhagen to Warsaw, which landed at Chopin Airport and had already been checked, a Warsaw-Chopin Airport spokesperson said, adding that the airport was continuing operations.
SAS said the aircraft landed safely in Warsaw and that its passengers had disembarked. Polish authorities said that the threat was not confirmed.
It was not immediately clear whether the two threats were linked.
Warsaw has two airports: Chopin is within the city limits and Modlin, mostly used by budget airlines, is about 36 kilometres from the capital.

Also Tuesday, a plane flying from Israel landed at Sofia Airport, in the Bulgarian capital, after a bomb threat was received by email. Counterterrorism units were checking the plane for possible explosive devices, the BTA news agency quoted Interior Minister Secretary General Lyubomir Nikolov as saying.
A Wizz Air flight from London to Sofia was also diverted to Budapest airport on Monday after receiving a bomb threat, Hungarian Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi said in a Facebook post.

articles.title: Judge orders Iowa to permit Satanic Temple holiday event at state capitol
articles.summary:
Federal court says group likely to win its free speech claim and tells officials to approve application within seven days

A federal judge ordered state officials in Iowa on Monday to permit…

blocks.text: A federal judge ordered state officials in Iowa on Monday to permit a local Satanic Temple organization to hold a holiday event in the rotunda of the state capitol after years of denying the group’s application.
The religious organization and Iowa Republican state officials have been in a legal battle over the group’s applications to hold a holiday event at the state capitol in recent years.

Republicans in Iowa, who currently control the governorship and majorities in the state house and senate, have cited the capitol building’s policies prohibiting gratuitous violence and obscene displays as justification for denying the applications.
According to the office of the attorney general, Brenna Bird, state Republicans intend to appeal the federal judge’s decision.
The Satanic Temple and Iowa chapter leader filed a lawsuit in August, alleging discrimination from former and current state officials.

Chief District Judge Stephanie M Rose stated in her court order that the group was likely to succeed on its free speech claim and ordered the current director of the Iowa department of administrative services to approve the holiday event application within seven days.

The Satanic Temple (TST), which was founded in Salem, Massachusetts, in 2013, characterizes itself as a “non-theistic religious organization” that advocates for secularism and emphasizes separation from the Church of Satan founded in 1966.

In December 2023, the group had a religious holiday display in the Iowa state capitol, but it was vandalized by a Christian military veteran. The Turning Point founder, Charlie Kirk, pledged $10,000 to the accused vandal’s legal defense. The following year, the Satanic Temple’s application for a holiday display and event was denied.

blocks.caption: A damaged Satanic Temple display is shown at the Iowa state capitol in Des Moines on 15 December 2023. Photograph: Scott McFetridge/AP

blocks.text: “State officials have made it clear that they denied TST permission to hold events in the Capitol rotunda because they disagreed with their religious viewpoint,” said Shefali Aurora, ACLU of Iowa staff attorney, in a statement on the court order. “It is a foundational principle that the government cannot restrict speech in this way, favor one religion over another, or discriminate against religious groups because they don’t agree with them.”

The group said its proposed holiday event would include costumes of the European folklore character Krampus, caroling, coloring for children and ornament making. In its denial of the application, state officials cited sticks included in the costumes that could be used as weapons and policies meant to protect children who might be present in the public space.

Judge Rose wrote that the state officials’ arguments did not justify the denials, noting the argument that the character Krampus might scare children was “not a permissible basis for excluding speech” and the argument about the sticks included with the costumes “cannot justify denying the entire event”.
The Iowa department of administrative services and the Republican governor, Kim Reynolds, have not yet commented on the court order.

In 2023, Governor Reynolds stated in response to the group’s holiday display at the state capitol, “like many Iowans, I find the Satanic Temple’s display in the Capitol absolutely objectionable. In a free society, the best response to objectionable speech is more speech, and I encourage all those of faith to join me today in praying over the Capitol and recognizing the nativity scene that will be on display – the true reason for the season.”

articles.title: Trump’s troubles with Iran could open the door to China
articles.summary:
Beijing launches diplomatic salvo to woo Gulf leaders and bolster its influence in the region

China has held a flurry of meetings with Gulf leaders in a sign that Beijing is stepping up its…

blocks.text: China has held a flurry of meetings with Gulf leaders in a sign that Beijing is stepping up its diplomatic efforts in the Middle East.

The diplomatic salvo comes before a highly anticipated meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping when the US president is expected to attend the Apec conference in Shenzhen, China, on 18 and 19 November.
Xi held talks with Haitham bin Tariq, Oman’s sultan, in a historic state visit to Beijing on Monday.
President Xi’s foreign minister, Wang Yi, met Saudi Arabia’s national security adviser, Musaad bin Mohammed Al Aiban, and the deputy secretary of Iran’s national security council, Ali Bagheri Kani.

Haitham’s trip to Beijing is the first time that an Omani head of state has visited China since the two countries established diplomatic relations nearly 50 years ago. According to a Chinese readout of the meeting, Xi warned that the Middle East should not become an arena for “great power rivalry and geopolitical conflicts”.
He said: “China has always been actively committed to stopping conflict and promoting peace, and hopes to contribute wisdom and solutions to resolving the regional security dilemma.”

Wang said after his separate talks that China was willing to “play a constructive role in helping the region emerge from the shadow of the pandemic and achieve lasting peace and stability”. In his meeting with Bagheri Kani, Wang said China supported Iran “in safeguarding its sovereignty and security”. According to China, the Iranian official said his country looked forward to China “playing a more important role in international and regional peace”.

blocks.caption: China’s foreign minister, Wang Yi, held talks with Iranian officials, telling them his country supported Iran ‘in safeguarding its sovereignty and security’. Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock

blocks.text: When the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February, China was credited with pushing Tehran toward ceasefire talks in Pakistan, bolstering its status as a regional mediator.

Beijing’s influence in the Middle East is “no longer what it used to be”, said Shen Dingli, a Shanghai-based scholar of international relations. But he added: “Given China’s increased investment and trade in the region … its influence cannot be ignored.”

As the war has dragged on, China’s diplomatic efforts have been muted. Its biggest economic leverage over Iran is the fact that it buys about 90% of the Middle Eastern country’s crude oil exports. Between April and June, it slashed its crude imports by 30%, with the total in June plunging to the lowest level in a decade. That saved the global economy from a major spike in inflation. According to some estimates, China’s cut in oil imports shaved $30 or more off barrel prices of Brent crude, a global benchmark.

Beijing has otherwise done little to broker peace in the Middle East. That is partly because it does not see the conflict as being its responsibility to resolve. In March, Wang said the war “should never have happened” and that the US and Israel would find “no popular support” for the strikes.
China is also a beneficiary from the damage that the fighting has done to the US’s global reputation.
According to findings published in July by the Pew Research Center, a Washington-based thinktank, China is now viewed more favourably than the US in a majority of 36 countries surveyed.

The pain caused by the long-term disruption to the strait of Hormuz, the waterway through which much of the world’s oil and gas flows, also poses a risk to China’s economy. Shortages of energy cause inflation, which risks reducing global demand for Chinese goods.

Tehran and Washington are locked in intensive talks to reach an agreement, which could include reopening the strait. Trump has repeatedly threatened to renew military action against Iran after Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US, a move which would cause alarm in Beijing.

Trump’s desperation to reach a deal in the Middle East may also provide an opportunity for China to present itself as a regional peacemaker, bolstering Xi’s status before their meeting. Beijing brokered a detente between Saudi Arabia and Iran in 2023 but since then its diplomatic impact in the region has been limited.
Shen said China’s desire to improve diplomatic relations with Middle Eastern countries as well as the US were “mutually reinforcing” trends.
China’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Mao Ning, said on Monday that China would send special envoy Zhai Jun to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia in early to mid-November.

articles.title: Europe on alert after supermarket freezers hit by cyber-attacks in nine countries
articles.summary: Supermarkets have reported problems from Estonia and Sweden to Portugal and Italy and many retainers have been forced to discard food.

blocks.text: The European Union has raised concerns about the attacks, which come three weeks after a cyber-attack disrupted as many as 700 French grocery stores, causing food losses estimated at tens of millions of euros.
The security of refrigeration systems as well as other devices that can be monitored remotely has heightened concerns about government-backed hybrid attacks.
The EU's food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the bloc was taking the incidents very seriously and warned of further disruption in the future.

Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier was careful not to attribute blame, but said: "These incidents of course show once again how cyber-attacks can disrupt essential services and affect citizens' daily lives."
"These are not isolated incidents and of course we have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents."

In Italy, Giorgia Meloni's government called a meeting with intelligence chiefs, but said the impact was "currently very limited" and most of the food distribution chain had up-to-date security systems able to fend off such attacks.
At least four Co-op supermarkets in Sicily and one business in Tuscany were affected, according to the national cybersecurity agency.
Meloni's office said those businesses affected were "mostly still equipped with obsolete security systems, with interfaces directly exposed to the internet and inadequate authentication mechanisms".
Belgian supermarkets were among those hardest-hit, with dozens of stores reporting refrigeration failures. Federal prosecutors have opened an investigation.

Mathieu Tilman, a manager at a Delhaize supermarket in Belgium, said he was shocked by this kind of attack: "I don't even understand how anyone could do this... How can we end up throwing away so much food? I find it truly distressing. In moments like these, you just feel like quitting your job."

In Ireland, 13 SuperValu stores were impacted by what the chain's owner, Musgrave Group, called a cyber-incident. "Replenishment of chilled and frozen ranges in the affected stores is well under way," a spokesman said on Monday.
A small number of corner shops in the Netherlands also suffered disruption. Last month, supermarket chain Albert Heijn had to take several services offline because of a separate cyber-attack.

In Portugal, the Mosqueteiros group said that incidents at seven Intermarché stores had been linked to a cyberattack, which "appears to have targeted an external service provider responsible for managing the refrigeration systems".

Swedish chain ICA also said "a limited number" of its stores had experienced refrigeration problems, without confirming a cyber-attack, and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.
In Finland, irregular temperatures were detected in a few smaller grocery stores belonging to the Kesko group, which said it was investigating the issue.
In Estonia, at least one supermarket was attacked by hackers who raised the temperature in the refrigeration units to 50C, public broadcaster ERR reported.

articles.title: Brazil wraps up COP30 with fossil fuel, forest roadmaps, urging shift from talks to action
articles.summary: 'We don't need more negotiations. What we need is for governments to start taking action,' says COP30 president Correa do Lago, who led last November's UN climate summit in Belem

blocks.text: DEADLOCK. COP30 President Andre Correa Do Lago speaks to the media during the UN Climate Change Conference (COP30), in Belem, Brazil, on November 21, 2025.
Anderson Coelho/Reuters
'We don't need more negotiations. What we need is for governments to start taking action,' says COP30 president Correa do Lago, who led last November's UN climate summit in Belem

items: Brazil is concluding its presidency of the UN climate process with plans to reduce deforestation and transition from fossil fuels, emphasizing the need for immediate government action.
The COP30 summit highlighted the challenges of achieving climate goals, particularly the need for increased funding for forest protection.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

BRASILIA, Brazil – Brazil is ending its year-long presidency of the UN climate process with roadmaps aimed at curbing deforestation and accelerating a shift away from fossil fuels to help governments deliver on past climate agreements.
COP30 president Andre Correa do Lago, who led last November’s UN climate summit in Belem, said governments must integrate climate goals into policymaking.

“We don’t need more negotiations. What we need is for governments to start taking action,” Correa do Lago told Reuters. “We need to completely change the way governments deal with climate change. To implement this, we need finance, infrastructure and transportation ministers at the table.”

Shifting away from fossil fuels and reducing deforestation are considered essential to limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, a goal set at the Paris climate talks in 2015.

But oil-producing nations have been reluctant to embrace measures that could undermine a key source of revenue while efforts to curb deforestation face a chronic lack of funding. A UN report last month showed 1.5ºC was increasingly out of reach.

This year’s climate summit, COP31, is due to get underway in Antalya in southern Turkey on November 9. Murat Kurum, the summit president and Turkish environment, urbanisation and climate ​change minister, told the UN in September the agenda would also focus on implementation rather than new ⁠pledges and was based on “dialogue, consensus and action.”

In Belem, Brazil sought to formalise an energy transition roadmap, after more than 100 countries agreed at COP28 in Dubai in 2023 to triple renewable energy capacity by 2030. But while the plan had European support, it failed to secure a consensus after opposition from major oil-producing countries.

Under the roadmap, countries would spend the period to 2028 assessing their energy systems, strengthening regulations and institutions, and developing national transition plans ahead of the second Global Stocktake, an evaluation of whether the world is heading in the right direction to contain global warming.

By 2030, infrastructure upgrades and renewable energy investments should be underway. A final phase between 2031 and 2033 would focus on accelerating renewable energy deployment, replacing fossil fuels and consolidating cleaner energy systems.
Global renewable energy capacity reached a record 5,149 gigawatts at the end of 2025, up 692 GW from the previous year, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency.
Brazil’s roadmap notes that most recent growth in renewable energy has gone toward meeting new demand rather than replacing fossil fuel use.
“My opinion is that it doesn’t need to be negotiated again because that negotiation has already taken place,” said Correa do Lago. “It needs to be implemented.”
A lack of consensus also kept Brazil’s proposed deforestation roadmap out of the final COP30 agreement, reflecting persistent disagreements over how to finance forest protection.
According to the United Nations Environment Programme, annual funding for forests must rise from $84.5 billion in 2023 to more than $300 billion by 2030.

Most current funding comes from national governments, which account for 88.3% of forest finance, with international public funding at only 3.4%, placing much of the burden on the developing countries where most of the world’s tropical forests are located.
Brazil has proposed a Tropical Forests Forever Facility that would use returns from a sovereign fund to provide ongoing payments to countries that preserve their forests.
The initiative had secured $7.6 billion by the end of COP30, against a target of $10 billion, according to Corrêa do Lago.

The roadmap also calls for expanding other funding initiatives, including strengthening carbon markets, improving direct access to finance for Indigenous peoples and local communities, and using debt-relief instruments.

“Public financing from developed countries is absolutely essential,” Corrêa do Lago said. “But we have a much more sophisticated and diversified way of financing the various activities that would reduce deforestation.”
He said the roadmap’s main value was in highlighting the complexity of tackling forest loss.
“It is not an easy task, and it is not just about financing. But financing is a central part of this process.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Brazil publishes first global ‘roadmap’ for phasing out fossil fuels
articles.summary:
Cop30 host sets out steps to break link with coal, oil and gas as it aims to move focus from negotiating to implementing

All countries can start to break their dependence on fossil fuels now…

blocks.text: All countries can start to break their dependence on fossil fuels now without needing to wait for new technologies or economic changes, Brazil’s government has said ahead of a global climate summit.

Brazil, the host of last year’s UN climate conference, set out the world’s first global “roadmap” for phasing out fossil fuels on Tuesday, showing that countries could boost their economies and pull people out of poverty while breaking the link with coal, oil and gas.

But Joeri Rogelj, a professor of climate science and policy at Imperial College London, said that although the Brazilian roadmaps represented a step forward, they were limited. “The roadmaps are valuable but fall short of clearly indicating the pace of change needed by including no timeline or key benchmarks,” he said.

“Because of this omission, they still leave much to be imagined about what is needed to achieve the Paris agreement’s ultimate goal: limiting global warming to well below 2C, and preferably to 1.5C, to avoid dangerous climate harm.”

André Corrêa do Lago, Brazil’s president of the Cop30 summit, said the roadmaps were intended to help move the annual UN Cops away from their previous focus on negotiating global agreements to tackle the climate crisis, and on to implementing the targets that had already been agreed. Cop31 takes place in Antalya, Turkey, this month.

“They are documents of implementation,” Corrêa do Lago told the Guardian in an interview. “There is a different group of people that negotiate and that implement. The problem we’ve had at many Cops is to think that the same people who negotiate might also need to coordinate the implementation – this is not the case.”
He said the roadmaps should be taken up by ministries of finance, transportation, energy and infrastructure to work on how they could be implemented in each country.

Brazil hosted the Cop30 summit last November in the coastal city of Belém, in the Amazon rainforest, where a bitter dispute broke out over whether the final set of resolutions should include pledges on fossil fuels. As a compromise, the presidency agreed to produce two roadmaps, one on “transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems in a just orderly and equitable manner” and the other on halting and reversing deforestation.

blocks.caption: An illegal mining camp in the Amazon rainforest in Suriname. Photograph: Iván Valencia/AP

blocks.text: These roadmaps are separate from similarly named plans from governments that met after Cop30 at a conference in Santa Marta, Colombia, in April, to discuss the transition away from fossil fuels. At that conference, nearly 60 countries formed a new “coalition of the willing”, separate to Cops, to set out their own national roadmaps to phase out fossil fuels. Several countries have since produced national plans, including Germany, France and the Netherlands.

The roadmaps produced by governments under the Santa Marta initiative are much more specific and prescriptive than Brazil’s, as each of those is written by the national government responsible for implementing the policies recommended.

The Brazilian roadmaps only set out steps that are possible. They are not binding, they contain no deadlines or milestones for actions, and they leave it to countries themselves to “diagnose” their degree of dependence on fossil fuels and select steps to reduce it.

“Every country will have a different rhythm [for moving away from fossil fuels] – it’s very important to concentrate on the diagnoses of countries’ circumstances,” Corrêa do Lago said. “Based on these diagnoses, they can choose their levers [of policy] and implement the transition.”
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: André Corrêa do Lago at Cop30 in Belém last November. Photograph: Anderson Coelho/Reuters

blocks.text: Among the steps Brazil suggests is for oil and gas producers to urgently cut the flaring and venting of gas from extraction sites. Methane is a greenhouse gas 80 times more powerful than carbon dioxide, so this would have an immediate impact. Other steps are for countries to reduce their subsidies to fossil fuel use or production, and building up renewable generation.

The roadmap on deforestation notes the large sums that are expected to be needed to help poor countries with heavily forested areas such as the Amazon, the Congo rainforests and south-east Asian tropical forests that are under threat from fires and palm oil exploitation.

About $300bn is likely to be needed every year for forests by 2030, and $500bn a year by 2050, according to the roadmap, citing UN figures. The current amounts available fall far short at about $85bn a year.
At Cop30 last year, Brazil set up the tropical forests forever facility, a fund aiming to preserve forests, to which the UK contributed £400m and other countries combined contributed about $7bn.

The deforestation roadmap also notes the importance of regulating trade between forested countries and consumer countries. At present, there are few trade checks to stop unscrupulous companies from selling goods from deforested areas.

In some cases, deforestation has appeared to be condoned or encouraged by local or even national administrations. Indonesia is being sued by civil society groups for “gross negligence” over the record-breaking fires over the last few months that have cleared swathes of forest and destroyed wildlife habitats, most likely to be replaced by palm oil plantations.

Brazil was able to publish the roadmaps after its president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, won a fourth election term just over a week ago. In the last four years under Lula, deforestation rates have fallen by about 70%. His defeated opponent Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the jailed ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, had been expected if elected to return to his father’s policies of rampant exploitation of the Amazon rainforest.

articles.title: Can US midterm election really change Trump's Iran policy?
articles.summary: The US midterms are at hand, but their impact on the Iran war remains far from clear. Analysts say the Washington political elite may not be as divided on Iran as it appears.

image.caption: Trump's Middle Eastern policy played a major role in the midterm election campaignImage: Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: The US election this Tuesday is shaping up to be one of the most consequential midterm votes in modern US history, with Washington's relationship with Israel and its war on Iran right at the center of the political standoff.
Many Democrats, including the party's rising stars such as Ohio Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, are outspoken critics of the Iran war, with El-Sayed calling the conflict "illegal" and "stupid."

US President Donald Trump sought to downplay the effects of the war during the campaign. Last week, he claimed only "one or two targets" remained in Iran and that those could be settled in 10 minutes. However, he immediately added that messages are still being exchanged, Tehran shows strong interest in a deal, and the US has plenty of time to deal with the crisis.

At the same time, there are reports of the US and Israel preparing to launch a new round of strikes on Iran just after the midterm election and pro-war Republicans such as Senator Ted Cruz are putting pressure on the White House to deal with "the threat" posed by Iran.
"I have urged arming the Iranian protesters to overthrow the regime," Cruz said in an online post after spending a day with Trump.

Behind the scenes, analysts warn that the Washington political elite may not be as divided on Iran as it appears. Moreover, even a resounding Democrat victory might not give them enough leverage on the Trump administration regarding the Iran war.
Democrats and Republicans broadly 'in consensus' on Iran

Talking to DW, former National Security Advisor John Bolton said the Democrats are likely to secure a majority in the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate, handing them control of the Iran war funding.
The US Congress "can allocate defense budgets or impose restrictions on the use of financial resources," Bolton said.
Iran conflict: Could a new phase of the war be imminent?
Nevertheless, Bolton points out that the US president can veto congressional legislation, which would then require a two-thirds majority in both assemblies to overcome.
"Even if Democrats hold a majority in both houses, their influence will be limited to the legislative and political tools of Congress," he said.
US diplomat and Iran expert Alan Eyre points to a kind of "bipartisan consensus" that Republicans and Democrats have on Iran.

"Both major US parties share significant common ground in their opposition to the political structure of the Islamic Republic and in their support for policies aimed at exerting pressure on Tehran to change its behavior," he said.
What does Tehran think?
While warning of a "crushing response" to any new strikes on underground sites, Tehran has confirmed ongoing indirect communication via Doha and Muscat, keeping its diplomatic option open.

Shahin Modarres, an international security analyst leading the Iran team at ITSS Verona, told DW that Tehran's actions are based on a miscalculation. The regime, he argues, assumes that a Democratic Congress can easily restrain the White House.

Tehran's strategy in dragging out peace talks, pressuring the Strait of Hormuz, and letting fuel prices weigh on US voters, aims to deny Trump a win before November. However, Modarres notes this strategy may backfire after the election, as the Trump administration will no longer have any reason to delay its moves.
This approach also ignores the fact that both US parties largely agree on not letting Iranian develop nuclear weapons, he said.
How serious are Iran's new threats of retaliation?
Will Trump launch new strikes and declare victory?
Trump's ally-turned-critic John Bolton believes that Trump will only decide on his next steps on Iran after the election, once the political pressure grows less acute.
"I cannot predict what the US President will do; even Trump himself does not know his final decision right now," he told DW.
Bolton cites as an example a possible US attack on "Kuh-e Kolang," the new nuclear site he claims the Iranian government is constructing near Natanz.
"In this scenario, Trump could damage these facilities, declare victory, and pull back."
Bolton: 'Regime change' only guarantee against Iran getting nukes

Trump has consistently emphasized that the US goal is to deny Iran the capability of acquiring nuclear weapons. Throughout the conflict, the US president has also repeatedly claimed his administration had succeeded in this regard.
Bolton, in contrast, believes that the Islamic Republic will continue to pursue nuclear weapons capability for as long as it remains in power.
The former Trump advisor views "regime change" as the only sustainable solution to keep Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons.
US military buildup: What message is it sending Iran?
US failing to communicate with ordinary Iranians

Eyre, the first Persian-speaking diplomat to be the spokesperson for the US Department of State, emphasizes the difficulty of using external tools to bring about sustainable change. In his view, even if there is a consensus in Washington opposing the Islamic Republic and demanding a change in its behavior, this US consensus alone cannot overcome the structural obstacles to political change inside Iran. He reiterates that any fundamental transformation must emerge from within Iranian society itself.
The veteran diplomat also points to the failure of "Washington's public diplomacy to convey a clear, coherent, and authentic message to Iranian society."
He notes that official US government messaging is only incompletely reflected in the media outlets that the vast majority of Iranian citizens rely on for news.
"Furthermore, targeted and principled engagement with the core of Iranian society has generally not been a priority for successive US administrations," he said.
"Iranian citizens see that the US takes certain positions at the rhetorical level, but behaves differently in practice."
According to Eyre, this gap between words and deeds in Washington is a structural phenomenon that is not limited to a single administration or a single election cycle.
Iran's regime: inside the system protecting its rulers

articles.title: Spanish soccer player dies after on-field collision in 2nd-division match
articles.summary: Tenerife forward Jesús de Miguel has died after he suffered cardiac arrest from an on-field collision in a Spanish second-division match, his club said Tuesday. He was 30.

image.caption: FC Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel is carried off the field on a stretcher after colliding with Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono during a soccer match in Santa Cruz de Tenerife, Spain, Monday. Tenerife said in a statement that De Miguel died on Tuesday morning. (The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Soccer
Tenerife forward Jesús de Miguel has died after he suffered cardiac arrest from an on-field collision in a Spanish second-division match, his club said Tuesday. He was 30.
Jesús de Miguel suffered cardiac arrest after incident on Monday
De Miguel was challenging for the ball near midfield on Monday when he was struck in the chest by the onrushing Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono during added time.
Owono was shown a straight red card for the incident.
De Miguel was taken to a hospital and the match, tied 2-2, was abandoned after the incident.

Tenerife said in a statement to Spanish media late Monday that De Miguel suffered cardiac arrest but that his pulse was restored in the ambulance to the hospital. However, it later said his condition had “worsened neurologically” and subsequently announced that De Miguel had died at 8 a.m.
The club located on Spain's Canary Islands said it was “heartbroken.”
De Miguel, a Madrid native, made his professional debut in 2015 with Leganés B and has since played for a number of lower-divisions clubs in Spain. He joined Tenerife last year.

“There are no words of comfort,” the club statement read. “There is absolutely nothing that can alleviate this profound sense of sorrow. We stand with his devastated family, his loved ones, and the entire Tenerife community.”

items: More soccer coverage

blocks.text: The heavy collision happened when Owono rushed out of his area all the way to midfield to challenge for a long ball that De Miguel was trying to reach.
De Miguel initially curled on his knees, clutching his torso for a few seconds, before he fell over onto his back, with his arms falling to his sides.
Owono was walking off the field after being shown the red card but turned around and joined the other players rushing to check on De Miguel.
Andorra, which is owned by former Barcelona star Gerard Pique, also offered its condolences, along with other clubs, the Spanish soccer federation and La Liga.
“We wish to extend our deepest condolences to the family of Jesús de Miguel, to all his colleagues and friends, and to CD Tenerife. May he rest in peace,” Andorra said in a statement.
The players of Real Madrid held a minute of silence for De Miguel during training, while fellow topflight club Espanyol postponed the presentation of its new coach.
English clubs Manchester United and Liverpool joined in offering their condolences on social media.
The Spanish soccer federation postponed two Copa del Rey matches and one Copa de la Reina matches to be held later on Tuesday.
Life-threatening injuries from collisions in soccer are extremely rare.

Last year in Spain, a 19-year-old goalkeeper died from head injuries suffered during a collision in a fifth-division match. Colindres goalkeeper Raúl Ramírez had two cardiorespiratory arrests, one on the field and then in the ambulance while being transported to a hospital. He was declared brain dead two days later.
In 2001, Ukrainian goalkeeper Serhiy Perkhun was playing for CSKA Moscow when he died from head injuries received in a collision during a match.

articles.title: PLDT’s longtime auditor SGV resigns, withdraws opinion amid accounting issues
articles.summary: PwC takes over the telco giant’s audits after SGV earlier identified a material weakness in financial reporting controls and withdrew its 2024 and 2025 audit opinions

blocks.text: PwC takes over the telco giant’s audits after SGV earlier identified a material weakness in financial reporting controls and withdrew its 2024 and 2025 audit opinions

items: SyCip Gorres Velayo & Co. (SGV) has resigned as PLDT's auditor after nearly 24 years, citing impaired independence under US SEC rules.
SGV withdrew its audit opinions on PLDT's 2024 and 2025 financial statements due to previously uncovered accounting errors and a material weakness in internal controls.
PLDT has appointed Isla Lipana & Co. (PwC) as its new external auditor, while still seeking an auditor for its international financial statements.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – After nearly 24 years of serving as PLDT’s auditor, SyCip Gorres Velayo & Co. (SGV) has resigned and withdrawn its audit opinions on the company’s 2024 and 2025 financial statements prepared for international reporting.

SGV, the country’s largest professional services firm and a member of Ernst & Young, informed PLDT on October 31 that it was resigning after determining that it was no longer independent under US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and auditing oversight rules.

“SGV has now concluded that its independence was impaired as of the issuance of its Fiscal 2025 Audit Opinions, and this impairment continues through today. Accordingly, SGV has submitted its resignation as the Company’s independent registered public accounting firm,” PLDT said in a disclosure.

An external auditor is supposed to independently examine a company’s financial statements and assure investors that these fairly present its finances. SGV concluded that its independence had already been impaired when it issued its 2025 audit opinions in April. While PLDT’s disclosure discussed the accounting errors and weaknesses in its financial controls, it did not specify what caused SGV’s independence to be impaired.

SGV’s resignation comes after accounting errors were earlier uncovered at PLDT. In August, PLDT acknowledged these errors arising from “deficiencies in controls over the accounting for certain structured hedge arrangements.” These hedge arrangements often protect companies from financial risks, such as fluctations in currency exchange rates. The errors involved how gains and losses from these contracts were recorded in its financial statements.
More seriously, SGV concluded that “a material weakness existed in the Company’s internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2025.”
SGV had initially issued unqualified, or clean, audit opinions on PLDT’s 2024 and 2025 financial statements before now withdrawing them following the discovery of accounting issues.

The auditor has since withdrawn its 2025 audit opinions, saying they “could no longer be relied upon.” On October 31, it also withdrew its 2024 opinion because it could not complete its assessment of additional accounting information before resigning.

PLDT said there had been no disagreements with SGV over accounting practices or audit procedures, apart from the unfinished assessment. The telco giant also stressed the revisions identified so far were not expected to materially affect its net income, EBITDA, earnings per share, cash flows, or key operating metrics.

Still, the August disclosure was serious enough for the Philippine Stock Exchange to halt trading in PLDT shares for one hour on August 14 as investors digested the news. PLDT shares later fell 4.49% to P1,170 by the end of that day.

It was not PLDT’s first controversy involving financial controls. In December 2022, the company disclosed capital expenditure budget overruns estimated at P48 billion covering 2019 to 2022. A later review found no evidence of fraud, but PLDT still introduced changes to its spending controls. (READ: PLDT cleans up, moves on from capex overrun mess)
Meanwhile, PLDT appointed Isla Lipana & Co., the Philippine member firm of PwC, as its new external auditor effective Monday, November 2.

PwC will handle its Philippine financial statements, but PLDT is still searching for an auditor to handle its international financial statements and internal control reporting required by US regulators. PLDT’s US reporting obligations arise from its listing on the New York Stock Exchange, where its American depositary shares trade.

PwC Philippines’ chairman emeritus, Alexander Cabrera, recently grabbed the spotlight as the forensic accounting expert who testified for the prosecution in Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial in October. – Rappler.com

articles.title: US urges Venezuela to release remaining political prisoners
articles.summary: The US secretary of state also discusses laying the groundwork for 'free, fair, and credible elections'.

blocks.text: The US has urged Venezuela to release the remaining political prisoners being held in the South American country.

More than 1,000 political prisoners have been freed since US forces seized Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro in a military raid on Caracas on 3 January and took him to New York, where he faces trial on drug-trafficking and torture charges.
But Venezuelan prisoners' rights group Foro Penal says 322 people remain in detention.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met his Venezuelan counterpart, Oliver Blanco, on Monday where he called for their release and discussed reforms aimed at laying the groundwork for free, fair, and credible elections, the US state department said.
The release of political prisoners has long been a demand made by Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado.

Machado, who was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2025, returned to Venezuela on 25 October after living in exile for almost a year. One of her first meetings was with relatives of political detainees.
Many of those in detention were arrested in the aftermath of the 2024 presidential election.

The National Electoral Council (CNE) - which is dominated by government loyalists - declared the incumbent, Nicolás Maduro, the winner of the election even though copies of the voting tallies collected by the opposition and verified by independent media suggested that the opposition candidate had won.
The Carter Center, which had sent independent observers to Venezuela, also said that the election "could not be considered democratic".

A UN fact-finding mission found, external that in the months that followed, the Venezuelan government orchestrated "a harsh repression against persons perceived as political opponents or simply because they express dissent or critical views against the authorities".
After US forces seized Maduro, his loyal vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, was sworn in as interim president.
While Rodríguez has the backing of the Trump administration, opposition parties within Venezuela have been expressing impatience with the slow pace of reforms.

In Monday's statement, the US state department stressed that it remained committed to US President Donald Trump's three-phase plan, consisting of "stabilisation, economic recovery and political reconciliation, and democratic transition".
A week ago, Rubio had told journalists that Venezuela's "election infrastructure" had to be replaced in order for fresh elections to be valid.
"Not in 10 years, not in five years, not in two years; it needs to happen quickly under the timelines that we've established," he insisted.
Days later, Rodríguez told Venezuelans in a televised address that "there will be elections" under a "renewed" electoral authority.
However, she did not give a timeline for when the election could be held.
Opposition leader Machado, on the other hand, has been pushing for elections to be held in 2027.
At one point she suggested 24 July 2027 - the anniversary of the birth of independence hero Simón Bolivar - but she has since returned to calling for a vote at some point in the next year.

articles.title: Defense’s list of witnesses in Sara Duterte trial expected this week
articles.summary: 'We issued an advisory last week which reminded the defense that it should provide the Court with a list of its witnesses at least five days before their intended date of presentation,' says Senate…

blocks.text: VEEP. Vice President Sara Duterte talks to supporters as she prepares to leave the Quezon City Regional Trial Court after the postponement of the arraignment for her grave threats case, on October 9, 2026.
Noel Celis/Reuters

'We issued an advisory last week which reminded the defense that it should provide the Court with a list of its witnesses at least five days before their intended date of presentation,' says Senate Secretary Renato Bantug Jr.

items: The defense counsel for Vice President Sara Duterte is preparing to present evidence in the impeachment trial and is expected to request subpoenas for witnesses this week.
The Senate impeachment court has a five-day rule requiring the defense to submit a list of witnesses before their presentation, and the trial is set to resume on November 9.

The prosecution has withdrawn most articles of impeachment, allowing the defense to focus on rebutting the remaining unexplained wealth case, while the court awaits the defense's formal comments on recent rulings.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The defense counsel of Vice President Sara Duterte is preparing to present its evidence in the ongoing impeachment trial, with the Senate impeachment court expecting it to seek subpoenas for its witnesses this week.

Senate Secretary and Clerk of Court Renato Bantug Jr. said on Tuesday, November 3, that the defense is expected to request the issuance of subpoenas for its list of witnesses ahead of the resumption of the proceedings.
This is in accordance with the five-day rule of the Senate impeachment court, which requires the defense to submit its list of witnesses at least five days before their intended presentation.

“We issued an advisory last week, which among others, reminded the defense that it should provide the Court with a list of its witnesses at least five days before their intended date of presentation,” Bantug said.

The impeachment trial was temporarily paused to give way for the Senate committee hearings on the proposed 2027 national budget. Trial will resume on Monday, November 9, with the defense beginning its presentation of evidence.
Prior to the break, the prosecution team in the impeachment trial withdrew all but one of the articles of impeachment to expedite the proceedings, a move that the impeachment court accepted.

Senate impeachment court Presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero said the defense team no longer needs to present counter-evidence for all the dropped cases, and can focus on rebutting the prosecution’s unexplained wealth case.

Escudero also lifted the sub judice rule covering the withdrawn articles, but the ruling drew objections from the defense team. The impeachment court said it would await the defense’s formal comment before deciding whether to reconsider the ruling, either in whole or in part.
Bantug said the defense had yet to submit its formal comment on the matter.
In a related development, the Senate impeachment court issued an advisory on the schedule of the trial for November.
The calendar for the trial is as follows:

November 11 — 10:00 am
