articles.title: Putin pushes the myth of Russian invincibility, seemingly to set his terms for peace
articles.summary: When Russian President Vladimir Putin recently declared that inflicting a "strategic defeat" on Russia is "unrealistic," it may have sounded like standard wartime bravado. But he might also be…

image.caption: Russian President Vladimir Putin attends the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on Sept. 1. Putin's recent remarks about Russia's past military successes are seen by some Kremlin-watchers as a precursor to peace talks. (Petr Kovalev/Sputnik/Reuters)

blocks.text: When Russian President Vladimir Putin recently declared to a television reporter that inflicting a "strategic defeat" on Russia is "unrealistic," it may have sounded like standard wartime bravado.
Instead, his boilerplate rhetoric may signal something deeper: positioning ahead of a diplomatic endgame as international pressure grows to end the war in Ukraine.
"It is impossible to defeat Russia on the battlefield," Putin told the reporter on Oct. 22.
He continued that "historical Russia" includes all Ukrainian territories and as such, the idea that Moscow could ever relinquish land it has conquered in Ukraine is impossible.
Analysts who've reviewed the Kremlin leader's comments suggest they're part of a deliberate strategy to shape an eventual peace settlement.
"Putin is using history to make a political statement and a political claim," said Eugene Maikinkov, a Canadian-Latvian scholar of Russian history who lectures at the University of Swansea, in Wales.
British Kremlin-watcher Mark Galeotti regularly parses Putin's speeches on his In Moscow's Shadows podcast and agrees Russia's leader is sending important signals.
"Everyone is moving into that kind of preparatory position of establishing their negotiating stances," he told CBC News.
Putin speaks with state television correspondent Pavel Zarubin following an event at the Bolshoi Theatre in Moscow, on Oct. 22 . (Gavriil Grigorov/Sputnik/Reuters)

Maikinkov says Putin's message to Russia's adversaries — Europeans especially — is that inflicting a humiliating defeat that fundamentally changes the trajectory of the Russian state will not happen and, one way or another, Russia's demands to end the war will have to be reckoned.
"Russia isn't going anywhere. It will have to be a partner in the future," said Maikinkov, suggesting there is no realistic way to rob Putin of negotiating power.
Intractable demands
After four and half years of combat, the war on the ground has largely bogged down into a stalemate, with Russia making only incremental territorial gains in Ukraine's Donbas region.
Some Western estimates suggest its military has suffered as many as half a million deaths and up to 700,000 wounded.

But despite the bloodbath, Putin has not noticeably moved on any of his key demands to end the invasion: Ukraine must turn over the last remaining 15 per cent of the territory of eastern Donbas region; it must demobilize its army; it must have nothing to do with NATO and must "de-Nazify," as the Kremlin puts it.

That last condition, along with the Nazi reference, reflects Putin's long-held position that the current Ukrainian government of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy — who is Jewish — is illegitimate and must be replaced.
Most Ukrianians believe Putin's real intention is to totally subjugate their country and erase Ukrainian statehood.

Ukrainian soldiers fire rockets toward Russian positions on the outskirts of the front-line city of Kramatorsk, in Ukraine's Donetsk region, on Sunday. (Iryna Rybakova/Press Service of the Ukrainian Armed Forces/Reuters)

The belief in Russian exceptionalism — that Russia is a historic empire which will always emerge victorious no matter how hard its enemies try to tear it apart — is one of Putin's most dominant narratives.
It's also one of the most intensely contested.
"There is a myth that has been successfully planted in the West that Russia always wins," said Poland's Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski, in response to Putin's comments.
"But things don't always go their way."

People carry candles past The Motherland Calls, a statue commemorating the Russians killed during the German invasion in the Second World War, in Volgograd, Russia, on June 21, 2021. Putin often cites the German defeat as an example of Russia's military prowess. (Kirill Braga/Reuters)
Russia was defeated in the Crimean war in 1856 which blocked its territorial ambitions in Europe.
In 1905, the country's Baltic navy sailed more than 25,000 kilometres around Africa to confront the Japanese navy in the Pacific only to be literally blown out of the water.
And the brutal Soviet-Afghan war, which started in 1979, turned into a decade-long quagmire that ultimately contributed to the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.
Curated history
Still, the rambling lectures that Putin frequently delivers to foreign guests and leaders, particularly Europeans, are always more curated.

His often sermon-like discussions tend to emphasize the defeat of invaders such as Napoleon and Hitler. Putin has also celebrated Czar Peter the Great who captured the territory that now makes up modern-day Estonia and St. Petersburg.
"Putin scours the historical landscape for legitimacy," said Maikinkov.
"One way to gain legitimacy is to create and sustain the narrative of victory and military success. That's why this narrative [of Russia's invincibility] is powerful and why it sticks."
European divisions
In recent days, Europe has been divided over engaging with Putin.

Finland's President Alexander Stubb took the lead and called Russia's leader last week — the first direct European outreach in years. The move was met with heavy criticism in many European capitals including those of Sweden and Italy, but Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Fredrickson was especially vocal, expressing deep skepticism over the overture.
Galeotti says the divisions revert back to a core disagreement over whether its possible to inflict an Afghanistan-style collapse on Putin that fundamentally changes the power dynamics of Europe.
"Putin is trying to inject himself into the debate, more or less saying, 'You can be serious [about negotiating] or you cannot be serious, it's your choice.'"
Municipal employees work at the site of private houses which were damaged during a Russian drone strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Odesa, Ukraine November 2, 2026. (Nina Liashonok/Reuters)

In recent weeks, the Trump administration has tried to incentivize Putin into a ceasefire, including by waiving sanctions on diesel exports. The Wall Street Journal has also reported some of his officials are trying to convince Europe to start buying Russian natural gas again.

So far, despite Trump's overtures, European nations have expressed little to no interest in re-establishing commercial ties with Russia before there's an end to the war. Nor are there any indications that restoring commercial ties could entice Putin to stop fighting.

Indeed, Maikinkov — the University of Swansea analyst — believes the likelihood the war will end with a peace agreement is remote and a "frozen conflict" akin to the situation on the Korean peninsula, is more likely.
North and South Korea are still technically at war and their border is one of the most heavily fortified and volatile places on the planet.

"At the end of the day, [it] may resemble something like the situation in Korea where we have a robust successful democracy backed by the West, and perhaps part of Ukraine that is under the Russian sphere of influence."
This is how residents of the besieged town of Oleshky stayed alive

While Zelenskyy has hinted he could live with such an outcome, Putin has insisted all of his maximalist demands must be met — including that Ukraine's army must leave the remaining parts of Donbas that it holds, and turn the territory over to Russia.

However, the area which includes the city of Kramatorsk, is arguably the most heavily defended part of the front. Known as the "fortress belt", if it falls into Russian hands, Ukrainians fear Putin's military would have an open path to capture Kyiv and other other Ukrainian cities.
The Donbas issue "is still an absolute block," said Galeotti.

items: Russia, Ukraine begin ceasefire in city of Oleshky as deadly strikes continue elsewhere
Trump's increasing support for Russia carries existential danger for Canada
Ukraine says its military did not violate Starlink terms, disputing Elon Musk claim

blocks.text: It is a reality that leaves other seasoned observers warning against false optimism.
"I struggle to imagine any scenario in which any Ukrainian leadership would agree to Putin's terms for ending the conflict,' wrote renowned Russia analyst Tatiana Stanovaya.
Instead, she predicts more dangerous geopolitical behaviour from Putin as the economic costs of the war on Russia escalate and the country's elites fight among themselves for survival.
She concludes with a bleak warning.
"I believe we should prepare for the worst," she said, suggesting there could more hybrid attacks or other Russian aggression.
"What appears to be a red line today may become the new normal tomorrow," she said, meaning potentially dangerous confrontations with European countries could become far more common.

Which is exactly why the Kremlin's projection of "battlefield invincibility" matters and why Russia's leader is heavily leaning into the narrative now — to shock exhausted Ukrainians and its Western allies into a state of resignation.

articles.title: Ottawa wants us all to have emergency supplies for 3 days. The good news is, that number hasn't changed
articles.summary: Public Safety Canada is maintaining its longstanding advice for Canadians to be prepared to go at least three days without running water or electricity, following recent calls in the U.K. and other…

image.caption: An ice storm knocked out power to more than a million residents in Quebec and Ontario in April 2023. Ottawa has reiterated its advice that everyone be prepared to go a minimum of 72 hours without power or water in case of an emergency. (Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Public Safety Canada is maintaining its longstanding advice for Canadians to be prepared to go at least three days without running water or electricity, following recent calls in the U.K. and other countries for their residents to do the same.
Similar calls in Europe and Japan have prompted online speculation

"Canadians have been encouraged for many years to ... be ready to take care of themselves and their households for a minimum of 72 hours during an emergency," Zarah Malik, a spokesperson for Public Safety Canada, said in a statement to CBC News.

Some U.K. retailers reported spikes in sales of essential goods after London launched its Be Ready campaign on Oct. 22. Officials warned that cyberattacks and severe weather could disrupt essential services, and encouraged residents to stockpile 72 hours of supplies including non-perishable food and bottled water.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said unexpected events "seem to becoming more common" and everyone should have "those supplies in the house."
Officials in Normandy, France, posted on social media on Oct. 27 that residents should prepare a bag containing essentials for 72 hours. "Don't wait for the emergency: prepare now!" the post reads.

And Japan launched a new national agency focused on disaster management on Monday which, as one piece of a much broader plan focused largely on earthquake preparedness, urged residents to evaluate their evacuation procedures and stock up on water and portable toilets for at least three days.
There is no indication that any of those announcements were co-ordinated or are connected to a particular expected event, but the timing has set off some speculation online.
Prep for one week: expert
Suzanne Bernier, faculty member of the Disaster Recovery Institute of Canada, says governments have been putting out the same messaging for at least three decades but it's a good time for an update.

She says it makes sense that the messaging is becoming more prominent, as natural and human-caused disasters are increasing, people are living in areas that used to be unpopulated and cyberattacks are becoming common.

A hacking attack on European supermarkets spread across the continent on Monday, hitting fridges and freezers from Sweden to Belgium and forcing stores to throw away food, echoing a similar ‌attack in France last month.
"We're just seeing that it doesn't really matter where we are, everywhere is a target. But particularly of concern is the cyberattacks on critical infrastructure," said Bernier.
"It's just a matter of time before everybody is either indirectly or directly affected by a cyberattack."
She encourages Canadians to aim for at least seven days' worth of supplies.
Getting prepped to deal with emergencies

"We need to really be preparing people for ... potentially not being able to have anybody respond to you or save your family within that first week," she said, adding people should also have a go-bag ready in case of evacuation.
Public Safety Canada says 72 hours is a minimum recommendation and notes it could take more time for some areas to restore basic services, or for emergency workers to reach all affected residents.
The government agency gives more detailed preparedness advice on its website.

Europe has generally ramped up its emergency preparedness messaging over the last two years. The European Commission's Preparedness Union Strategy, released in March 2025, warns of growing geopolitical tension and threats from natural disasters.

items: Another cyberattack on supermarket fridges sweeps Europe, leaving food spoiled
Canada's new national security strategy will shield economy, modernize military
U.K. opts against joining Canada-led defence bank, pledges co-operation

blocks.text: Scott Cameron, co-founder of Emergency Management Logistics Canada, says Canadians should also be paying more attention to emergency preparedness, given talk of national sovereignty and growing climate-related concerns, including recent mass evacuations from wildfires and floods.
Cameron says stockpiling for 72 hours is a good idea for personal preparedness, but more work needs to be done on a community level, like identifying local supply chains and resources.

"Where is our local, our community capacity and resilience, to move beyond 72 hours?" he said. "And what are we as Canadians all prepared to be able to help with, as opposed to being the recipients of aid?"
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kevin Maimann is a senior writer for CBC News based in Edmonton. He has covered a wide range of topics for publications including VICE, the Toronto Star, Xtra Magazine and the Edmonton Journal. You can reach Kevin by email at kevin.maimann@cbc.ca.
With files from Reuters and The Associated Press

articles.title: 24 hours in Antigua: Mark Carney's priorities at this year's Commonwealth Summit
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney's oft-stated determination to keep his government focused on what Canadians can control could be tested today, as he meets with leaders from the 55 other member countries…

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney and Diana Fox Carney arrive in St. John's, Antigua and Barbuda, ahead of the 28th Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, on Monday. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Prime Minister Mark Carney's oft-stated determination to keep his government focused on what Canadians can control could be tested today, as he meets with leaders from the 55 other member countries of the Commonwealth in Antigua.

As he boarded his flight with his wife Diana on Monday, Carney gestured as if he couldn't hear reporters yelling for clarification on where things stand following his conversation with U.S. President Donald Trump over the weekend.

Trade negotiations could return to a full boil, but for now they remain on a back burner while the White House focuses on the verdict about to be rendered by American voters in their midterm elections.

The future of the Canada-U.S. relationship hangs so heavy over the Carney government's agenda that it could be hard to focus on anything else. But this week's Commonwealth talks are the first in a series of multilateral summits this month where Canadian officials will pursue alternative partnerships in trade, security and diplomacy.
Here are five things to watch for:
1. Push to double intra-Commonwealth trade
The Commonwealth has three main priorities leading up to 2030: democratic resilience, economic resilience and environmental resilience.

On that first priority, ministers, including Foreign Minister Anita Anand, met Sunday to welcome the restoration of an elected government in Gabon, the central African country which had its membership partially suspended following a military coup in 2023.

But the main focus at this summit is trade partnerships: specifically the association's ambition to lower trade barriers and double trade between member countries by the time they meet for their next biennial summit.
That dovetails perfectly with the Carney government's attempt to pivot away from the U.S.

items: Canada's next budget to be unveiled this week amid U.S. trade war, economic uncertainty
Experts suggest Canada lock in gains with EU amid 'associate member' confusion

blocks.text: "I think people don't realize the economic clout of the Commonwealth. There's almost a trillion dollars of trade," said Arif Lalani, a former diplomat who served as a senior official the last time a Canadian prime minister attended the Commonwealth Summit, in 2022.

"There are studies which show that it's cheaper to do business between Commonwealth countries because we have the same practices, same language, generally the same set of regulations. So it's definitely a place to pursue the economic diversification agenda," Lalani said.
Carney should see Commonwealth as trade opportunity: secretary-general
His fear, however, is that the Commonwealth's "relevance is growing faster than its capacity to deliver."
Leaders need to get more outcome-oriented on trade, he said. He agrees with Carney's efforts to expand this focus to defence and security co-operation too.

At a time when conflicts over choke points like the Strait of Hormuz are restricting global trade, "Commonwealth countries have a lot of coastline, they have strong navies, and so I think there's something that can be done to increase maritime co-operation," Lalani said.
2. Evolving Caribbean relationships
This is Carney's first trip to the Caribbean as prime minister.

That diplomatic deficiency will be addressed this morning in a bilateral meeting with this year's Commonwealth host, Antigua and Barbuda's Prime Minister Gaston Browne, followed by a working breakfast Canada is hosting for all the Caribbean leaders attending this year's summit.
While not a complete gathering of CARICOM leaders, officials briefed reporters that this breakfast is a chance to discuss trade and investment, climate action and regional security.
Prime Minister Mark Carney and Diana Fox Carney are met by a greeting party as they arrive in Antigua. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)
Vandana Kattar, who worked in the prime minister's office under former prime minister Justin Trudeau, says Carney's approach so far makes sense to her.

"Multilateralism is important to him," she said. Carney went after some of the bigger pieces of his puzzle first, she reckons — pursuing the "low-hanging fruit" of a closer relationship with Europe, attempting to resolve tariff tensions with China.

"Those are big pieces of the puzzle that he's been able to put together," she said. But he also needs to fit smaller pieces into that puzzle, like nurturing Canada's relationships in the Caribbean, "otherwise that doesn't complete the whole picture."
3. Climate finance commitments
"You can't go to the Caribbean countries and not talk of climate resiliency," Kattar said. "They're the ones impacted the most."

Canada's already contributed $4.65 million over three years to the Commonwealth's climate finance access hub to help small island states. It's also made a bigger $13-billion commitment to support all developing countries adapt to the consequences of climate change — like stronger and more frequent hurricanes — over the next five years.

items: Netherlands must cut CO2 to protect Caribbean island of Bonaire, court rules
Small island nations want largest emitters to pay for catastrophic effects of climate change

blocks.text: Canada hopes to amplify the voices of smaller Commonwealth partners on climate issues, officials told reporters prior to the trip.

"That's what actually builds the trust, and that's what ensures that Canada is seen as a reliable and a trustworthy partner that actually listens to the concerns of their partners and [is] not just forcing their own agenda onto them," said Climate Action Network's Soomin Han.

Han believes conversations on climate financing between big and small Commonwealth partners might be more productive than at United Nations climate conferences, where a few large countries can block progress.
"Countries should not have to take out more debt simply to survive a crisis they contributed comparatively little to creating," she said.

items: Climate change past the point of no return, UN says, as worst impacts are now unavoidable

blocks.text: 4. Tensions, debate on reparations

While the Commonwealth has 56 members, King Charles is the head of state in only 15 of them. Half of those are Caribbean countries, and for the week leading up to this summit, he's been touring the region, amid ongoing political pressure for the Crown and the government of the United Kingdom to apologize for its historical role profiting off the slave trade in British colonies.
So far, the King has acknowledged "the great suffering and injustices of the past in these islands and beyond," but he has not apologized.

Canadian officials briefing reporters prior to the trip said Canada acknowledges the generational and lasting impact of slavery, and supports "open and respectful dialogue" on reparations, but noted there are a "diversity" of perspectives on reparatory justice among Commonwealth members.
King Charles will confront 'shameful aspects' of Britain's role in slavery

Nicholas Marcus Thompson, an advocate for reparations for Canada's Black communities, says the current U.K. government's opposition to negotiating reparations for slavery is "simply a non-starter" for Caribbean nations.

"Reparations is not giving away a freebie. It's repaying what you took, right? Wealth extracted from enslaved Africans built businesses, financial institutions, universities," said Thompson, who is also the president and CEO of the Black Class Action Secretariat.
"It would have been billions of dollars in today's currency."
5. The Trump factor

Former diplomat Lalani said he believes Canada is heading into this summit with more credibility than it's had in the past, thanks to the "provocative vision" Carney laid out in his speech on middle powers at the World Economic Forum in Davos last winter.

Carney's conversations today won't be limited to people he's close to, like Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. It's also a chance to talk to leaders with whom he doesn't have full agreement — without being overshadowed by superpowers like the U.S. or China.
"Canada can have a discussion with other countries without the baggage of having the United States at the table," he said.
"The biggest destabilizing power in the world right now is the United States. … That requires a candid discussion."

articles.title: Ryan Wedding's $40M US motorbike collection to go up for auction
articles.summary: A $40 million US collection of rare and high-performance motorcycles seized from Canadian alleged drug lord Ryan Wedding will go up for auction next week in Mexico. The 61 bikes include models from…

image.caption: The FBI released pictures of motorcycles seized by Mexican law enforcement during raids targeting Ryan Wedding. On the right, Wedding is seen after being flown from Mexico to an airport in Ontario, Calif., following his arrest in January 2026. (FBI)

blocks.text: World·New

A $40 million US collection of rare and high-performance motorcycles seized from Canadian alleged drug lord Ryan Wedding will go up for auction next week in Mexico. The 61 bikes include models from Ducati, Honda, Kawasaki, MV Agusta, Suzuki and Yamaha. Some were previously used in professional racing, according to the FBI.
Bikes seized in December 2025 amid international manhunt for Canadian former Olympic snowboarder
A $40-million US collection of rare and high-performance motorcycles seized from Canadian alleged drug lord Ryan Wedding will go up for auction next week in Mexico.
The 61 bikes include models from Ducati, Honda, Kawasaki, MV Agusta, Suzuki and Yamaha. Some were previously used in professional racing, according to the FBI.
The motorcycles were uncovered during raids in the Mexican capital and nearby Mexico state last December at addresses linked to Wedding, who was then one of the FBI's most wanted fugitives.
The former Team Canada Olympic snowboarder was arrested in Mexico City the following month and flown to the U.S., where he remains in custody.

items: Canadian fugitive Ryan Wedding arrested after a decade on the run

blocks.text: The Mexican public agency known as INDEP — translated as the institute to return stolen assets to the people — shared pictures of the motorcycles on its website and social media accounts ahead of next week's auction.
A red Ducati motorcycle — set to be auctioned off — was among those seized in raids on properties linked to Ryan Wedding in Mexico last December. (INDEP)
Proceeds from the agency's auctions typically go to fund social services.

INDEP didn't name Wedding, but announced the motorcycles were now subject to forfeiture after they were seized by law enforcement last December. Some of the models pictured on the auction site match those seen in images previously shared by the FBI.
Mexican media also reported the link to Wedding.

Following last year's raids, the FBI said in a social media post the "large number" of motorcycles seized were believed to be owned by Wedding, with an estimated total value of about $40 million US. The U.S. agency said the operation was the result of co-operation with Mexican authorities, the RCMP and the Los Angeles Police Department.

Mexican authorities said more than 60 motorcycles, as well as medals, artwork and drugs were seized in a series of raids in December 2025. The FBI later said the operation targeted Ryan Wedding, then considered a most-wanted fugitive. (Mexican government)
'Amazing collection'

Racing enthusiasts who examined pictures of the seized bikes last year said some were identical to those used in Grand Prix road races, including a Ducati driven by Spanish world champion Marc Márquez.
The FBI previously confirmed to CBC News some of the models had been used in professional racing.
"There are maybe 10 or 15 of them that are literally the two-wheeled equivalent of Formula 1 cars," said Simon Patterson, a North Ireland-based journalist who covers MotoGP, told CBC News.
"All in all, [this is] just an absolutely amazing collection of machines that Wedding has somehow been able to amass."
The FBI said the December raids resulted in the seizure of a 'large number' of motorcycles. (FBI)
The U.S. Treasury Department has said Wedding laundered his vast wealth through an "extensive transatlantic network" involving associates, businesses and luxury assets including cars and motorcycles.

The FBI in Florida also seized an ultra-rare 2002 Mercedes-Benz CLK-GTR Roadster, said to be worth $13 million US. The silver two-seater had been purchased by Toronto-area jeweller Rolan Sokolovski — described by U.S. authorities as one of Wedding's two chief money launderers.
Big-ticket assets seized by U.S. federal law enforcement are also often auctioned off, but it's unclear what will happen to the Mercedes.
An FBI spokesperson declined to comment on Monday when CBC News asked whether more Wedding-linked items would be sold off.
Canadian Ryan Wedding was arrested in Mexico in January 2026 and flown to California to stand trial. (U.S. Embassy in Mexico, FBI Los Angeles/X)
Bids start at $1,600

As for the motorcycles, INDEP said in a news release the models going up for auction range from the 1960s to the 2020s, with starting bids going from roughly to $1,600 to $192,000 Cdn., depending on the bike.
Bidders must register by Nov. 10. The live auction is set to begin the following morning.
The raids last December also netted other items, including Canadian snowboarding medals, artwork and two vehicles, authorities said at the time.

items: Ryan Wedding ally 'Tupac,' who allegedly offered cosmetic surgery to locate murder target, requests bail

blocks.text: Next week's auction, set to be held at a banquet hall in the Mexican capital, will feature 620 lots in total, including armoured vehicles, boats and aircraft. It's unclear whether any of the other goods may be connected to the Canadian.

U.S. authorities have said Wedding — also known as "El Jefe" (The Boss) — fled to Mexico around 2015, when the RCMP in Montreal sought his arrest. The Thunder Bay, Ont., native then allegedly expanded his purported cartel-linked drug-smuggling operation to a $1-billion US empire.
Motorcycles seized from Ryan Wedding used for pro racing: FBI
Wedding has pleaded not guilty to charges related to drug trafficking, money laundering and murder.
The 45-year-old is set to stand trial in Los Angeles next year.
Prosecutors have linked Wedding's purported criminal network to multiple killings, including the mistaken-identity shooting of a family in Caledon, Ont.
CBC News senior reporter Thomas Daigle has covered the case of Ryan Wedding extensively. He can be reached by email at thomas.daigle@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Millions of fish died at an Ontario nuclear plant in 2025. Now its operator faces federal charges
articles.summary: Bruce Power, the private company that operates the Bruce Nuclear Generating Station, faces two federal Fisheries Act charges after millions of Lake Huron fish died over a period of two months in 2025.

image.caption: Gizzard shad gather beneath the ice in the warmer waters of Lake Huron by the millions near Bruce Nuclear Generating Station. The cold-sensitve fish seek out warm water refuges in winter, including the thermal discharge from the plant. (Zack Melnick/Inspired Planet Productions)

blocks.text: Canada·New

Bruce Power, the private company that operates the Bruce Nuclear Generating Station, faces two federal Fisheries Act charges after millions of Lake Huron fish died over a period of two months in 2025.
Fisheries and Oceans Canada said Bruce Power exceeded annual fish kill limit by 200 times
The private company that operates the Bruce Nuclear Generating Station faces two federal Fisheries Act charges after millions of fish died in the plant's cooling water intake system in 2025.
The charges against Bruce Power come after a CBC News investigation revealed publicly, for the first time, the extraordinary scale of what happened.

An estimated 8.1 million gizzard shad massed near the power plant during a sudden cold snap on Feb. 13, 2025, according to an internal report from Bruce Power. The small, cold-sensitive fish were drawn to the warm water discharged into Lake Huron near Tiverton, Ont., by the nuclear power plant over a two-month period, between February and March of 2025.

The fish subsequently became trapped and died against the plant's intake screens in such large numbers that one reactor had to be shut down and another had to reduce power, straining the province's electrical grid during a prolonged winter cold spell.
The company's own findings said the massive fish kill was the result of an "organizational failure" to adapt to changing environmental conditions caused by climate change.
Dead gizzard shad lie along the Thames River in 2021. The same temperature-sensitive species washed ashore along Lake Huron for days during the 2025 fish kill at Bruce Power. (Colin Butler/CBC)
Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO) estimates between 3.3 and 4.3 million fish died between February and March of 2025 — more than 200 times Bruce Power's annual authorized limit by weight.

Gizzard shad carcasses washed ashore in nearby communities for days, while Bruce Power used a crane to scoop millions of dead fish from the plant's cooling water channels before hauling them to a landfill, provincial records showed.

Under the federal Fisheries Act, Bruce Power was charged last month with causing the death of fish through non-fishing industrial operations and violating the conditions of its environmental permit, which limits the company to 6,600 kilograms of dead fish annually.

"As this matter is before the courts, we cannot comment on how we intend to plead or provide additional commentary relating to the charges," Megan Adams, Bruce Power's director of corporate communications, wrote in an email.
The company will appear in Ontario provincial court on Nov. 24.
Fines pay for environmental restoration

In a recent news release, Bruce Power said it was transparent with regulators, including DFO and the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission, as well as nearby First Nations and municipalities about the fish kill.
An aerial image of the Bruce Power site located near Tiverton, Ont. (Submitted by Chad Richards)

Still, prosecutors don't have to prove the company meant to kill fish in order to establish an offence, according to Theresa McClenaghan, a lawyer and the executive director of the Canadian Environmental Law Association (CELA).
"The courts consider Fisheries Act offences to be serious offences," she said.
Fines for a first offence can range from a few thousand dollars to $200,000, she said, and are intended to deter violations and express the court's condemnation.
When a fine is issued by the court, the money goes into the federal Environmental Damages Fund to support conservation, habitat protection or restoration, McClenaghan said.
The court can also recommend directing the money to a particular organization or project, including an Indigenous nation or for environmental research.
'A giant fish trap'

Since the fish kill, Bruce Power has spent more than $10 million on mitigation measures, including nets to keep fish out, acoustic and strobe-light deterrants, sonar, cameras and artificial intelligence to monitor fish movements, along with expanded lake research.
Rare 'fish city' footage reveals hidden world

Ryan Lauzon, a fisheries biologist who advises Saugeen Ojibway Nation, whose traditional territory includes the nuclear plant, said during a recent onsite visit last year he saw gaps in the mitigation measures.

"I did see fish that were swimming right up to that sound and acoustic deterrent system. There was gaps in the nets that were being used to exclude the fish. They ended up having to take the net out because they were so full of algae and dead fish."

Invasive zebra and quagga mussels have depleted the plankton that supports Lake Huron's food web, Lauzon said, leaving less food for other species and making the loss of millions of gizzard shad concerning. They are a prey species for trout, pike and walleye.

Lauzon, who has written a paper on the fish kill, said smaller die-offs happened at the plant in 1977 and 2023. He said while Bruce Power may have spent millions on mitigation measures, they don't address the warm-water discharge that attracts the fish in the first place.

items: Rare footage reveals 'fish city' near an Ontario nuclear plant on Lake Huron
Lake Huron's 'fish city' is a sign of trouble at nuclear plant, says Ontario First Nation

blocks.text: "Unfortunately, the plant acts as a giant fish trap," he said. "Until we establish the effectiveness of mitigation measures and try to deal with this attractant issue, I still think there's real danger."

The cooling systems that draw those fish also face growing challenges as the climate changes, said McClenaghan, who noted the incident may point to a need to rethink how nuclear plants are cooled in a changing climate.
"On the list of possibilities are cooling towers or cooling loops as opposed to what happens right now," she said. "The lakes are acting as a heat sink."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Colin Butler is based in London, Ont., where he reports for Ontario and national audiences. He covers investigative, science, public policy and government accountability with a particular interest in using public records to uncover hidden stories.

articles.title: PNP debunks viral photo of Dela Rosa at Digos cemetery as 'old'
articles.summary: Police say the Digos cemetery image was taken in 2023.

blocks.text: November 3, 2026 | 4:51pm
Sen. Bato dela Rosa poses for a photo with unidentified individuals in this 2023 file photo that recirculated on social media on Nov. 1, 2026.
Redacted social media image

MANILA, Philippines — A viral photo supposedly showing fugitive senator Bato dela Rosa at a cemetery in Digos City was taken in 2023 and does not show a recent public appearance, the Philippine National Police said.
"Wala pong katotohanan na nagpakita siya," PNP spokesperson Col. Allen Rae Co said Tuesday, November 3. ("It is not true that he surfaced.")
Co said the PNP's technical team verified that the photo was old, while the original uploader also clarified that it had been taken three years ago.
He also warned those who deliberately share misleading information. "For them, if this was meant to mislead, there will be possible consequences," Co said.
The PNP continues to receive tips through hotlines set up for information on Dela Rosa's whereabouts as he remains at large, Co added.
Police are validating the information but have declined to disclose whether any patterns have emerged.
"Mayroon po tayong tinatawag na 'operations secrecy' ... Tama po 'yong sinasabi ni Sen. Lacson na secrecy is key in our operations," Co said.
("We have what we call 'operations secrecy' ... Sen. Lacson is right that secrecy is key in our operations.")
Manhunt continues. The viral photo circulated days after the expiration of a one-week deadline for Dela Rosa to surrender.
Authorities have since intensified the manhunt and organized tracker teams across the country. A P50-million reward has also been offered for information leading to his arrest.
The International Criminal Court issued a warrant for Dela Rosa in November 2025 that was unsealed in May 2026.

The ICC prosecutors allege that Dela Rosa, who served as PNP chief during the administration of former President Rodrigo Duterte, bears criminal responsibility for the alleged crime against humanity of murder in connection with the government's anti-drug campaign.
The ICC says the alleged crimes covered by the warrant occurred from July 2016 to April 2018 and involved at least 32 killings.

articles.title: US midterm elections 2026 live: Americans go to the polls in referendum on Trump’s agenda
articles.summary: Polls open across the US where key Senate and House races will decide which party controls Congress for remainder of Donald Trump’s second term

blocks.text: Key events

items: 45s agoWhat are the races to watch in the US midterm elections?
22m agoAmericans vote in midterms that will determine control of Congress and Trump’s agenda

blocks.text: What are the races to watch in the US midterm elections?

blocks.caption: David Smith

blocks.text: David Smith
in Washington

Donald Trump will still be US president on the morning of 4 November. But he could be facing a very different political landscape, depending on the results of the midterm elections held the previous day.

As the name implies, midterm elections fall nearly halfway through a president’s term. They are often a telling referendum on the sitting president’s performance, something Trump is actively encouraging by telling voters “pretend I’m on the ballot”. In this case, voters will decide whether Trump’s Republican party can retain its grip on Congress.

Democrats are hoping to capitalise on growing discontent with Trump to seize control of the US House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate. Republicans are fighting to preserve their congressional majorities and prevent a fresh period of legislative paralysis and investigations into the White House.

Several Senate contests have emerged as key battlegrounds. In Michigan, progressive Abdul El-Sayed is seeking to hold an open seat for Democrats against Republican Mike Rogers, who received a last-minute endorsement from Democrat Haley Stevens. In Georgia, Jon Ossoff, a Democratic senator, enjoys a healthy poll lead over Republican challenger Mike Collins.

blocks.caption: In Michigan, Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed has been locked in a heated Senate race against Republican ‌Mike Rogers. Photograph: Zach D Roberts/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: In Maine, a state won by Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024, Susan Collins, the Republican senator, is defending her seat against Democrat Troy Jackson. Ohio offers another major test, with Democrat Sherrod Brown seeking to return to the Senate against Republican Jon Husted.

Texas has become especially closely watched. Democrat James Talarico is taking on Republican Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general. Republicans have spent about $210m to help the scandal-plagued Paxton. No Democrat has won a statewide election in Texas since 1994. Trump won Texas by nearly 14 points in 2024.

blocks.caption: James Talarico speaks to supporters during a rally at the University of Texas on 23 October 2026 in Austin. Photograph: Sergio Flores/Getty Images

blocks.text: In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola’s Senate race against Republican incumbent Dan S Sullivan sparked controversy after Republicans accused the candidate of planting a second Dan Sullivan to confuse voters. A judge dismissed a Trump-backed lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s Senate race results if Dan Sullivan loses.

Other contests in Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina and New Hampshire could help determine which party controls the chamber (if there is a 50-50 split, JD Vance, the vice-president, a Republican, wields the tiebreaker vote). Latest polls show Democrats ahead in Maine, North Carolina and Kansas, and competitive in Ohio. Also on the map this year are South Carolina and Mississippi, two reliably Republican states that have seen aggressive Democratic challenges this year.
Americans vote in midterms that will determine control of Congress and Trump’s agenda

It’s Tuesday 3 November, which means that after months of campaigning, debate and analysis, the critical US midterm elections that will take the political temperature of the nation halfway through Donald Trump’s second term – and determine the trajectory of the remainder of his presidency – are finally upon us. Americans, who have already voted early in record numbers, will decide the balance of power in Congress and, therefore, Trump’s ability to advance his agenda for the next two years.

With the US president almost unprecedentedly unpopular, Democrats are aiming for what would be stunning victories in seats where, for decades, turning blue would have been unthinkable. Trump is not on the ballot, but this election is very much a referendum on the direction of the country under his Republican party.

Trump’s agenda has thrown the US into a deeply unpopular – and expensive – war alongside Israel against Iran, sparking a global energy crisis and regional conflict that remains unresolved. The war has exacerbated inflation and the cost-of-living crisis, which had already been worsened by Trump’s chaotic tariff policies. The un-affordability of basic living costs from groceries and gas to childcare, housing and healthcare has been a defining issue of this election, with concerns over the economy turning even deeply conservative seats competitive.

blocks.caption: The Republicans hold power in the White House and both chambers of Congress: the House of Representatives and the Senate, but their majority is thin and at risk of erosion. Photograph: Bonnie Cash/UPI/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The second Trump administration has also overseen violent surges of federal immigration enforcement across Democrat-led cities, deeply divisive operations that killed two Americans earlier this year. The administration has pursued an aggressive and cruel mass deportation policy, slashed federal government agencies and Medicaid funding, supported the restriction of abortion rights in many states, and expanded presidential power in unprecedented ways.

And now, after months of gerrymandering, efforts to curtail voting rights, and scaremongering over election integrity as Republicans cling to power, also looming over this election is the question of whether Trump and his allies will accept the results.
This will be a defining moment for American democracy, so stick with us as we bring you all the latest news, analyses and commentary as it all unfolds.

articles.title: Zelenskyy to make unexpected visit to Berlin for talks with Merz – Europe live
articles.summary:
Merz said the German push to increase defence spending was triggered by Zelenskyy and Trump’s meeting last year

Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy is set to make an unexpected…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 13m agoMorning opening: Zelenskyy to make unexpected visit to Berlin for talks with Merz

blocks.text: Morning opening: Zelenskyy to make unexpected visit to Berlin for talks with Merz

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa

Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy is set to make an unexpected visit to Berlin for talks with German chancellor Friedrich Merz ahead of next week’s trilateral talks with Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi.

blocks.caption: German chancellor Friedrich Merz welcomes Ukraine's president Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Berlin, Germany in April. Photograph: Ebrahim Noroozi/AP

blocks.text: The rumours about Zelenskyy’s potential visit started swirling last night, with Merz confirming the visit during an industry speech this morning. The Ukrainian president’s trips are usually kept secret until the last moment for security reasons.
Recalling the infamous showdown between Zelenskyy and Trump at the White House last year, Merz said:
“He’ll be here ‌with me just after midday, and things will be a bit different then.”
In his speech, Merz said the German push to rapidly increase its defence spending last year was triggered by the scenes in the Oval Office.
“What we experienced last year … led me to conclude that we must ensure, on our own, that we are capable of defending ourselves in Europe,” he said.
He added that this was not meant to question Nato, but strengthen it. “We are making Nato more European so it can remain transatlantic,” he said.
Elsewhere, we are expecting updates from Sweden, with a second parliamentary vote on the new government, which is expected to fail once again (51 days on from elections).

We should also get some lines from Spain, where transport minister Óscar Puente is will present new ideas on reforming high-speed rail after last week’s tragic crash in Toledo before facing a parliamentary committee.
We are also likely to see developments in Poland after last weekend’s protests over the country’s constitutional tribunal, and in Belgium amid continuing uncertainty about Bart De Wever’s government.
Lots for us to cover.
It’s Tuesday, 3 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: Australia seeks to change visa deal with UK after influx of Britons
articles.summary:
Australia says easing of rules has led to surge in British visitor numbers, putting pressure on local workforce

The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has told Andy Burnham he is…

blocks.text: The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has told Andy Burnham he is looking at changing rules for British backpackers in Australia, after an increase in the number of travellers visiting popular hotspots such as Sydney.

Albanese, who met Burnham on Monday evening at the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) in the Caribbean, told reporters he wanted to discuss changing the agreement between the UK and Australia that removes a regional work requirement for British travellers.

Backpackers had previously been required to do about three months of regional work as part of visa conditions to help with the country’s work shortages in some occupations. But under the free trade agreement signed under Boris Johnson, Britons do not have to undertake the rural work that many other nationalities do as a condition of their visas. It also extended the maximum period for the visa to three years and the age limit to 35.

The Australian government has said the changes have led to traveller numbers more than doubling, from 40,000 two years ago to 87,000 last year, the majority concentrated in Sydney and beachside suburbs. The easing of visa restrictions also applies to Australians coming to the UK but fewer than 10,000 came last year.

Albanese told the Australian parliament that the numbers of Britons arriving to a small destination was putting pressure on the local workforce. “They are staying at Bondi Beach or Coogee or around particularly the capital cities and working in hospitality there. That’s placing enormous pressure because it’s distorting the labour market in these areas as well,” he said.
Burnham confirmed to reporters that he was meeting Albanese but declined to comment on any potential changes, saying “we’ll see” when asked if it would be on the agenda.
A Downing Street spokesperson said there had been discussions about the visas at a bilateral between the two leaders in Antigua at the summit but stopped short of making any commitments.

“The leaders discussed the increasingly uncertain global landscape and agreed that strong partnerships between close allies like the UK and Australia are more important than ever,” a readout of the meeting said.

“Turning to the close relationship between the UK and Australia, the leaders underlined the importance of ensuring opportunities for young people both at home and abroad. On broader migration, the prime minister updated on the new rules being rolled out for migrants looking to settle in the UK, and the leaders discussed how best to drive down illegal migration.
“They both looked forward to continuing their discussions during Chogm and staying in close contact.”

articles.title: Objection of VP Sara's lawyers vs offer of evidence not based on truth - Ridon
articles.summary: The objection made by Vice President Sara Duterte"s defense team on the House Prosecution"s offer of evidence in relation to her impeachment trial is not based on the truth, said House prosecution…

blocks.text: Published November 3, 2026 4:36pm

The objection made by Vice President Sara Duterte’s defense team on the House Prosecution’s offer of evidence in relation to her impeachment trial is not based on the truth, said House prosecution team member Representative Terry Ridon on Tuesday.
According to GMA News’ Bea Pinlac, Ridon said they already expected the defense lawyers to object to all pieces of evidence they submitted before the Senate impeachment court.

“Expected na po namin’yung pag-object ng depensa, but that is an objection that is not based on truth, it is not based on what we had seen in the last couple of weeks. So tignan natin kung ano ‘yung gagawin nilang paglalatag ng ebidensya at depensa nila,” he told reporters.

(We already expected the defense to object, but that is an objection that is not based on truth—it is not based on what we have seen in the last couple of weeks. So let's see how they will present their evidence and defense.)

The formal offer includes all documentary evidence and witness testimonies presented by the prosecution in support of Article 2 of the impeachment complaint, which alleges that Duterte accumulated unexplained wealth through assets not declared in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN).

Ridon said Duterte’s defense lawyers actually objected to all the evidence they submitted including SALNs, bank records, insurance records, records from the Bureau of Internal Revenue and the Anti-Money Laundering Council, among others.
“The defense has objected, we will leave it to the Senate impeachment court to make a determination on all the pieces of evidence,” he said.
In their response to the Prosecution’s offer of evidence, the Defense said the evidence submitted is the result of an "impermissible fishing expedition and, thus, inadmissible as evidence."
For his part, Ridon said the House prosecutors questioned the defense team’s “blanket objection.”
“Medyo nakakatawa na meron po silang blanket objection sa lahat ng piraso ng ebidensya na isinumite ng prosekusyon…That the defense is defenseless is probably a good description of it,” he said.
(It is somewhat laughable that they have a blanket objection to every single piece of evidence submitted by the prosecution… That the defense is defenseless is probably a good description of it.)
GMA News has reached out to the defense team for a comment. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: NCR chief prosecutors endorse Zalameda for chief justice
articles.summary: Zalameda is among five justices shortlisted by the JBC to succeed Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo, who retires November 6.

blocks.text: November 3, 2026 | 4:35pm
Supreme Court Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda on the sidelines of an Integrated Bar of the Philippines in Roxas City in August 2023.
SC PIO
MANILA, Philippines — Metro Manila's chief prosecutors have endorsed Supreme Court Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda to become the country's next chief justice.

In a resolution unanimously adopted by its members and trustees, the NCR Chief Prosecutors Association Inc. expressed its full support for Zalameda, citing his legal background, leadership and record in public service.

"WHEREAS, the Supreme Court Chief Justice, as the highest judicial officer, must possess outstanding legal credentials with exceptional moral, administrative and leadership traits," the association said.
The group then declared its sole endorsement of Zalameda for the post.

"RESOLVED, that the Association shall give its full support and solely endorse Supreme Court Associate Justice Rodil V. Zalameda as Supreme Court Chief Justice vice Hon. Alexander G. Gesmundo," the resolution read.
Gesmundo is set to retire on November 6 upon reaching the mandatory retirement age of 70.

The Association of Retired Regional Trial Court Judges of the Philippines, meanwhile, has endorsed Associate Justice Jose Midas Marquez for chief justice. The group cited his experience as court administrator and his work with judges and court personnel.
The Judicial and Bar Council submitted its shortlist for chief justice to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on October 29.
Aside from Zalameda and Marquez, the shortlist includes Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen and Associate Justices Alfredo Benjamin Caguioa and Japar Dimaampao.
Under the Constitution, the vacancy in the Supreme Court must be filled within 90 days from the time it occurs.

articles.title: Major Queensland hospital to close pathology labs amid potential formaldehyde exposure investigation
articles.summary:
About 400 staff affected by closure at both Mater’s Brisbane and Springfield hospitals, with financial sustainability of pathology business a factor

  • Get our

blocks.text: In-house pathology services at one of Queensland’s biggest hospitals will permanently close amid an investigation into potential formaldehyde exposure and continual financial strain.
The closure, which affects 400 staff across Mater’s Brisbane and Springfield hospitals, includes the lab which handles foetus and newborn tissue and cell testing for unexpected deaths.
This Brisbane facility was closed with short notice on 24 September due safety concerns over potential formalin exposure.

Formalin is a liquid comprising water and formaldehyde and is considered a hazardous chemical, making it subject to strict workplace safety protocols. Exposure can cause eye, nose and respiratory irritation, trigger allergies, and is associated with increased risk of some cancers.
Mandatory ventilation standards and safe specimen handling protocols are used to manage exposure among laboratory staff.

Anatomical pathology laboratory staff at the Mater Brisbane were also required to wear protective respiratory equipment as a precaution. Wearing respiratory gear is not standard protocol for laboratories except in the cases of a formalin spill, or where there is concern levels might be above exposure standards.

Staff also wore personal exposure monitoring devices and, after 17 samples were taken on 21 September, an employee returned a result above workplace exposure standards, prompting the lab to be closed on 24 September with staff not told when it might reopen.
A Mater spokesperson said an investigation is ongoing into the abnormal result.

On 2 November, after questions from Guardian Australia about the closure, a Mater spokesperson said all pathology services at Mater’s Brisbane and Springfield hospitals will be outsourced through specialist providers, including Sullivan Nicolaides Pathology and Pathology Queensland.
This includes not only the anatomical pathology laboratory, but also all other pathology services at both hospitals, the spokesperson said.

An internal email sent to staff across the pathology departments on Tuesday, seen by Guardian Australia, said: “At the end of last month, we identified infrastructure and safety concerns within our anatomical pathology service and made the immediate decision to suspend that service.
“It has become clear there is no quick or simple solution.”
The spokesperson said that, while a number of controls were introduced to mitigate safety risks, significant long-term infrastructure changes and investment would be required to reopen the lab.

This work “cannot be considered in isolation from the broader sustainability of Mater’s pathology business”, the spokesperson said, adding that it was the overall review of all challenges facing pathology services that prompted the permanent closure and outsourcing.
“The pathology sector has changed significantly in recent years and is increasingly reliant on scale, specialist workforces, technology, infrastructure and logistics,” the spokesperson said.
“Mater’s current operating model is not sustainable over the longer term.”
after newsletter promotion
The decision will have no impact on the high-quality patient care, the spokesperson said, and will allow more resources to be directed to clinical care of patients.
Mater Brisbane is a not-for-profit major tertiary hospital jointly funded by Queensland Health and Mater Private Hospitals. The Springfield hospital is a public and private facility.
The internal email said staff had “lived with questions about the future of the service for some time”.
A Queensland Health spokesperson said Mater Health is responsible for decisions regarding its pathology services.

“While most services have transitioned to private pathology providers, Pathology Queensland has taken on a small increase in perinatal autopsies, which is being managed within existing capacity,” the spokesperson said.
“Queensland Health will continue to work with Mater to ensure patients have access to the pathology services they need.”

United Workers Union Queensland secretary, Fiona Scalon, said staff will be significantly affected if redeployment opportunities are not available, and said different employers operate under different enterprise agreements and conditions.
“This is not simply a change of employer,” she said. “It could mean workers losing a substantial part of their income and conditions, despite continuing to perform the same work.”

articles.title: No date yet on Pax Silica legal framework signing, says BCDA chief
articles.summary: The Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) said Tuesday there is is no specific date yet when the legal framework for the planned Pax Silica initiative will be signed, originally targeted…

blocks.text: Published November 3, 2026 4:08pm

The Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) said Tuesday there is is no specific date yet when the legal framework for the planned Pax Silica initiative will be signed, originally targeted this November —the same month that US President Donald Trump is in the Philippines for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit.
In a chance interview with reporters, BCDA president and CEO Joshua Bingcang said the legal framework for Pax Silica was already submitted to Malacañang.
Last month, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro announced that the BCDA has submitted to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. the legal framework for the Pax Silica.
The Pax Silica framework deal is targeted to be signed by November, the same month that Trump is in the Philippines.
Asked regarding the status of the framework’s signing this month, Bingcang said, “Nothing concrete, nothing is finalized.”
However, the BCDA chief said that the government is keen on pushing through with the Pax Silica initiative.
“We want this project to push through starting with the signing of an agreement,” Bingcan said.
EXPLAINER: What is Pax Silica and why are people worried?

Philippine officials are expected to include a clause that explicitly preserves sovereignty over projects in the Pax Silica initiative in New Clark City, stating that expatriates employed in the area will have no diplomatic immunity.

The initiative, announced in April, is a US-led effort to build a network of allied supply chains for critical technologies and minerals, which the Philippines will host in the New Clark City in Tarlac.

Officials have clarified that there will be no data centers included in the Pax Silica initiative, as its main objective is to process the country’s minerals and to make high-tech components for AI and semiconductors. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: DOLE opens '15/30' hotline for workers' labor concerns
articles.summary: The Department of Labor and Employment launched Hotline 15/30, a new 24/7 hotline for workers' concerns, including those related non-compliance with the agency's El Niño guidelines.

blocks.text: November 3, 2026 | 4:05pm

Workers are seen performing their duties at a construction site in Taguig on February 7, 2024. The labor department encourages workers to report non-compliance with El Nino advisories released late-October.
STAR / Ernie Penaredondo
MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Labor and Employment launched a round-the-clock hotline for labor and employment concerns on Tuesday, November 3.
Hotline 15/30 — named after workers' semi-monthly pay on the 15th and 30th — replaces the former 1349 service.
DOLE said issues that can be brought to the 1530 hotline include unpaid or delayed wages and benefits, illegal dismissal or termination issues and violations of labor standards, among others.
Employees can also flag workplace safety and health concerns through the hotline, including risks related to extreme heat amid a strong El Niño, according to the department.
Access to the 24/7 hotline is currently limited to PLDT subscribers, but Labor Secretary Francis Tolentino said the department is working to expand services.
DOLE said its 1530 hotline operators will refer the concerns they get to the appropriate DOLE regional or field offices.
Tolentino urged the public to refrain from making prank calls that would distract hotline operators from attending to legitimate concerns.

"Baka mabulunan 'yong linya. Baka 'yong tunay na concerns, lalo (na) 'yong mga riders natin sa El Niño (ay) mahirapang makatawag ... 'Yong mga seryosong mga pangangailangan, lalong lalo na sa workplace: kulang ang ventilation, walang patubig, hindi sumunod sa mga labor advisory tungkol sa El Niño," Tolentino said.

(The lines might get clogged. People with genuine concerns — especially our riders, given the El Niño situation — might find it difficult to get through... There are serious needs, particularly in the workplace: inadequate ventilation, a lack of water supply, and failure to comply with labor advisories regarding El Niño.)
Employers are also allowed to avail of assistance through the hotline, Tolentino added.

The department outlined several advisories in late October to address and manage heat stress during the El Niño period. Included in the advisories are heat index-based guidelines on work arrangements, as well as key protections for delivery riders.
The weather pattern is projected to peak in December 2026 and persist through the first half of 2027.

articles.title: US midterm election: How it works, why it's important and races to watch
articles.summary: US voters are electing a new Congress. The results will be decisive for the future of the United States, and a judgment on Donald Trump's second term as president.

image.caption: Can the Republicans hang on to their majority in Congress?Image: Blake Fagan/AFP

blocks.text: On November 3, United States citizens will vote in the midterm elections. These won't decide who gets to sit in the White House; instead, Americans will be voting on who they want to see in the Capitol.

Midterm elections are held every four years, at the exact halfway point between presidential elections. The people of the United States decide who will represent them in the two chambers of the US Congress, the House of Representatives and the Senate. Some states are also voting for their governor. These are the decisions on the ballot paper — but they are not the only thing voters will be taking into account.

J. Miles Coleman, an election analyst at the Center for Politics at the University of Virginia, explained before the last midterms that they were "often a referendum on the president and party currently in power." If the people are content, the party of the leader in the White House does better than if the people are predominantly dissatisfied. President Donald Trump's approval ratings are currently at a record low.

blocks.caption: President Donald Trump's approval ratings have sunk to an all-time low: More than 60% of Americans view him negativelyImage: Jacquelyn Martin/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Who are Americans electing in the midterms?

All the seats in the US House of Representatives are up for election. Its 435 members are elected by eligible voters across the country. Each member represents one electoral district. These are allocated based on population size. As a result, relatively large US states where few people live, such as Wyoming, have only one seat in the House of Representatives. New Jersey, a much smaller state by surface area but with a larger population, has 12. Representatives are elected for a two-year term of office.

US senators, on the other hand, are elected for a six-year term. The Senate, the other chamber of the US Congress, has 100 seats: two for each of the 50 US states, regardless of size. Around one third of these senatorial seats come up for election every two years. This year there are 35, meaning that not every state will be electing a senator in these midterms.

Separately, voters in 36 states will elect their governor, whose term of office is four years in most states. Many decisions in the US are taken at state level, on everything from abortion law to education and electoral procedure. It can therefore make a considerable difference to people's lives whether Democrats or Republicans are the ones making these decisions in their state.
Who currently has a majority in the US Congress?
At present, the Republicans, the party of President Trump, have a majority in both houses of Congress — but its margin is slim.

The House of Representatives currently has 218 Republican deputies, 214 Democrats, and one independent, who usually votes with the Republicans. Two seats are vacant. Observers think it likely that the Democrats will seize the majority in this chamber in the upcoming elections. "It would be a surprise if the Democrats don't at least take the House [of Representatives]," Coleman told the American broadcaster CBS at the end of October.

In the Senate there are currently 53 Republicans, 45 Democrats, and two independent senators who usually vote with the Democrats. When a vote in the Senate is deadlocked 50:50, the US vice president has the deciding vote. This means that currently, Trump's Vice President JD Vance would tip the scales if there were a tie in a Senate vote.

blocks.caption: Republicans and Democrats are vying for seats in the two chambers of the US CongressImage: Graeme Sloan/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Why are the midterms so important?

Voter turnout is typically lower for midterms than for presidential elections, but the results will decisively influence US politics for the next few years. Despite the significant executive power delegated to the presidency, the majority of federal political decisions have to be approved by Congress before they can be implemented.

It is therefore considerably easier for Trump to govern the country as he chooses if the Republicans have a majority in both chambers of Congress. If the Democrats win a majority in one or both chambers, it will be more difficult for him to make changes to either domestic or foreign policy.
Which races are crucial?

The Democrats only need to win four more seats in the House of Representatives to gain a majority. They would then have 218 representatives. Out of the 435 races, only a few are still considered toss-ups. These include districts in Iowa, Virginia and Montana.

One senatorial race to watch is the one in Texas. Current polls put Democrat James Talarico level with his Republican rival, Ken Paxton. The Democrats need four more seats in the Senate to win a majority. The possibility that Texas could be one of them is already a sensation. No Democrat has won here at state level since 1994. Talarico now even has the support of some members of the Bush family, the Texas Republican dynasty of former presidents George H.W. Bush and George W. Bush, his son.
Many US voters are undecided, disillusioned or disengaged

In the gubernatorial elections it is possible that, for the first time in US history, a Black woman could become state governor. In Minnesota, the Democrat Amy Klobuchar and the Black Republican Lisa DeMuth are vying for the position, while in Georgia the Black Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms is up against the Republican Rick Jackson.

DeMuth is unlikely to win in Minnesota: The state generally votes Democrat, and Klobuchar, who has been state senator there for almost two decades, is much better known than her rival. In Georgia, however, the latest polls suggest it's neck-and-neck. Bottoms has a realistic chance of winning.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.summary: The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) on Tuesday said a total of 80 Chinese vessels were monitored at a number of key features in the West Philippine Sea (WPS) in October 2026.

blocks.text: Published November 3, 2026 3:50pm
The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) on Tuesday said a total of 80 Chinese vessels were monitored at a number of key features in the West Philippine Sea (WPS) in October 2026.
The figure is lower compared to the 101 Chinese ships seen in the disputed area in September 2026.

In an update, AFP spokesperson for the WPS Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad said People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) and China Coast Guard (CCG) vessels were seen in WPS features from October 1 to 31:
• Ayungin Shoal – 11 CCGs, 13 PLANs
•Bajo de Masinloc – 30 CCGs, 11 PLANs
• Escoda Shoal – three CCGs, eight PLANs
• Pag-asa Islands – three CCGs, one PLAN

Tensions continue as Beijing claims almost all of the South China Sea, a conduit for more than $3 trillion of annual shipborne commerce, including parts claimed by the Philippines, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brunei.
Parts of the South China Sea that fall within Philippine territory have been renamed by the government as the West Philippine Sea to reinforce the country’s claim.

The West Philippine Sea refers to the maritime areas on the western side of the Philippine archipelago, including the Luzon Sea and the waters around, within, and adjacent to the Kalayaan Island Group and Bajo de Masinloc.
In 2016, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague ruled in favor of the Philippines over China's claims in the South China Sea, saying that it had "no legal basis."
China has refused to recognize the decision. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: DA, civil society groups find coordinate discrepancies in 8 of 1,669 proposed 2027 FMR projects
articles.summary: The Department of Agriculture (DA) has tightened its review of project documents, including those for farm-to-market roads (FMRs), to prevent errors in project information.

blocks.text: Published November 3, 2026 3:37pm
The Department of Agriculture (DA) has tightened its review of project documents, including those for farm-to-market roads (FMRs), to prevent errors in project information.

Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. ordered a comprehensive review of project descriptions, supporting documents, and validation procedures after senators flagged errors in the coordinates of proposed FMR projects for 2027 submitted by the agency.
“We are reviewing the data and working with civil society groups to make sure the technical descriptions are accurate and verifiable,” he said in a statement on Tuesday.

“If there are errors in the technical descriptions, whether typographical or otherwise, we will take responsibility and correct them. Public funds must go to the projects they are intended for,” Tiu Laurel added.

The DA said it immediately coordinated with the People's Budget Coalition, Bisto Proyekto.ph, and the Bureau of Agriculture and Fisheries Engineering to address discrepancies traced to typographical errors.
The DA and civil society groups identified coordinate discrepancies in eight of the 1,669 entries for proposed FMR projects.
"Upon close inspection, it showed one or two numbers in the coordinate were mistyped from the correct coordinates," the DA said.
Tiu Laurel also ordered improvements in geotagging, internal reviews, and third-party validation of project documents.
The DA maintains an online portal for transparency and monitoring of FMR projects nationwide at fmrwatch.bafe.gov.ph.
“Public funds must be backed by accurate project information. That is our accountability to Congress, our farmers and fisherfolk, and the Filipino people,” Tiu Laurel said.
Under the proposed P198.45-billion budget for the DA in 2027, P16 billion is earmarked for FMR projects. This is half the P33 billion allocated for the program in the 2026 budget.
Since President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. assumed office in 2022, a total of 537 FMR projects have been completed, the Department of Agrarian Reform earlier said.
These projects cover a combined distance of 435.807 kilometers and benefit 155,123 agrarian reform beneficiaries (ARBs). —VBL, GMA News
