articles.title: Why a US-Russia showdown left Morocco celebrating
articles.summary: An impasse between the US and Russia at the UN means its peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara has ended after 35 years.

blocks.text: Western Sahara, on Africa's north-west coast, was a Spanish colony until 1975. It has significant phosphate reserves and valuable fishing grounds along its Atlantic coast.
As Spain prepared to withdraw, both Morocco and Mauritania claimed the territory.
The International Court of Justice found historical ties of allegiance but no territorial sovereignty that overrode the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination.

Morocco's then King Hassan II responded by organising the Green March. On 6 November 1975 about 350,000 Moroccan civilians entered the territory in a mass demonstration intended to put pressure on Spain.

Days later, Spain signed the Madrid Accords with Morocco and Mauritania, agreeing to transfer administrative control. Morocco took the northern two-thirds and Mauritania the southern third. The agreement did not settle the question of sovereignty.
The Polisario Front, an independence movement founded in 1973, opposed the deal. It saw it as replacing Spanish colonial rule with Moroccan and Mauritanian control.
Mauritania renounced its claim in 1979, but Morocco continued fighting Polisario.
Morocco's royal palace welcomed the failure to renew Minurso's mandate.
In Laayoune, the territory's largest city, footage showed people celebrating, waving Moroccan flags and displaying portraits of King Mohammed VI.

"The decision is an opportunity for Rabat to challenge what it sees as an international mechanism that has failed to resolve the dispute," Issam Laaroussi, a Moroccan expert in international relations, tells the BBC.
He said Morocco would now have more room to push its autonomy proposal and shift negotiations away from a referendum on independence towards autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty.
The decision does not, however, change Western Sahara's legal status or amount to international recognition of Moroccan sovereignty.
Western Sahara remains on the UN list of non-self-governing territories, while the African Union officially recognises its independence, as the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (SADR).
But the decision comes after several countries backed the position of Morocco, which in recent years has made securing international support for its claim a central part of its foreign policy.
In 2020, the US recognised Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara as part of an agreement to establish diplomatic relations between Morocco and Israel.
France also backed Morocco's autonomy plan as the basis for resolving the dispute in 2024.
The fear is that Minurso's departure could lead to renewed fighting.
The mission has monitored military developments and helped reduce the risk of escalation.
Aid organisation Oxfam warned that losing its monitoring and de-escalation role could undermine stability, with serious consequences for civilians.
Laaroussi admits that the mission's departure could create security gaps.
"Minurso's departure does not create the original conflict, because the conflict is already there, but it could aggravate an already fragile security environment," he says.
The UN decision has also fuelled nationalist rhetoric online.
Several Moroccan users have shared AI-generated images of themselves in military uniform, declaring their readiness to fight for Morocco's sovereignty over Western Sahara.

In Morocco, Western Sahara is widely regarded as a national cause. Political parties that are often divided on other issues are united in supporting the country's claim to sovereignty over the territory.
Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita has said the end of the mission does not mean the end of the ceasefire, and that Rabat remains committed to it "within respect of its security and sovereignty."
Polisario has not said what it will do next.
Any resumption of fighting could well draw in Algeria, as tensions with Morocco remain high.

According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), both countries significantly increased military spending last year, with SIPRI citing their dispute over Western Sahara as a key driver.
Algeria spent an estimated $25.4bn, more than four time Morocco's $6.3bn.

articles.title: 'Walang pasok' powers amid site-specific conditions given to schools by Marcos EO
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has signed an executive order (EO) that gives schools an authority to independently declare onsite class suspensions during bad weather or hazardous conditions. Under…

blocks.text: Published November 3, 2026 3:20pm
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has signed an executive order (EO) that gives schools an authority to independently declare onsite class suspensions during bad weather or hazardous conditions.
Under EO No. 130, schools can impose granular suspension even when there is no suspension declared by national or local government.

“In the absence of an applicable automatic suspension or localized suspension declared by the concerned LCE (local chief executive), an educational institution or learning center may, through its duly authorized official, declare granular suspension, in coordination with the concerned LCE, upon the determination that an actual or imminent threat to the safety, health, or welfare of learners and personnel exists based on documented site-specific conditions,” the EO read.

Aside from granular suspension, schools may automatically suspend onsite classes and work upon issuance by PAGASA, PHIVOLCS, DENR-Environmental Management Bureau of any warning, advisory, alert level, and forecasts.
Moreover, local officials may declare suspensions based on the specific, verified disaster or risk levels within their respective city, municipality, or province.
However, the EO provides that schools should implement learning continuity measures despite the suspension of in-person classes or activities.

“Educational institutions and learning continuity measures consistent with the policies of the ECCD Council, DepEd, CHED TESDA, and other agencies operating or supervising specialized educational institutions and learning centers, to ensure that learning continues despite the suspension of in-person classes,” it read.

Further, EO No. 130 also allows individual schools to seek the early resumption of classes ahead of an LGU-wide order, provided a documented site-specific assessment proves the school grounds are safe and the local mayor or governor concurs.

Amid the threat of El Nino, the Department of Education said a school can suspend both physical and online classes once the local temperature hits 42 degrees Celsius, upon coordination with the concerned local government.

articles.title: Schools may reopen during LGU class suspensions under new Marcos order
articles.summary: Schools will be allowed to resume in-person classes even while a mayor's or governor's class suspension is still in force, under an executive order signed by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. that…

blocks.text: November 3, 2026 | 3:13pm

Students walk across the gutter-deep flood along the corner of Taft and UN Avenues in Manila following a heavy downpour brought by the enhanced southwest monsoon on Monday, July 21, 2025. The city of Manila on Monday suspended classes at all levels in public and private schools starting at 12 noon.
The STAR / Edd Gumban

MANILA, Philippines — Schools will be allowed to resume in-person classes even while a mayor's or governor's class suspension is still in force, under an executive order signed by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. that updates rules on calling off classes during disasters.

Executive Order 130, signed on October 28 and originally proposed by the Department of Education (DepEd), lets a school reopen earlier than a city- or province-wide suspension if an assessment shows its campus is safe and accessible, and the local chief executive concurs.
The new order replaces Executive Order 66 of 2012, signed under former President Benigno Aquino III.
The order recognizes a need to "rationalize and harmonize" the different rules governing the suspension of in-person classes and on-site government work.
EO 130 covers all public and private schools and learning centers, including colleges and technical-vocational schools.
What is new
EO 130 spells out three kinds of suspensions:

items: Automatic suspensions, triggered without "need of further declaration," upon the issuance of a warning, alert level or forecast by PAGASA, PHIVOLCS, and other relevant government agencies. These are based on "prescribed technical thresholds" to be detailed in later guidelines.
Localized suspensions, which can be decided by the local chief executive in the absence of an applicable automatic suspension, based on local risk assessments.

Granular suspensions, which are suspensions called by the school itself in the absence of the first two kinds. This is done "in coordination" with the local chief executive and upon the "determination" of an actual or imminent threat to the safety, health or welfare of students and personnel. DepEd gave public school heads similar authority in 2024.

blocks.text: The executive order stated that schools can also, in turn, decide to resume classes on their own during a local suspension with a documented site assessment and the concurrence of the mayor or governor.
This option applies only to localized suspensions declared by local officials, not to those triggered automatically by hazard warnings.
Local chief executives also must now name the areas a suspension covers, down to barangays and, where practicable, individual schools, and state how long it will last.
They are to consult barangay captains, the schools division superintendent and private school heads as needed.
Classes resume once a suspension lapses or a warning is lifted, downgraded or expires, but only after required safety inspections.
The order also states that suspending in-person classes "shall not automatically suspend learning."
Schools must shift to alternative delivery where feasible, and staff to alternative work arrangements.

The order no longer spells out which grade levels are to suspend in-person instruction under each storm signal. Previously, EO 66 called off preschool under Signal No. 1, classes up to high school under Signal No. 2, and all levels and government work under Signal No. 3 or higher.
Those thresholds will instead be set in guidelines that DepEd must issue within 30 days of the order taking effect.

blocks.text: The two-day Berlin Security Conference is kicking off in the German capital for the 25th time on Tuesday.

This year, the focus will be on what many see as the biggest challenge toRussia's war in Ukraine European peace for decades: the threat of Russian aggression as reflected in its invasion of Ukraine and hybrid attacks on other European countries.
The conference's partner country this year is Lithuania, a country that shares an uncomfortable border with Russia and fears greatly for its own security.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda is to open the event and later to meet with Chancellor Friedrich Merz, with not just security issues but also Lithuania's upcoming presidency of the Council of the European Union on the agenda.
The program for the conference also includes a speech by a still unnamed "special guest" to be held mid-morning.
The conference has been taking place annually since 2001.

articles.title: St. Luke's Medical Center probing cybersecurity incident on mobile app
articles.summary: Private healthcare provider St. Luke's Medical Center has said it is investigating a "cybersecurity incident" that it detected on its mobile application.

blocks.text: Published November 3, 2026 2:27pm
Private healthcare provider St. Luke's Medical Center has said it is investigating a "cybersecurity incident" that it detected on its mobile application.

In a statement issued Monday, the company said, "On October 29, 2026, St. Luke's Medical Center identified a cybersecurity incident affecting a portion of the platform that supports our mobile application, which is managed by a third-party service provider."
St. Luke's did not specify the extent of a potential data exposure, but assured that critical patient data records are intact.

"Our Electronic Medical Records (EMR) and other core clinical systems are unaffected. The EMR is the heart of our patient information, holding the records our team relies on to care for our patients," the statement read.
The healthcare provider added that it carried out immediate mitigation protocols and reported the matter to National Privacy Commission.

"Upon detection, we immediately initiated containment and remediation measures. The affected platform was isolated and secured, and the mobile app was taken offline. We engaged independent cybersecurity experts to conduct a comprehensive forensic investigation and to further strengthen our security safeguards," it added.
St. Luke's said it is currently notifying people whose personal information may have been affected. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: PNP: No shoot-to-kill order vs Bato dela Rosa
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Tuesday denied reports that it had issued a shoot-to-kill order against Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa.

blocks.text: Published November 3, 2026 2:26pm
The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Tuesday denied reports that it had issued a shoot-to-kill order against Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa.

“May I remind the public that only share or believe information coming from verified and official sources. Wala pong shoot-to-kill order na inilabas,” PNP spokesperson Police Colonel Allen Rae Co told reporters in an interview.
(May I remind the public that only share or believe information coming from verified and official sources. No shoot-to-kill order has been issued.)
Co pointed out that the PNP would carry out its operations against Dela Rosa within the bounds of the law.
In a separate statement, PNP chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. also stressed that the police do not subscribe to a shoot-to-kill approach in serving arrest warrants.

“The PNP does not subscribe to a shoot-to-kill approach. Our mandate is to enforce the law, not to take the law into our own hands. Every operation must be guided by due process, respect for human rights, and the rule of law,” Nartatez said.
All operations must observe maximum restraint, proportionality, and respect for human rights, according to the PNP.
Due process
This came after Cagayan de Oro 1st District Representative Lordan Suan denied social media posts falsely attributing to him a supposed call for a shoot-to-kill resolution against Dela Rosa.
“It has come to my attention that several social media pages are amplifying a false and malicious statement falsely attributed to me,” Suan earlier said in a Facebook post on Monday.

“The quote circulating online claiming I threatened a House hearing and a ‘shoot-to-kill’ resolution against Senator Ronald ‘Bato’ dela Rosa is FALSE, FAKE, FABRICATED. I never made that statement. I stand firmly for due process and the rule of law,” he added.
Dela Rosa is wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) in connection with the crimes against humanity case arising from former President Rodrigo Duterte’s war on drugs.
The senator is accused of being a co-perpetrator in the alleged crimes.

Earlier, the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) claimed that Dela Rosa was hiding in Mindanao under the protection of an “armed and powerful group,” but did not identify the group.
A P50-million reward is being offered for information that would lead to the senator’s arrest.

articles.title: DOLE OKs minimum wage hike in Western Visayas, SOCCSKSARGEN
articles.summary: The Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) has approved a minimum wage hike in Western Visayas and SOCCSKSARGEN, which will be implemented in November.

blocks.text: Published November 3, 2026 2:21pm
The Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) has approved a minimum wage hike in Western Visayas and SOCCSKSARGEN, which will be implemented in November.
According to Manny Vargas' report on Super Radyo DZBB,there is a P40 to P45 increase for minimum wages in Western Visayas, which will be effective on November 19.
From P550, this will raise the current minimum wage to P590 a day for workers in non-agriculture, industrial and commercial establishments with more than 10 employees

For establishments with less than 10 employees, their new minimum wage would be P565 a day from P525. This is also the same new wage rate for agriculture workers, who had previously been at P520 a day.
Household helpers will also receive an additional P500 a month, which raises their monthly minimum salary to P7,000.
Meanwhile, the DOLE also announced a wage hike in SOCCSKSARGEN.
The prevailing minimum wage for the region is P443 to P460. There will be an additional P41 a day, which will be implemented in two tranches.
The first tranche, P16 a day, will be implemented on November 19. This will raise the SOCCSKSARGEN minimum wage to P459 a day for agriculture workers, and P476 a day for non-agriculture workers.
The second tranche, P25 a day, will be implemented on January 1, 2027. This would again raise the region’s minimum wage to P484 for agriculture workers, and P501 for non-agriculture workers.
DOLE also announced a P450 monthly raise for household helpers starting November 19, which raises their total monthly wage to P6,450. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: UK ministers told not to engage formally with Indian mega-zoo after lobbying
articles.summary:
Guardian and Mongabay reveal approaches to officials and MPs on behalf of Vantara zoo ahead of UK-chaired Cites meeting on endangered animal imports

British government ministers were…
articles.byline: Patrick Greenfield, Elisângela Mendonça and Phoebe Weston

blocks.text: British government ministers were told not to engage formally with Vantara, the controversial mega-zoo run by the Indian billionaire Anant Ambani, after lobbying efforts by the private animal sanctuary in the run-up to a UK-chaired meeting on the trade in endangered species, according to documents.

This week, the UK heads a 32-country committee meeting in Geneva of Cites, the United Nations body that regulates trade in endangered species. The meeting will examine how India has responded to compliance concerns about imports of endangered animals.
Documents obtained by the Guardian and the news outlet Mongabay under the UK’s Freedom of Information Act reveal Vantara’s efforts to lobby British officials and ministers before the meeting.

Ambani, 31, is the heir to the oil and gas fortune of one of India’s richest men, Mukesh Ambani. He set up a 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo near his family’s oil-refining facilities in Gujarat, where more than 150,000 animals have reportedly been amassed since 2022. Vantara boasts high welfare standards for animals in its care, including facilities such as an elephant hydrotherapy pool, where more than 260 elephants can also receive oil therapies and Ayurvedic massage.

But conservation groups have repeatedly questioned how such a vast number of species, many of which are endangered, were gathered so quickly. Last year, India’s supreme court cleared the zoo’s operators of any wrongdoing.

A subsequent Cites fact-finding mission looking into the zoo raised concerns about India’s compliance with international rules on animal imports in 2025. It recommended temporary restrictions on India, although the recommendation was later withdrawn.

Its November 2025 report said: “There is a need for caution to ensure that imports of large numbers of animals by these facilities are not inadvertently creating a demand for illegally sourced animals.”

blocks.caption: British officials were invited to visit the controversial zoo.  Photograph: P Paranjpe/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: In May, officials from the UK’s Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) met a representative from Vantara and the US lobbyist firm Checkmate Government Relations, founded by Ches McDowell, a hunting friend of Donald Trump Jr.

Before the meeting, internal briefing documents said Checkmate was “seeking to persuade the UK to take a more sympathetic view of India’s handling of imports to Vantara and of Checkmate’s argument that responsibility for verifying legality sits primarily with exporting or re-exporting parties rather than with India as importer”.

blocks.caption: Vantara boasts high welfare standards for animals in its care. Photograph: P Paranjpe/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: During the meeting, the Vantara representative invited UK officials to visit the zoo – an invitation that was subsequently declined to ensure the impartiality of the UK’s Cites chair role.

After the meeting, a representative from another lobbying firm, Atlas Strategy, working on behalf of Vantara, approached the then secretary of state, Emma Reynolds, and then nature minister, Mary Creagh, also raising the prospect of a visit to the zoo.
When Reynolds asked for advice, a note was issued recommending that ministers did not engage formally with Vantara.

The government documents also reveal concerns about an application by Vantara to import falcons and falcon hybrids, after an unnamed organisation made a £50,000 “donation” to a breeder in the UK, whose identity was also not disclosed. British Cites officials classified the transaction as commercial, according to the documents. The falcons were not exported to India.

A spokesperson for Vantara said it had not imported falcons from the UK, nor had the zoo hired or paid a lobbying firm. It is understood that Checkmate and Altas Strategy were working pro bono for Vantara and not required to register with the Office of the Registrar of Consultant Lobbyists.

blocks.caption: Elephants at a veterinary hospital in Vantara. Photograph: Punit Paranjpe/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: After recent scrutiny, Vantara has sought to “reset” its activities by voluntarily suspending animal imports for a year and hiring John Scanlon, a former Cites chief, to oversee its operations. In an interview with the Sunday Times this year, Ambani said he only brought animals to Vantara legally to ensure their welfare, mentioning a group of hippos he had saved from a hunting lodge in South Africa and jackass penguins saved from a shopping centre in Qatar.
“I think since I was a baby I have been taking care of animals. It’s always been a passion,” he said.

Vantara was used to host Ambani’s lavish pre-wedding celebrations in 2024, which were attended by celebrity guests and politicians. In September, Newcastle University awarded the oil heir a professorship of practice for “his work in conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship”, sparking a backlash from conservationists.

A Defra spokesperson said: “The UK has strict rules in place to protect endangered species and ensuring international wildlife trade is legal and sustainable, with every application assessed individually against internationally agreed and domestic requirements.”
Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

articles.title: North Korea denies role in record Binance hack, calls US charge 'provocation'
articles.summary: Kim Yo Jong dismissed FBI claims that North Korean hackers stole more than $6 billion from Binance, as the exchange began reopening withdrawals on more networks.

image.caption: Binance said it replaced most of the stolen assets out of its own fundsImage: Sk Mijanur Rahaman/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: North Korea has hit back at US accusations that its hackers drained more than $6 billion (more than 5.36 billion euros) from cryptocurrency exchange Binance. Kim Yo Jong, sister of leader Kim Jong Un, called the charge "a grave political provocation," according to state media agency KCNA.
Kim described the US claim as "absurd rhetoric and nothing new.”
What do we know about the hacking?
The accusation came from the FBI, which blamed a state-tied hacking group called TraderTraitor over the weekend.

This was reportedly the biggest crypto-exchange heist on record, well above the roughly $1.5 billion Bybit raid in 2025, which was also attributed to North Korean hackers. TRM Labs linked the attack to the same group and said it shifted most of the money out within 20 minutes, German news agency DPA reported.
Cryptocurrency giant Binance hit by $6.3 billion hack
Kim Yo Jong said Pyongyang now had "issues to reconsider" because of Washington's hostility.

North Korea has so far stayed silent on Trump's overtures about reviving summit talks. Analysts in Seoul told Reuters news agency the speed of the denial points to concern that Washington could step up efforts to cut off a funding source widely believed to bankroll arms development.
Is Binance working again?

Separately, Binance announced Monday that withdrawals will restart for additional assets across several blockchains, among them Binance Smart Chain, Ethereum, Solana, XRP and Sui, from 04:00 GMT Tuesday.
Selected tokens on Arbitrum, Optimism, Tron and Base are part of the same rollout.
Binance said it replaced most of the stolen assets out of its own funds.

articles.title: US strikes Iran ahead of midterm elections
articles.summary: US officials described the attacks on Qeshm Island as limited and defensive, according to CBS, the BBC's US partner.

blocks.text: The US has launched strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials have told CBS, the BBC's US partner.
Iranian state news agency IRNA reported several explosions on the island on Monday.
The US officials described the strikes as limited and said they were in response to the Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) firing upon a US aircraft.
The BBC has contacted US Central Command (Centcom), the part of the US military responsible for operations in the Middle East, for comment.
It comes ahead of the US midterm elections, which will determine whether the Republicans or Democrats control Congress.
Trump has been facing falling polling numbers and pressure from within his party to end the war, which began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.
Earlier on Monday, he told reporters that he was in "no rush" to ramp up strikes on Iran.

"One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush. We crippled them financially," he told news outlet Axios. "They have no money, no gasoline and their people are getting very tired of it."
He also said the US "might need to go after Pickaxe", a site linked to Iran's nuclear programme, in an interview with Fox News on the eve of the midterm elections.
This was "not a big deal" and could be done in "one hour", Trump added.

There has been mounting speculation in the last few days that the US may resume significant strikes in Iran again after the midterms. But asked by a reporter on Monday if that was the case, Trump said "no".
Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi told the IRNA earlier that "very intensive" talks to try and end the war are under way with the US via mediators.

He also said Tehran was prepared for both diplomatic and military scenarios "more than ever before" and that it was up to the US to choose between a "wise path" of negotiation or the "mistake of military aggression".

articles.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump's request to stop California counting disputed votes
articles.summary: The ruling, which comes on the eve of the midterm elections, essentially ends the Trump administration's bid to disqualify the ballots in the state.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
BySareen Habeshian
Reporting fromLos Angeles
The US Supreme Court has rejected a last-minute request by the Trump administration asking it to intervene in California's midterm election vote count.
The justice department wanted 20,000 ballots to be set aside that it alleged may have been issued to non-US citizens in the state.
Two lower courts had already rejected the request. State election officials had questioned the federal government's claims - saying the process used to identify alleged non-citizens was inaccurate.
The Monday ruling comes on the eve of the midterms, which will determine which political party controls the US Congress for the last two years of President Donald Trump's second term.
The Supreme Court announced its decision in a one-line order, saying it was denying the justice department's request for an injunction.
"The application for injunction pending appeal presented to Justice Kagan and by her referred to the Court is denied," it reads.
Its means rulings made in lower courts will stand and essentially ends the Trump administration's bid to disqualify the ballots.

California is the most populous state in America with some 23 million people on its voting register. As of Sunday night, more than six million mail-in ballots had already been received, according to the California secretary of state's office.

The justice department sent letters to the California secretary of state and Los Angeles County Registrar last month, demanding they set aside the ballots of 20,000 registered voters whom the Trump administration "believe" are "likely" non-citizens, according to court documents.

About a week later, armed officials from the Department of Homeland Security delivered letters to county officials and employees across California threatening criminal charges if they didn't sequester those ballots.
In a 22-page brief reviewed by the BBC, the justice department maintained that ballots cast by non-citizens could "debase or dilute valid votes".
On Friday, a federal appeals court declined the government's request to segregate the ballots.
California election officials have questioned the accuracy of the government's claims, and have said the list of names the government has provided is riddled with inaccuracies.
They have expressed concern that eligible voters could be disenfranchised and said segregating ballots whilst voting is underway is unfeasible.
What are Americans voting for this election?
The attempts are a part of a years-long campaign by Trump and his administration to fight alleged voter fraud that they believe is widespread, despite research showing that it is extremely rare.

President Trump has repeatedly claimed that Democrats steal elections by allowing immigrants to vote illegally, and he blames much of it on the so-called "mail-in" or postal voting that is permitted in many Democratic states.

Last week in a scathing ruling, district judge David Carter said the government's move in California was indicative of an "ongoing pattern of attempted election interference" on the part of the Trump administration.

The judge added that "never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the executive branch".
With additional reporting by the BBC's David Willis

articles.title: US reportedly strikes Iran’s Qeshm Island as Vance voices optimism about a deal
articles.summary:
Iranian state media reported the sound of explosions on the island in the strait of Hormuz, coming on the eve of crucial US midterms

The ⁠US launched limited strikes on ​Iran’s Qeshm Island…

blocks.text: The ⁠US launched limited strikes on ​Iran’s Qeshm Island late on Monday, ⁠according to reports in US media, hours after US vice-president JD Vance said he was optimistic diplomatic efforts to end the war were moving in the right direction.

The strikes were reported as being “defensive”, and not thought to be a signal of a return to full hostilities, but came on the eve of crucial midterm elections in which Donald Trump’s Republican party is expected to be punished by voters for the cascading effect the war has had on the US cost of living.
When asked earlier on Monday whether he had considered resuming strikes on Iran after Tuesday’s midterm elections, Trump replied “no”.

Several explosions were ⁠heard ⁠on Qeshm ​Island on Monday evening, according to Iranian state media, with local outlets describing their cause as unclear. The strikes – first reported by the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) – targeted surface to air missiles being used against US assets, according to Reuters and the Associated Press.

US Central ‌Command did ​not immediately ⁠respond to ​a request for ​comment from the Reuters news agency, and the WSJ described the attacks as part of a series of strikes carried out against the country in recent weeks that have not been made public.

The paper said that sources suggested the recent strikes have been carried out on a smaller scale and purposefully kept secret by the Trump administration so as not to signal ‌any intent of resuming the military campaign against Iran.

The US has targeted Qeshm Island on multiple occasions throughout the war. Positioned in the mouth of the strait of Hormuz, the island has been used in the past to launch attacks on shipping in the waterway.

Despite attacks having ceased in recent weeks, Iran has continued to enforce its closure of the strait by targeting oil tankers, shipping containers and other vessels attempting to transit the waterway.

If confirmed, the attack would mark the first publicly known strike by the US on Iran in weeks. On Monday Vance said that he and Trump were optimistic about securing a deal with Iran, after Tehran revealed indirect negotiations with Washington.

“The president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement,” Vance told reporters. “We’ve certainly made some progress. We’ll see if we can make some more.”
Speaking to Fox News hours before the polls opened in the US on Tuesday, Trump continued to play down the significance of the conflict and its effects on the US economy.
“There’s no war raging. It could happen if they don’t make a deal, but they want to make a deal very badly and there’s a very good chance we make a deal.”

Speaking from Washington in his closing message of the midterms campaign, Trump hailed a sharp drop in oil prices that came as his administration touted a renewed diplomatic efforts being made to end the war. Rising petrol prices have caused by the war have become a signature issue of the midterm elections, with polls showing voters likely to punish Republicans for the effect on the cost of living.

articles.title: Trump to remove Rwanda and South Africa from US trade deal
articles.summary: The move comes barely a week after Rwanda's defence ministry was hit with sanctions by the US Treasury.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has notified Congress of his intention to remove South Africa and Rwanda from a preferential trade programme, from 1 January 2027.
The African Growth and Opportunity Act (Agoa) allows eligible African countries to export thousands of products to the US duty-free.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement that an annual review had found that both countries were engaging in practices inconsistent with the programme's eligibility requirements.
He added that the Trump administration had additionally notified the two countries of the decision.
The Trump administration cited barriers to US trade and investment, as well as concerns over national security and foreign policy interests in the region.
For South Africa, the US pointed to corruption.
"The Trump administration is working to ensure our African partners take the necessary steps to meet the eligibility criteria," Greer said.

South Africa's Trade Minister Parks Tau described the decision as "unfortunate", saying Washington was raising new issues that had not featured in trade negotiations between the two countries, which began in 2025.
"We will continue to accelerate the diversification of South Africa's export markets to protect jobs," Tau said.
US Ambassador to South Africa Leo Brent Bozell III said it was regrettable that South African policies led to its termination from Agoa.
"This was a predictable and preventable outcome resulting from the rejection by South Africa's government of real concerns raised by the US," he wrote on X.
The announcement comes amid strained relations between Washington and both countries, with the proposed termination threatening their access to preferential trade arrangements with the US.
Last year, Trump accused South Africa of persecuting its white minority and launched a programme for white Afrikaners to get asylum in the US.
Trump also repeated widely discredited claims of a genocide of South Africa's white population.

articles.title: DepEd procures over 170,000 Macbooks for teachers, staff
articles.summary: The Department of Education has purchased 170,000 Apple MacBook Neo laptops, in what Apple's chief executive called the company's biggest education deal ever for the Mac.

blocks.text: November 3, 2026 | 10:51am
MANILA, Philippines (Second update, 12:48 p.m.) — The Department of Education has bought 172,654 Apple MacBook Neo laptops for public school teachers and administrative staff at about P43,000 each.

DepEd said on Tuesday, November 3, it had concluded competitive bidding for the laptops. Of the total, 169,008 will go to teachers and 3,646 to administrative officers. Deliveries are scheduled from this month through March 2027.

"For the longest time, our teachers have carried the heavy personal burden of buying their own laptops or maintaining outdated equipment just to keep up with lesson plans," Education Secretary Sonny Angara said in a statement. "Under the vision of President Marcos, we are changing the narrative."
The MacBooks bring the number of teacher laptops DepEd has contracted so far under its computerization program to 231,725, including 62,717 Windows-based units.
That is enough for roughly one in four of the country's nearly 900,000 public school teachers.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has pledged that every public school teacher will have a laptop before his term ends in 2028, and DepEd had planned to buy more than 250,000 laptops for teaching personnel under its 2026 budget.

The pace of the program has drawn criticism, particularly from the teachers' group the Alliance of Concerned Teachers (ACT). In a statement in August, the group faulted DepEd for handing out voice amplifiers while teachers were still waiting for their own laptops, and said the planned 250,000 units would still leave most teachers without one.
At the time, DepEd replied that the laptop purchase was taking longer because the devices had to meet standards for performance, durability, battery life and warranty.
Price and warranty
DepEd said the P43,000 price covers the laptop, built-in productivity software, delivery and teacher training, and is about P6,900 below the base model's suggested retail price.
At that price, the order is worth about P7.4 billion. The department did not disclose the exact contract amount.
The five-year warranty on the MacBook Neos is a first for DepEd's laptop purchases, the department said. Retail units carry one year of coverage.
The unit price is about P15,300 lower than what DepEd paid in 2021, when the procurement service of the Department of Budget and Management bought 39,583 laptops for teachers at P58,300 each.
The Commission on Audit later flagged that P2.4-billion purchase as overpriced given the laptops ran on outdated processors.
Apple's biggest Mac education deal
Apple chief executive John Ternus shared the deal during the company's fourth-quarter earnings call early Tuesday, Manila time, his first since he succeeded Tim Cook in September.

"I'm feeling great about the opportunities ahead for Apple, from our product roadmap and broad range of services to promising areas like health, emerging markets, enterprise and education," Ternus said. "As one example, we recently secured our biggest education deal ever for Mac with the Department of Education in the Philippines. They're going to deploy 170,000 MacBook Neos to teachers and staff."
"Opportunities like this bring more users into our ecosystem and help fuel growth across our business," he added.
Apple launched the MacBook Neo in March as its cheapest laptop. It runs on the A18 Pro, a chip first used in iPhones.
It also raised the laptop's Philippine retail price by P10,000 in June amid a global shortage of memory chips.
Apple also told analysts that Mac supplies would remain constrained through the October-to-December quarter, when DepEd's first deliveries are due.

articles.title: North Korea denies being behind record $6.3bn Binance hack
articles.summary: US government agencies and cyber analysts have blamed Pyongyang for the record-breaking heist.

blocks.text: North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance, calling the allegations an "absurd rhetoric".

Kim Yo-jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage the country's public image.
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack - which has been described as the largest in history.
Pyongyang has also been blamed for a number of major cyber attacks - accusations that it has consistently denied.
Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor.
The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group.
"The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement.
"It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she said.
The incident is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its economy.
The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.

Pyongyang has systematically built its cyber operations, recruiting promising students from universities and sending them to hacker units overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, research groups like the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies think tank have said.
The country has consistently denied such claims.
Kim Yo-jong said "it is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace".
The BBC has contacted Binance for comment. Since the hack, the crypto giant has largely focused its public statements on the technical nature of the breach and its response to protect users.
The company said initial checks indicated that an engineer's laptop had been compromised, enabling an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals.
Trading in major cryptocurrencies on Binance has since resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze assets impacted by the hack.
Binance said on Sunday that its customers pulled out more than $3.6bn of assets from its exchange as it reopened after suspending all transactions in the wake of the hack.
The company has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack and that it has so far covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach.

articles.title: Russian bombing of Ukrainian aid centre kills at least 26, Kyiv says
articles.summary:
Ukrainian president Zelenskyy says attack on aid hub was ‘vile’ and shows Russia does not want to de-escalate

Russia on Monday bombed an aid distribution centre and neighbouring shelter in…

blocks.text: Russia on Monday bombed an aid distribution centre and neighbouring shelter in southern Ukraine, killing at least 26 ​people, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the country’s emergency services said.

Emergency services said two members of a rescue crew and four police officers were among the dead in the village ⁠of Komyshuvakha, in south-eastern Zaporizhzhia region. Five people were being treated in hospital, including two rescue workers.
Zelenskyy, in his nightly video address, said Russian forces initially dropped bombs on a school in the village that was used as a shelter and for ⁠distributing humanitarian assistance.
There were no classes at the school, he said, as the village, lying south-east of the region’s main city, ​also called Zaporizhzhia, was too close to the frontline. ‌
“The Russians struck first ‌just as people were arriving – a few aerial bombs,” he said. “Then there was a second strike – more air bombs, this time on ‌the shelter. A vile terrorist strike.”

As night fell in Komyshuvakha, emergency responders used torches to search through the rubble of collapsed buildings, according to photos and video posted online by local officials. Regina Kharchenko, secretary of the Zaporizhzhia city council, said that 27 people were missing in the attack.

Efforts to rescue people Monday evening were hindered as Russian drones launched additional attacks in the area that had been bombed, according to Mykhailo Semikin, a military official in Zaporizhzhia.
Zelenskyy said the Russians could not have been unaware that residents remaining in Komyshuvakha gathered each week to pick up humanitarian packages from the site.

blocks.caption: Ukrainian soldiers stand among the rubble after a Russian airstrike on the humanitarian aid hub. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: The attack, he said, had shown that Moscow was intent on killing people instead of building on the past week’s ceasefire in the embattled southern city of Oleshky, brokered by US first lady Melania Trump.
“Russians continue to demonstrate, time and again, their hatred of Ukraine and everything that exists here,” he said.
“If Russia genuinely ‌wanted de-escalation, there was an opportunity following the situation in Oleshky to continue taking humanitarian steps. We proposed this. But Russia continues to kill people.”
The ceasefire last week enabled an evacuation of the Russian-occupied Oleshky.
It was the longest pause in fighting between the neighbours in the war, now in its fifth year, which has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
The Kremlin said that no other similar missions were being planned “at the moment”.
US-led talks between Russia and Ukraine are set to resume next week, US special envoy Steve Witkoff said on Monday.
President Donald Trump has pushed for a settlement to the dragging war but there has been no breakthrough.
The talks – to be held 10 November and 11 in Abu Dhabi, Witkoff said – come as Kyiv and its European allies worry that Trump has increasingly sided with Moscow.
*With Reuters, Associated Press and Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Thousands of European troops to rehearse Ukraine deployment in event of peace
articles.summary: Western officials stress that any force sent to Ukraine would not take part in any offensive operations.

blocks.text: Britain and France are to lead a military exercise to test a multinational force's ability to deploy to Ukraine, if there is a peace deal.
Nearly 3,000 military personnel from 12 European nations will take part in the rehearsal in neighbouring Poland this month.
Plans for a reassurance force for Ukraine were set out last year as one of the long-term security guarantees being proposed by European nations.

But there are still more questions than answers as to how such a military force might work in practice. Western officials stress that any force sent to Ukraine would not take part in offensive operations or be involved in peacekeeping or ceasefire monitoring missions.
Nor would they be operating under the command of Nato or on the front line.
Officials say their presence would be to provide reassurance to Ukraine and to help rebuild its armed forces.
The US has been involved in discussions, but is not contributing to the mission.
Russia has already voiced opposition to foreign troops being stationed in Ukraine and, last year, President Vladimir Putin said they would be "legitimate targets".
Western officials have declined to spell out the rules of engagement if any international troops were to be attacked in Ukraine. Though they say the force would be able to defend itself.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the exercise showed Britain, France and their allies were stepping up preparation for the day when peace came to Ukraine.
He said: "This is not a hypothetical plan, it's a real force, ready to help Ukraine once the fighting stops."

Lt Gen Tom Bateman, the UK commander of the Multi National Force – Ukraine (MNF-U), said the exercise represented an important step in translating political commitments into credible military readiness.
He said it was a "real, capable, readily deployable force that represented a serious commitment from Coalition of the Willing nations to Ukraine's long-term stability and security".

Exercise Koalicja - which takes place from 9-22 November - will be a rehearsal of how to move, protect and supply a force in Ukraine. It will also be a test of their command and control to ensure troops from different countries can work together.
Some 2,800 military personnel will take part across land, sea and air, with the UK contribution including 300 troops and a pair of RAF Typhoons.
Fighter jets will simulate how they would reassure commercial aircraft once Ukraine's skies can be reopened.
Turkey has agreed to lead the maritime mission, with the eventual goal to clear mines and allow the resumption of trade in the Black Sea.
As well as the UK, troops will come from France, Belgium, Estonia, France, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain, Sweden, and Turkey.
However, Western officials could not comment on the final make-up and shape of the force that could be deployed to Ukraine if the fighting stops.
In the past, military experts have suggested that Western nations might have to send tens of thousands of troops to Ukraine to guarantee its security.
Officials acknowledge that the countries' commitment and contributions will depend on the circumstances of a cessation of hostilities and individual nations' political decisions.
It is also unclear what training role Western forces could provide to battle hardened Ukraine.
Ukrainian soldiers are already in high demand training Nato forces - passing on their expertise in drone warfare.
Above all, Russia has shown no sign of wanting to end its war.

articles.title: US: Trump labels Democrats 'dangerous' ahead of midterms
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump said the Democrats nominated "the most extreme and dangerous" candidates in US history in the midterms. He also lowered expectations by saying a sitting president "doesn't…

image.caption: Trump spoke in front of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, where he also discussed rusty pipes and algae extensively.Image: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump labeled the upcoming midterm elections as the most important "in our lifetime."

Trump did seem to lower his supporters' expectations by saying on Monday that an incumbent president "doesn't win the midterms," while also adding that his Republican party "gave this a very strong shot."
"Usually, whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, good or bad, good president, great president. For some reason, the sitting president doesn't win the midterms," Trump said.
According to the US president, the Democrats nominated "the most extreme and dangerous" list of candidates in the country's history.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer responded to Trump's accusation by calling his last message ahead of the midterms "pathetic."
"Donald Trump's pathetic closing message as his illegal war rages, his corruption mounts, and the inflation he caused persists," Schumer posted on his X account.
Trump's last-minute attempt to block 20,000 California ballots was rejected by the US Supreme Court.
Referendum on acting president
This comes as the vote to decide control of Congress for the rest of Trump's term as president will take place on November 3.
Millions of voters will head to the polls, with surging costs of living and energy prices as a result of the Trump-led war in Iran taking center stage.
Trump said he hoped that voters would realize the risks of Iran having nuclear weapons heading to the polls.
"If we allowed Iran to have a nuclear weapon, this country could never function the same way," he argued.
Oil prices dropped significantly as the US and Iran renewed the talks over ending the war between the two countries.
The midterms are largely seen as a referendum on the current US president's policies.
The Democrats are expected to retake the House of Representatives from the Republicans' control, but the fight for the Senate is considered to be close.
The election's outcome is bound to influence both parties' strategies going ahead to the 2028 presidential election.
Democrats get boost from sour mood on Trump, Republicans

articles.title: Canadian dentist detained by ICE in Minnesota ordered released by federal judge
articles.summary: A Canadian dentist detained by U.S. federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents in Minnesota during a green card interview has been ordered released by a federal judge.

image.caption: A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) vehicle seen in New Jersey. A federal judge ordered the release of a Canadian dentist detained by ICE in Minnesota last month, saying his constitutional rights were violated. (Shannon Stapleton/Reuters)

blocks.text: Canada·New
A Canadian dentist detained by U.S. federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents in Minnesota during a green card interview has been ordered released by a federal judge.
Dr. William Lizardo was arrested Oct. 23 at a green card interview
U.S. District Judge Michael J. Davis wrote in his ruling that the arrest and detention of Dr. William Lizardo, 32, originally of Mississauga, Ont., violated his constitutional rights.

Lizardo moved to the U.S. on a student visa in 2019 to study at the University of Minnesota School of Dentistry, according to court documents. He graduated in 2023 and married an American that same year. They had a daughter two years later.

Lizardo's wife filed a petition for an alien relative in September 2023, while Lizardo applied to adjust his status to permanent residency. The relative petition was approved in January 2025, according to the court.

Lizardo practiced dentistry in federally-designated shortage areas until his work authorization was revoked, at which time he started volunteering at a low-cost clinic in Burnsville, Minn., according to the court documents.
New bodycam video shows aftermath of ICE shooting in NYC

In January, his request for permanent residency was denied because he had failed to provide a certfied document from Ontario. Orders to appear at subsequent hearings were sent to the wrong address. Lizardo missed the hearings and was subsequently arrested by ICE Oct. 23, detained at Sherburne County Jail, and ordered removed from the U.S.

The judge called the facts of the case "appalling" — noting that while the couple moved several times, each time Lizardo "filed changes of address with the post office and with USCIS [U.S. Citizen and Immigration Services]. In turn, USCIS communicated with Petitioner at each new address."
The judge also noted that Lizardo had never been arrested during his time in the U.S.

items: Canadians caught up in Trump voter fraud crackdown as U.S. accuses Canada of election interference
Edmonton-born man held for months in ICE detention centres returns to Canada

blocks.text: Lizardo filed to have the order of removal rescinded as he had never received the notices for the hearings. That request was granted by an immigration court on Oct. 28 after it found he had provided sufficient evidence of lack of notice.
ICE argued Lizardo should be kept in custody while the green card case was being decided.
The judge ruled ICE agents had no reason to believe Lizardo was a flight risk and ordered him immediately released.

"Because the facts presented here are so appalling and so well supported, the Court could issue a long order, complete with colorful details about, and commentary on, the abuses suffered by Petitioner," the judge wrote. Instead, he said he simply wanted to make sure Lizardo didn't spend another night in jail.

articles.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump bid to block 20,000 California ballots
articles.summary: The Trump administration had appealed to the Supreme Court over claims that a list of more than 20,000 ballots in California include non-US citizens.

image.caption: Early voting has been underway in California since October Image: Mario Tama/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: On the eve of the US midterm elections, the administration of President Donald Trump made a last ditch attempt to sideline over 20,000 mail-in ballots in California, claiming non-US citizens are attempting to vote.
The US Justice Department (DoJ), which is run by Trump's former personal attorney Todd Blanche, has claimed to have a list documenting non-US citizens on California's voter rolls.
In mid October, the federal government first filed a lawsuit based on the allegations, which was rejected by a California district court.
On Monday, the DoJ asked for a "limited injunction" directing the state of California to "stop commingling suspected illegal ballots with legal ones" pending the verification of voters' status.
However, hours after the appeal was filed, the Supreme Court said it would decline to stop California from counting the votes.

When the initial lawsuit was filed by the Trump administration earlier in October, Los Angeles District Judge David Carter had warned that singling out ballots would "wreak havoc" on the election process and harm voters' trust in the democratic process.
"If the executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger," Carter wrote in rejecting the initial suit.
Early voting has been underway in California for several weeks, with hundreds of thousands of ballots already processed.
Battle for US midterm elections heats up
Analysis shows thousands of eligible voters on ballot blacklist

The voter list had been compiled by the US Department of Homeland Security. In its response to the federal government's lawsuit, California defended its election integrity, and said the process used by the Trump administration to identify non-citizen voters was likely flawed and full of errors.
Last week, another federal judge ordered the DoJ to share its list with an immigrant rights group, and a voting rights watchdog based out of the University of California Los Angeles (UCLA).

A legal filing of the analysis found that thousands of US citizens on the list appear to be inexplicably flagged as ineligible to vote. US District Judge Carter said people recently flagged as noncitizens on voter rolls in other states have repeatedly turned out to be naturalised US citizens.
Trump's fixation on voter fraud
Trump has made unfounded claims of election fraud for years, despite multiple investigations finding such malfeasance is exceedingly rare.
For the current midterm election cycle, Trump has zeroed in on claiming non US citizens are trying to vote, despite these claims being repeatedly debunked by research and investigation.

"Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own ​constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the executive branch," US District Judge Carter wrote in October.
The most populous US state, California, leans heavily Democratic, and is not expected to be a competitive state for Trump's Republicans in the midterms.
California governor Gavin Newsom is an outspoken critic of Trump, and has warned the president's administration against trying to interfere in the state's voting process.

Ahead of the midterm voting on Tuesday, Newsom announced the deployment of election law experts, poll observers and a help line for voters to report any attempts of intimidation or interference at the polls.
What could a Democrat win mean for Trump's presidency?

articles.title: Indonesia's toxic haze is giving its neighbours a political headache
articles.summary: Governments in Singapore and Malaysia are split between anxious citizens and an irascible neighbour.

blocks.text: The haze billowing out from wildfires in the Indonesian regions of Kalimantan, Papua and Sumatra knows no borders.
Carried by winds to nearby Singapore and Malaysia, the toxic smog has in recent weeks impacted populations across maritime South East Asia, triggering respiratory illnesses and headaches.
It's also giving the region's governments a different kind of headache - split between the mounting frustrations of their citizens and the risk of souring diplomatic ties with Indonesia.

"People are fed up, angry and anxious," Eugene Tan, associate professor of law at the Singapore Management University, tells the BBC. "The governments have to respond to them, or else what is more an external issue has become an internal one with ample headroom for politicisation."
Indonesia's wildfires are a yearly occurrence, widely associated with industrial-scale land clearing to make way for crops like oil palm.
But the blazes this year have been particularly difficult to tame due to a strong El Niño, which has exacerbated drought conditions in the country's forests and peatlands.
Whereas previous haze episodes in Singapore and Malaysia have typically lasted for a few days, this time it stretched into weeks.

In Malaysia, locals started a boycott of Indonesian products in protest against the haze, after lawmaker Syed Saddiq called for sanctions on companies linked to the wildfires and said Malaysians should "treat them as an outcast in the region".
There have also been complaints in Singapore, a country that has come to expect seamless efficiency from its leaders.

"There appears to be the view that the government dropped the ball in dealing with the haze, given that it was known that the El Niño weather phenomenon would be severe and that early warning was given," says Tan.
"Clearly, Singaporeans expect the government to decisively deal with the polluters."
As the haze spiralled into yet another crisis for Prabowo's beleaguered administration, some officials pushed back against criticism.
One senior official ruffled feathers when he said the wildfires were out of human control and that oxygen in neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia "also comes from our forests".
That remark was "disappointing" and "not right", according to Singaporean senior minister K Shanmugam - a rare rebuke from the city state, which prides itself on its diplomatic prowess.

"The haze is affecting our health seriously, and it's really unacceptable," Shanmugam told reporters. Since the haze impacts citizens on both sides of the border, there should not be "any bilateral issues" in addressing it, he added.
"The Indonesian public is suffering as well, and it is in Indonesia's interest as much as ours to deal with the companies that are causing these problems."
Days later, Indonesia announced it would reduce gas exports to Singapore, citing domestic energy needs - a move that many saw as retaliation to Singapore's rhetoric.

To be sure, Indonesia has faced recent electricity shortages in parts of the country. Singapore also says the reduction, which amounts to less than 2% of its total daily demand, will have little impact on its gas supply.

But the abrupt announcement came just days after Indonesia's energy minister warned that they could halt gas exports to countries that don't "respect Indonesia". That same day, Prabowo made reference to "countries that like to insult Indonesia" when talking about the wildfires.

"It's a tired playbook of using Singapore as the bogeyman, driven by the 'abang-adik' [big brother-little brother] syndrome," Tan says, referring to a historical dynamic that Singapore's leaders have long tried to shrug off: the expectation that it should defer to its larger neighbours.
"Singapore leaders expressing concerns about the haze and how it affects the people of both countries have been taken to mean that Singapore has been disrespectful to its neighbour."
In contrast, Malaysia's official rhetoric on the haze has been relatively muted.
Its foreign minister Mohamad Hasan has ruled out lodging a formal diplomatic protest with Indonesia or taking legal action, saying such actions "would mean we were prepared to sever relations".
For now, Malaysia has agreed to explore a memorandum of understanding with Indonesia to strengthen wildfire prevention efforts.
It would also rely on diplomatic mechanisms, Mohamad said - like the Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution.
The agreement, which came into effect in 2003, commits members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) to collaborate on tackling the recurring haze.
But many see it as toothless, as it is unable to punish agricultural companies linked to wildfires or to force individual governments to do so.
The agreement has turned out to be "just not worth the paper it was signed on", says James Chin, professor of Asian studies at the University of Tasmania.
"The moment the haze disappears, the moment the political pressure's off, it's back to business as usual."
In 2016, Asean countries had set a goal to eliminate haze in the region by 2020. When that deadline drifted quietly by, they set a new target of achieving the goal by 2030 instead.

Complicating Malaysia's position is the fact that it is also a major palm oil producer. The commodity is often linked to commercial "slash-and-burn" practices that are widely blamed for the region's wildfires.
Malaysia has at times dealt with acute haze stemming from blazes on local land.

In 2019, when Malaysia pointed to hotspots in Indonesia's peatlands as the cause of the haze shrouding the region, Indonesian authorities pointed the finger back at Malaysia, claiming the smog came from their side.
"As long as we place a lot of importance on oil palm planting, [the haze] is going to recur," says Ei Sun Oh, principal adviser at the Pacific Research Centre of Malaysia.

And even if Malaysia were to speak up, Oh adds, it's unlikely to wield the same "leverage" over Indonesia as Singapore, which is Indonesia's largest foreign investor and an offshore financial hub for many wealthy Indonesians.
For now, Malaysia "doesn't want to unduly provoke Indonesia", says Oh.
"The government is just wringing their hands till the wind blows [the problem] over. Because eventually it will blow over."

articles.title: Former Alberta junior hockey executive charged with sex offences against players
articles.summary: Tyler King, 39, has been arrested and charged with sexually exploiting three players. The complainants, all under 18 at the time, were junior A players from Saskatchewan and Alberta.

image.caption: Tyler King, who worked with various teams in Alberta and British Columbia, oversaw non-hockey operations for the Okotoks Oilers with the British Columbia Hockey League. (Okotoks Oilers)

blocks.text: Calgary
Tyler King, 39, has been arrested and charged with sexually exploiting three players. The complainants, all under 18 at the time, were junior A players from Saskatchewan and Alberta.
Three alleged victims are all minors, say RCMP
A former junior hockey executive in Alberta has been arrested and charged with sexually exploiting three players.
RCMP say Tyler King had been working at SUNY Oswego in New York state and was arrested Friday at a U.S. border crossing in Kingston, Ont.
The 39-year-old has been charged with luring, sexual exploitation, and making child sexual abuse and exploitation material.
The three complainants, all under 18 at the time, were junior A players from Saskatchewan and Alberta and part of the Okotoks Oilers Athletic Association.
King, who worked with various teams in Alberta and British Columbia, oversaw non-hockey operations for the Okotoks Oilers and with the British Columbia Hockey League.
Mounties say the Oilers informed them about the allegations against King in June 2024.
On June 21, 2024, the Oilers issued a statement on their website announcing King’s departure from the organization and wishing him well. The page has since been taken down.
"The Okotoks Oilers would like to thank Tyler King for his tireless efforts during his three seasons in our organization as Assistant GM, Business Operations," said the statement.
It said King had been in charge of overseeing all off-ice operations.
Speaking to the media on Monday afternoon, Cpl. Dan Campbell said he could not confirm if the Oilers knew of the allegations against King before he left the organization.
“I'm not aware of how the timeline lines up. However, I do know that the Okotoks Oilers reported this as soon as they became aware of it, and we became engaged.”
In a statement released Monday afternoon, a spokesperson for the Oilers said the organization had been made aware of charges against a former employee, but did not name King.
"The Okotoks Oilers were not aware of these allegations while this individual was with our organization," said Brent Lauinger, chairman and governor with the Oilers.
"After his departure, we received information that, while unverified at the time, raised enough concern that we felt it needed a closer look. We reviewed it carefully and passed it to the RCMP."
King was hired by the Nanaimo Clippers in June 2024 as the vice-president of business operations, according to a release on the organization's website.
Campbell said the Clippers were “likely not aware” of the allegations against King at the time.
RCMP say the investigation is ongoing.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Kylee is a reporter with CBC Calgary. You can reach her at kylee.pedersen@cbc.ca
