articles.title: Ukraine: At least 26 killed in Russian strikes on aid center
articles.summary: At least 26 people were killed in Russian airstrikes on a school that was serving as an aid distribution center in Zaporizhzhia, a southern Ukrainian region. DW has more.

image.caption: The local school in Komyshuvakha served as a humanitarian aid hubImage: Press service of the National Police of Ukraine in Zaporizhzhia region/REUTERS

blocks.text: November 2, 2026
Zaporizhzhia: At least 26 killed in Russian strikes on aid center

At least 26 people were killed and five more injured on Monday when the Russian air force launched repeated strikes on a school which was functioning as an aid distribution center in the southern Ukrainian region of Zaporizhzhia.

The multiple attacks, in which Russian planes reportedly launched more than 10 glide bombs, took place in the village of Komyshuvakha, about 35 kilometers (31 miles) east of the city of Zaporizhzhia and a dozen kilometers away from the frontline.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the attacks as "utterly horrific" and accused Russia of being well aware of the humanitarian purpose of the site.
"After the first aerial bomb strike, there was a double-tap strike with nine more bombs, specifically targeting the shelter where people were taking cover," he wrote on social media.
"The Russians could not have been unaware that every week, local residents who had remained in Komyshuvakha received humanitarian aid at that very location."

Ukrainian emergency services said two ‌members of ⁠a ⁠rescue crew were among the dead after falling victim to the so-called "double-tap" strike in which a location is targeted again with the aim of hitting first responders.
The attacks came less than 24 hours after a localized six-day humanitarian ceasefire in and around the town of Oleshky in the neighboring region of Kherson had expired.
Zelenskyy said the temporary truce could potentially have led to further steps toward a possible deal to end the ongoing Russian invasion, but said after Monday's strikes:

"This is yet further proof that Russia does not want any kind of ​de-escalation or any real justice... With these killings, Russia has sent a completely opposite signal; Russia is counting on further killings."
The Zaporizhzhia region has been targeted repeatedly for months by heavy Russian airstrikes.

articles.title: Woman, 48, and boy, 12, arrested after air cadet leader assaulted while selling poppies in Hamilton
articles.summary: The 59-year-old victim is a commanding officer and was supervising young cadets selling Remembrance Day poppies on Sunday. Police said the 12-year-old and another boy approached them and 'blew a loud…

image.caption: Hamilton police arrested a 12-year-old boy and a 48-year-old woman after the assault of a man selling poppies, police say. (Hamilton Police)

blocks.text: Hamilton

The 59-year-old victim is a commanding officer and was supervising young cadets selling Remembrance Day poppies on Sunday. Police said the 12-year-old and another boy approached them and 'blew a loud air horn directly into [the young cadets'] ears' and an altercation ensued.
The man suffered 'life-altering' injuries, police said
A man helping young air cadets sell poppies in Hamilton suffered "life-altering" injuries after an alleged assault by a 12-year-old boy and a 48-year-old woman, Hamilton police say.

The man, 59, is a commanding officer for the Royal Canadian Air Cadets and was supervising the selling of Remembrance Day poppies on Sunday when two boys approached them and "blew a loud air horn directly into [the young cadets'] ears," police said in a release on Monday.

They were outside a restaurant at The Centre on Barton, near Barton and Ottawa streets, at about 1:45 p.m. on Sunday. The man followed the boys into the restaurant "to confront them about their actions," police said on Monday.
According to police, "a struggle ensued" and a woman who was not initially involved started assisting the boys and assaulted the victim, causing him to fall.
One of the boys hit the victim "several times," police said, before leaving the scene. The woman also left before police arrived.
Police said when officers arrived, the man was suffering from serious injuries, which paramedics attended to before taking him to hospital.
The 12-year-old boy was arrested and charged with aggravated assault and assault level one. Police found him and the other boy later that day after reports of "a new, unrelated disturbance."
The second boy was not arrested, police say "as officers were able to see footage of the incident and determined his role/actions."
The woman was arrested Monday morning and charged with aggravated assault.
'Unsettling' seeing kids so young involved in assault

Veronica Formosa, who says she saw the aftermath of the incident, was arriving at the Mandarin restaurant at the Centre on Barton when she saw two kids running from the restaurant to Boston Pizza next door.

When she went inside the Mandarin, a hostess at the restaurant told her she couldn't be seated due to an "incident that involved a man and some youths fighting." People at the restaurant were telling her what happened when the same two kids ran back into the Mandarin and left shortly after.
Formosa said she later saw the man, who seemed to be wearing military-style clothing, being cared for by paramedics.
Formosa said the boys looked "really young."
"And to be involved in something like this, that's unsettling," she said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Aura Carreño Rosas is a reporter at CBC Hamilton. She's originally from Venezuela. She has extensive experience in covering stories about immigrants and migrant workers as well as interesting people with diverse journeys. You can contact her at aura.carreno.rosas@cbc.ca

articles.title: US midterms campaign 'shattering' spending records to be most expensive ever
articles.summary: The 2026 campaign is projected to cost nearly $12bn - BBC Verify looks into where all that money has come from.

blocks.text: The top 40 donors gave $2.4bn up until 14 October, according to the liberal-leaning think tank Brennan Center for Justice, external, which is a record high for that point in a midterms cycle.
"Spending in the 2026 midterms is shattering records, with more of the money coming from the wealthiest donors and groups this election," says Michael Beckel, a US campaign finance expert.

As well as individuals, organisations can also give to Pacs. For example, Geosor Corp and Fund for Policy Reform, both founded by the billionaire financier George Soros, have given a combined $102m to liberal groups.
Aside from Soros, former New York City mayor and businessman Michael Bloomberg has been the biggest Democratic donor, giving more than $60m.

Several billionaires including Jeff Yass, who runs one of the world's largest trading firms, and Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein, the owners of a US business supply company, have given over $100m this campaign to Republican causes, according to FEC filings.
But Musk has given by far the most of any individual, donating almost half a billion dollars as of October.

articles.title: Man guilty of stealing cash from farm owned by South African president
articles.summary: The case, part of the "Farmgate" scandal, has left President Cyril Ramaphosa mired in an impeachment saga.

blocks.text: A court in South Africa has found a man guilty of stealing more than $500,000 (£372,822) in cash from a farm owned by South African president Cyril Ramaphosa, in a case that mired the head of state in an impeachment saga.
Imanuwela David was found guilty of theft on Monday, as well as conspiracy to commit housebreaking with intent to steal at Phala Phala farm in the Limpopo province in 2020.
Froliana Joseph, a cleaner at the property, was also found guilty of conspiracy to commit housebreaking with intent to steal.
Her brother, Ndilinasho Joseph, was acquitted on all charges.

David was accused of breaking into the cattle farm in February 2020 and taking $580,000 (£432,000) in cash from a sofa on the property. David then went on a spending spree, buying a range of cars including three Mercedes - among them one for his girlfriend - a Porsche, two Volkswagens as well as diamond-encrusted Rolex watches and a house.

David told the court he had made the money through businesses including diamonds and Bitcoin, claims the court rejected. The court also found that David was the only one of the two convicted who had any of the stolen cash in his bank account.
Pre-sentencing will take place on 13 November.
There have been many twists and turns in what is known as the Farmgate scandal.

The theft was largely unknown until 2022 when it was brought to light by Arthur Fraser, South Africa's former intelligence chief and an ally for the former president Jacob Zuma, when he claimed that Ramaphosa hid the theft from the police and tax authorities.
Ramaphosa admitted the theft took place but denied any wrongdoing.
An independent panel that same year found Ramaphosa could have questions to answer over the burglary. MPs voted against establishing an impeachment inquiry.

In May this year, the constitutional court ruled that parliament had acted unlawfully by shelving the panel's report, and in July Ramaphosa blocked the parliamentary inquiry through a provincial court.

articles.title: Fossilised red blood cells found in 115m-year-old dinosaur’s bone, say scientists
articles.summary:
Chemical tests on Aratasaurus bone identify presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around body

It could be the opening of a Jurassic Park…

blocks.text: It could be the opening of a Jurassic Park rip-off: scientists examining ancient dinosaur bones find what appear to be fossilised red blood cells, and traces of the molecule that gives the beast’s blood its distinctive crimson hue.

But that is what researchers are claiming to have discovered after analysing the hind leg bones of a small, meat-eating dinosaur called an Aratasaurus that lived and died in what is now north-eastern Brazil 115m years ago.

Electron microscope images of the dinosaur bones revealed small, round structures that resemble red blood cells in fine channels where blood vessels once ran, while chemical tests identified the presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around the body.

Such claims are controversial because biological tissues and molecules can break down fast, leaving little or no trace in ancient fossils. But if confirmed, it would open up entirely new avenues for scientists, allowing them to investigate dinosaur blood, metabolism and even their activity levels.

“We are seeing a mineral and molecular echo of the dinosaur’s original biology,” said Prof Kliti Grice at Curtin University in Western Australia who led the research team. “Fossilised red blood cells with distinct chemistry related to heme have never been found in situ in any fossil, let alone a dinosaur. This is a world first.”

The fossilised remnants of the Aratasaurus were discovered in a mine in 2008 and have since been held in the National Museum of Brazil, where researchers continue to study them. While analysing the dinosaur’s hind leg bones, Grice spotted the structures that resembled red blood cells.

The scientists’ suspicions that they were looking at red blood cells were bolstered when chemical tests came back positive for heme and its breakdown products. Tests also found traces of the amino acid building blocks for collagen, a key protein in connective and other tissues.

blocks.caption: A portion the Aratasaurus’s hind limb. The remains were discovered in a mine in 2008 and have since been held in the National Museum of Brazil. Photograph: Curtin University

blocks.text: If the structures really are fossilised red blood cells, as the researchers contend, it raises the question of how they were preserved. According to Grice, a manganese compound called hausmannite, which formed in and around the blood cells, may have lent a helping hand by stabilising them prior to fossilisation. The same process might have helped preserve the amino acids, she added. The study appears in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

The work is already stoking debate. Prof Mary Schweitzer at North Carolina State University in the US, who has discovered remnants of blood vessels and soft tissues in dinosaur fossils, is not convinced Grice and her colleagues have found red blood cells. One reason for her doubt is that the dinosaur’s red blood cells should have a “nuclear bulge” making them appear dome-like on both sides. The structures Grice found are concave, suggesting they might be something else.

Schweitzer was more persuaded by the discovery of heme and collagen amino acids in the bone and said there was so much more to learn from exceptionally well-preserved fossils. Schweitzer added: “The conventional wisdom in palaeontology that all endogenous organics would disappear in a million years or less is being routinely challenged, and will continue to be as technological approaches to palaeontological specimens are more routinely applied.”

Another question the research raises is what other biological material might lurk in fossils collections around the world. On this, Grice urges extreme caution, adding that her work does not imply that large biological molecules such as proteins or DNA live on in ancient fossils. “Any extraordinary claim needs extraordinary analytical evidence,” she said. “The aim isn’t to find Jurassic Park DNA, it’s to determine how much genuine molecular information deep time can preserve.”

“The really exciting implication is that extraordinary molecular information may already be sitting in museum collections around the world, waiting for us to ask new questions of old fossils,” she added.

articles.title: Legal challenge to Australia's social media ban to start in High Court
articles.summary: A rights group will argue the world-leading policy robs under-16s of their right to free communication.

blocks.text: Two days of hearings on a challenge to Australia's landmark social media ban for children will begin at the country's highest court on Tuesday.

In a major test of the world-leading policy, a digital rights group will argue that the ban for under-16s robs children of their right to free communication. A separate challenge launched by platform Reddit will be jointly heard.
Introduced last December, the ban is a key part of sweeping changes the Australian government has spearheaded in recent years on online safety.
Supporters say the ban protects children from harmful content but critics say it is too blunt an instrument and efforts should focus on improving online safety.

The constitutional challenge in Australia's High Court was filed by the Digital Freedom Project a few weeks before the ban started on 10 December last year. The group is lead by New South Wales parliamentarian John Ruddick.
Two teens who originally spearheaded the case, Noah Jones and Macy Neyland, have since withdrawn as plaintiffs though Jones is still expected to attend Tuesday's hearing.
Speaking about the legal challenge last November, Jones told the BBC that there were bad things online but a blanket ban for under-16s was not the right answer.
"We shouldn't be using the resources and money of these social media platforms to try to avoid fines from our government," he said.
"They should be using this money and resources to try to get rid of the predators and harmful content out there."
Reddit also launched a High Court challenge to the ban, arguing the policy has serious implications for privacy and political rights.
Communications Minister Anika Wells last year said the government would not be "intimidated by legal threats."
"We will not be intimidated by big tech. On behalf of Australian parents, we will stand firm," she said last November.

Under the ban, ten platforms - Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, Snapchat, X, Kick, Threads and Twitch - must take "reasonable steps" to ensure no one under 16 years old can access its site.
Platforms risk fines of up to A$99m (US$70m, £52m) for serious or repeated breaches, but since the ban started, no company has been fined.

articles.title: U.S. Supreme Court rejects Trump administration's bid to set aside California mail ballots
articles.summary: The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday rejected a push for California to set aside thousands of mail ballots from people U.S. President Donald Trump's administration claims are non-citizens, a decision…

blocks.text: What happens to Trump if the Democrats crush the midterms

The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday rejected a push for California to set aside thousands of mail ballots from people U.S. President Donald Trump's administration claims are non-citizens, a decision that comes on the eve of the final day of voting in the pivotal midterm elections.
The high court refused to intervene in a case involving 20,000 people the Republican administration flagged as likely non-citizens on the largely Democratic state's voter rolls.

The swift rejection was the latest in a flurry of election-related litigation the day before the elections, which will decide control of Congress for the last two years of Trump's second term. No justices publicly dissented.

In California, the Trump administration had asked the high court to set aside the challenged ballots until the citizenship status of the voters could be verified. But state officials said the list appeared to be filled with errors and that setting the ballots aside could effectively disenfranchise legal voters.
Voters enter the C. Blythe Andrews Jr. Public Library to cast their ballots on the final day of early voting for midterm elections in Tampa, Fla., on Sunday. (Octavio Jones/The Associated Press)

The high court did not detail its reasoning, as is common in emergency decisions. The justices previously rejected Trump's push to restrict mail ballots around the country in September, even though the justices have sided with his administration in a series of other emergency docket appeals.
The Trump administration has prioritized identifying non-citizen voters this year, despite them being rare.
A district court judge previously denied the U.S. Justice Department's request and warned that the demand could disenfranchise citizens.

Also on Monday in Washington, another federal judge ruled against the administration's efforts to make last-minute demands of California election officials, finding they violated the U.S. Constitution.

items: Economic frustration set to boil over in U.S. midterm elections
Election denial has gone mainstream in the U.S. What does that mean for the midterms?

blocks.text: "The Executive Branch has likely violated the Constitution's Elections Clause, which commits authority over election rules to the states and Congress alone," wrote Chief Judge James Boasberg.
The administration, for its part, said segregating the ballots was a modest request that would eventually allow legal votes to still be counted.

The administration has faced a remarkable string of losses in court in its push, as well as criticism for waiting until a few weeks before the election to make its demands of California election officials with a list that even the Department of Justice admits is not entirely reliable.
LISTEN | The CBC's Jonathan Montpetit on what Trump might protest:
Day 69:26How will Trump’s voter fraud claims affect the midterms?

During a hearing over whether to lift her own order forbidding the administration from threatening to prosecute election workers who let potentially illegal voters cast ballots, District Court Judge Trina Thompson drilled down on reports of widespread inaccuracies in the Justice Department's data.
"Would you agree there's a high error rate?" Thompson asked Kenneth Kao, a Justice Department attorney.
"That's a fair statement," Kao said. "That's why we ask for the registrars' aid in verifying these are all valid voters."
What would a U.S. midterms win look like for Democrats and Republicans? | Hanomansing Live

At the same time, Bill Essayli, the federal prosecutor running the U.S. Justice Department's Los Angeles office, said at a news conference that he was highly confident the people on the list were not entitled to vote.
"This isn't speculation. This isn't a theory," Essayli said, later conceding there may be errors on the list.

Voting has been underway in California, a largely Democratic state, since early October. All of the state's roughly 23 million registered voters are mailed a ballot. Hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been processed. California election officials have said that finding and setting aside the challenged ballots now would be logistically impossible.

items: Canadians caught up in Trump voter fraud crackdown as U.S. accuses Canada of election interference
5 reasons why the Democrats might not take control of Congress in U.S. midterms

blocks.text: California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, said the appeal "reeks of desperation and is another attempt to undermine our elections and trample on the rule of law."
Lower courts have sided with the state, with a district judge warning that segregating ballots would "wreak havoc" on the midterm elections and erode trust in the democratic process.

"If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger," wrote U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, who was nominated by president Bill Clinton, a Democrat.

A 2-1 appeals court panel upheld his order, with one judge appointed by Trump and another appointed by president Joe Biden, a Democrat, voting in favour. The third judge on the panel, also appointed by Trump, argued in a dissent that California's unwillingness to separate the ballots encourages the "violation of federal law."
The Justice Department has sought to move the case along quickly, unsuccessfully asking an appeals court to intervene early.
Alaska setback for Trump administration

The administration has taken an increasingly aggressive approach ​toward how states run elections. The Justice Department has told ⁠election officials in all 50 states that they could face criminal prosecution if they knowingly allow non-citizens to remain on their rolls or cast ballots.
It has lost a series of lawsuits seeking to obtain voter rolls, including sensitive personal information, from dozens of states.
Trump slams Democrats for Alaska's double Dan Sullivan drama
The administration has also vowed to appeal a ruling in Alaska.

Alaska has become a particularly intense legal battleground after the New York Times reported that Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign was involved in recruiting retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan to challenge Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.

The Justice Department lawsuit, which Trump said he directed the department to file, asked a court to halt certification and order an investigation if the margin suggested voter confusion could have affected the outcome.
U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason, in Anchorage, dismissed the case on Sunday, finding ​Alaska could not conduct such a probe while preserving the secrecy of ballots.

items: Dirty tricks or much ado about nothing? Why Alaska, for once, is front and centre in midterms
Canada is in the U.S. midterm spotlight. Will the results be a blessing or a curse?

blocks.text: The lawsuit marks a rare federal intervention in the voting process and signalled a willingness by the administration to contest the election results in court.

Separate from the election result, the Justice Department has vowed to investigate whether any laws were broken in the effort that saw the politically inexperienced Dan Sullivan qualify for the ballot.

The administration already sought to restrict voting by mail for this year's midterms — a mode of casting ​ballots used more often by Democratic-leaning voters — but the Supreme Court in September rebuffed that effort.
According to an NBC News tracker, more than 24 million mail-in ballots have been cast so far, as of Monday.

articles.title: If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?
articles.summary: Dozens of shops across European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their fridges.

blocks.text: Supermarkets across Europe have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting their fridges and freezers, and raising concern about the vulnerabilities of internet-connected hardware from industrial machinery to humble domestic appliances.
Smart devices which are connected to the internet can include fridges, central heating, and even washing machines.
And while that makes them easier to control remotely, in theory, any device which goes online can potentially be exploited by malicious actors.
However, that doesn't mean hackers can easily take control of it, and big brands generally go to great lengths to make sure their tech is secure.
Exploits have been found before in some devices. In 2015, researchers demonstrated how a vulnerability in a Samsung smart fridge could allow them to intercept internet traffic.
But there's no evidence domestic appliances are being targeted in the cyber-attacks which targeted supermarkets in November.
Ciaran Martin, former chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says manufacturers needed to do more to make connected devices secure.
"There's a lot more that we need to demand of big tech to give us safer devices and products in the first place," he said.
He advised consumers to keep devices updated and enable multi-factor authentication wherever possible.
"I know it's a pain, but it only takes a few seconds," he said.
Since April 2024, UK law has required manufacturers of certain consumer smart devices to meet minimum cyber security standards, including requirements around passwords and security updates.
The NCSC said it was working with international partners and industry to understand the supermarket incidents, but it was unaware of any impact on the UK.
However, researchers from UK Cyber Defence have identified more than 800 refrigeration and building-control interfaces associated with British retailers that can be accessed over the public internet.
That doesn't necessarily mean they can be hacked, but it could leave them exposed to attackers exploiting weak passwords or software vulnerabilities.
The government has already held talks with senior food retailers about cyber resilience, following earlier attacks on supermarkets.

Helen Dickinson, chief executive of the British Retail Consortium, has said cyber incidents are a major concern for retailers, with businesses working alongside the NCSC to share intelligence and strengthen their defences.
It would not be the first time that hacks have raised concern about impact on food supply.
When UK supermarkets M&S and the Co-op were targeted by ransomware hackers in May 2025, the retailers struggled to stock some shop shelves with fresh deliveries.
Customers across the UK complained of empty shelves in the days following the attack.
Tom Hegel, a researcher at cyber-security firm SentinelOne, said retailers must be clearer about responsibility.
"The question retailers need to answer is who owns the security of that equipment, not just who repairs it," he said.
He said internet connectivity can make everyday technology more convenient, but security needed to keep pace.
"Once an attacker can operate those controls, legitimate functions such as defrosting become tools for disruption," he said.
"Changing a setting can destroy physical stock, not just interrupt a computer system."
Could cars, power plants and water supplies be vulnerable?
Outside of the home, connected tech is used to remotely manage industrial machinery and vehicles.

Cyber security expert Ken Munro pointed to a 2015 demonstration in which researchers remotely hacked a Jeep through its internet-connected entertainment system, prompting improvements in vehicle security.
"Fortunately, the vehicle industry woke up to this and fixed the problem," he said.
Mobile connections are also widely used to monitor equipment in power plants and water networks, allowing engineers to manage systems remotely.
Munro said UK utilities were generally good at securing these connections, but standards varied around the world.
His biggest concern was smaller, poorly funded utility companies which may still be relying on older, vulnerable equipment.

Without proper protections, "any factory or equipment" connected to the internet - ranging from carmakers to electricity or transport infrastructure - could face similar risks, said Olivier Daloy, a cybersecurity expert at Zscaler.

articles.title: Russian bombing kills 18 people at Ukraine aid centre, Kyiv says
articles.summary: Local officials say 27 people are missing after at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit a village in southern Ukraine.

blocks.text: At least 18 people waiting to receive humanitarian aid in a Ukrainian village have been killed in a Russian attack that Ukraine's leader has called "utterly horrific".

Five people were injured and another 27 are still missing after at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit the village of Komyshuvakha in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, regional head Mykhailo Semikin said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said that after the first strike on the local school "used for humanitarian needs", there was a second attack on the place where people were sheltering.
He posted a video showing a huge crater left after Monday's attack, and rescue teams searching through the rubble.
"The Russians could not have been unaware that the local residents who remained in Komyshuvakha received humanitarian aid there every week," the Ukrainian president wrote in a post on social media.
"This is yet another proof that Russia does not want any de-escalation."

He said that after a recent a successful joint Russian-Ukrainian operation to evacuate civilians from the Russia-occupied southern city of Oleshky, "there was a moment when the next steps could show that peace is possible".
"With such killings, Russia is sending the exact opposite signal - Russia is counting on further killings," Zelensky said.
Meanwhile, Semikin said rescue teams were working at the scene, confirming "people were still under the rubble".
The Russian military has not publicly commented.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

articles.title: 'All this food is now useless': Piles of rubbish after shop freezers hit by cyber-attack
articles.summary: Dozens of supermarkets in seven European countries dumped huge quantities of food after refrigerators and freezers were targeted in a cyber-attack.

blocks.text: In dozens of supermarkets across several European countries, a huge amount of food has been dumped after refrigerators and freezers were targeted in a cyber-attack.
Belgium and Luxemburg saw some of the worst damage, with 40 Delhaize supermarkets affected, and incidents also took place in stores across Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.

In a branch of supermarket Delhaize in Hoeilaart, just outside the Belgian capital Brussels, the BBC's Europe correspondent Nick Beake found frozen pizzas and ice cream among a mountain of food having to be scrapped. This branch estimated the cost of the damage running to more than €100,000 (£83,500).

articles.title: Fighting returns to Kherson region after longest Ukraine war ceasefire
articles.summary: Though unprecedented, the six-day truce has done little to alter the wider trajectory of a war that continues to grinds on.

blocks.text: ByLaura Gozzi and Vitaly ShevchenkoChief analyst, BBC Monitoring
Fighting has resumed in Ukraine's Kherson after a six-day truce brought quiet to the front-line region for the first time in years.

The ceasefire - the longest since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - allowed hundreds of people trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky and its surroundings to be evacuated.

On Monday morning, local authorities confirmed that strikes had resumed, saying Moscow had hit a medical facility in Kherson city centre. They also said a 62-year-old woman and a 73-year-old man were injured when a Russian drone attacked the car they were travelling in.
Ukraine also accused Russian forces of using the humanitarian ceasefire to strengthen their military positions, rotate units and deliver ammunition.

"The enemy used the humanitarian pause to set up their positions," said Ukraine's General Staff, adding they had recorded rotation of Russian units, expansion of anti-drone equipment on the roads, and delivery of ammunition.
The Kremlin appeared to corroborate this when spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was "reasonable to assume that the Ukrainian army also used this period for the necessary regrouping".
"It is a completely standard practice in such situations," he added.
The ceasefire had been brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump. Both Kyiv and Moscow thanked her repeatedly, though no details of her involvement were shared.

An unusual show of cooperation came from Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart Dmytro Lubinets. The pair oversaw the ceasefire, travelled into Oleshky and were filmed speaking to residents together. They publicly thanked each other for their work, often highlighting that no violations of the ceasefire had been observed.
Both Lantratova and Lubinets called for the initiative to be repeated elsewhere, and Ukraine repeatedly said it would be prepared to observe similar ceasefires on a national level too.
But many have questioned whether this will lead to more cooperation and further truces.

In fact, the Kremlin swiftly dismissed the idea even as the ceasefire was under way, calling Oleshky "an isolated case" which would not affect the "settlement process" – a euphemism for the stalled peace talks. "There are no similar plans or initiatives," Peskov reiterated on Monday.
And although last week the guns fell silent in Kherson region, elsewhere in Ukraine Russia's air strikes continued, killing scores of civilians and destroying crucial infrastructure.
The decision to observe an unusually broad and comparatively lengthy ceasefire in and around Oleshky was therefore a notable exception.

The ceasefire's observance appears, at least in part, to have been linked to Melania Trump's reported involvement. By violating the truce, Moscow would have risked undermining its own efforts to cultivate the crucial relationship with her husband, US President Donald Trump.
Some commentators have argued that Trump himself would be interested in presenting the Oleshky ceasefire as a foreign policy achievement scored days before the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
"I totally get why our official representatives need to 'play along' with the US first lady on Oleshky," said Artyom Sheynin, a prominent figure on Russian state TV.
"I understand why it's so important to create a 'success story' ahead of the elections for the US president, whose wife 'achieved a ceasefire' in Oleshky."

Kyiv, too, had its reasons to be fully compliant. Although relations with the US and its president are often fraught, Ukraine continues to rely heavily on US intelligence and US-made Patriot air defence missiles to counter Russian aerial attacks. Ahead of another tough winter of war, continued American support is essential to protect Ukrainian skies from Russia's assaults.
But though the ceasefire may have been born out of political calculation rather than purely humanitarian compassion, it also resulted in hundreds of civilians escaping.

There were emotional scenes when hundreds of Oleshky residents arrived in northern Ukraine on Saturday. Many were met by tearful relatives they had not seen in years. To the journalists waiting, the evacuees told of years of hunger and hardship in a destroyed town.
The hundreds of residents who decided to stay behind will receive monthly humanitarian aid deliveries, Lantratova said, adding that decision too was the result of Melania Trump's mediation.
Yet the troop rotations and resupply efforts show that neither side is expecting Oleshky to be a blueprint for lasting respite in the future.

As Kherson came under fire again, Ukrainian drones hit several energy facilities across four Russian regions. In Samara, residents reported hearing explosions and seeing black plumes of smoke rising into the sky as an oil refinery was hit for the fifth time in a month.
If the truce brought a rare moment of relief to Oleshky, it has done little to alter the wider trajectory of a war that grinds on for now.

articles.title: Oil price falls amid hope of a breakthrough to end Iran war
articles.summary:
Brent crude drops by more than 6% to $105.55 a barrel, the lowest level in more than two weeks

The oil price has fallen to its lowest level in more two weeks amid new hopes of a breakthrough…

blocks.text: The oil price has fallen to its lowest level in more two weeks amid new hopes of a breakthrough to end the Iran war.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, dropped by more than 6.5% to as low as $105.55 a barrel on Monday, the lowest since 16 October, sending shares in airline companies higher and pushing down government borrowing costs.
Oil prices fell after Tehran revealed that contacts between Iran and the US to end their eight-month war were continuing.

“Consultations through mediators are very ⁠intensive. We have presented our conditions and ⁠proposals and everything depends on the political ​rationality of Washington,” the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said, according to the state media outlet IRNA.
Over the weekend, Qatari officials tried to negotiate the release of more than $6bn (£4.5bn) in Iranian assets, so that Tehran might allow the strait of Hormuz to reopen.
Donald Trump had earlier taken a belligerent tone, telling voters in Iowa on Sunday that Iran would receive “the hammer” unless there was progress.

“The only reason why I’m not finished with Iran is I want to be nice. I want to try and save all those lives if I can ... But at some point we’re going to have to give them the hammer,” he said during a campaign rally in the run-up to the US midterm elections.
But investors were cheered by reports on Monday that Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, had granted “powers” to his government in its talks with the US seeking to end the Middle East war.

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “The news is manna from heaven for stock markets, which have felt increasingly pressured by oil’s rise, but of course there is still a risk that Trump will try one last throw of the iron dice after the midterms.”
after newsletter promotion

The drop in the oil price sparked hopes of a break in the inflationary pressures gripping the global economy. Government borrowing costs dropped, with the yield – or interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds down 10 basis points, or 0.1 of a percentage point, to the lowest since 22 September.
Shares in British Airways’ parent company, IAG, rose by 4.2% in London, while United Airlines jumped 7% in New York.

articles.title: U.S. federal investigators to provide update after Florida plane crash that killed 9

image.caption: First responders attend the scene of a deadly plane crash in Palm Beach County, Fla., on Sunday. The crash, which killed nine people, is being investigated by federal officials. (Mark Elias/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

A business jet crashed into a South Florida neighbourhood and erupted into a ball of flames, killing all nine people on board and leaving a fiery crater. The cause was not immediately clear, but federal investigators are expected to provide an update at 1 p.m. ET on Monday.
Officials have not yet identified those on board the Bahamas-bound aircraft
A business jet crashed into a South Florida neighbourhood and erupted into a ball of flames, killing all nine people on board and leaving a fiery crater.

The cause was not immediately clear, but federal investigators are expected to provide an update during a news conference at 1 p.m. ET on Monday in West Palm Beach. CBC News will be carrying it live here.

Video recorded by passersby captured the terrifying moment on Sunday afternoon, when the Bahamas-bound aircraft plunged from the sky before slamming into the ground and exploding in Green Acres, about 11 kilometres southwest of West Palm Beach. Flames flickered around chunks of pavement lining the crater as shocked residents looked on in horror. Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site.

"Debris was everywhere. Debris hit my house. Everything was on fire. The road was on fire," Anthony Blackmon, who lives near the crash site, told NBC affiliate WTVJ. "I've always seen it on the news, never thought it would happen so close to somebody, like how it happened today."
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said there were no immediate reports of anyone on the ground injured or killed. Authorities have not yet released the names of the people who died.

items: All 9 aboard killed after plane crashes in Florida, officials say

blocks.text: Palm Beach County authorities were evacuating about 600 people from a nearby mobile home community while the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigate the crash.
Authorities have not provided any information about what caused the Bahamas-bound Learjet 60 to crash.

The jet began its journey at the Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas, and airport spokesperson Jim Reynolds described it as a private aircraft. He could not immediately provide details about who was on board.
The plane was heading east at about 35,000 feet when the pilot started to report problems.

The pilot said ice was accumulating on the jet and that turbulence was jolting it by as much as 700 feet (210 metres), according to air traffic control recordings captured by LiveATC.net. Rain pounded the region on Sunday.
"We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence," the pilot told controllers.
The situation rapidly deteriorated.
Jet lost altitude at alarming rate
The pilot requested permission to climb another 2,000 feet (610 metres), then quickly declared an emergency as the jet lost altitude at an alarming rate.
"We're descending 8,000 — mayday, mayday — we're descending 10,000 feet per minute," the pilot radioed.

"We are in an overspeed condition, descending 20,000 feet per minute," the pilot radioed, before delivering a devastating acknowledgment of what was about to happen. "We're going to crash into the ground."
Mayday call captures final moments before Florida jet crash
The plane banked sharply to the right before crashing and exploding.
"It was a cataclysmic plane crash," DeSantis told reporters at the scene. "It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road."

articles.title: Ice hockey officials considering options after CAS order to reinstate Russia
articles.summary: Ice hockey's ruling body is deciding how to respond to a decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport that allows Russia back into international competition. Germany hasn't ruled out pulling out as…

image.caption: Russian players could soon again be seen at IIHF-sanctioned international ice hockey tournamentsImage: Kirill Kukhmar/ITAR-TASS/IMAGO

blocks.text: The president of the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF), Franz Reindl, announced shortly after the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) on Friday, that he had called a meeting of its main decision-making body for this Monday and Tuesday.

The Lausanne-based court had ruled that the IIHF must allow Russian national teams to take part in ice hockey world championships again. They had been barred from doing so since shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
"Our task now is to implement this ruling responsibly," said Germany's Reindl, who was elected IIHF president just last month.

"Several championships are only weeks away, and changes to participation affect many people; players, teams, organizing committees and host cities. We will work closely with all of them to find practical solutions."

blocks.caption: Franz Reindl, 71, was elected president of the IIHF in early OctoberImage: ActionPictures/IMAGO

blocks.text: The first tournament the CAS decision applies to is the World Juniors, to be held beginning on December 26 in Canada. Just how it will affect the tournament is not clear. Hockey Canada said it was in contact with the IIHF and had briefed Prime Minister Mark Carney's government on the decision.
Canada to 'maintain restrictions' on Russian athletes
Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand told public broadcaster CBC that she is "not comfortable" with allowing a Russian team to take part in the tournament in Alberta.

"This is a very unwelcome decision given the geopolitical situation, given the actions of Russia," she said. "All options are on the table, and I will say, again, I greet this decision with great disappointment."
Canada's secretary of state for sport, Adam van Koeverden, appeared to rule out Russian athletes being granted visas for the tournament

"Canada will maintain restrictions on the participation of Russian athletes at events hosted in Canada that receive funding from the Government of Canada and explore further options to ensure that the Russian government is held accountable," he said in a statement.
German hosts mull 'possible consequences for Worlds
Germany is also considering its options as it prepares to host the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in Gelsenkirchen, Düsseldorf and Mannheim next May.
"The German government takes a very critical view of the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport, a government spokesman said on Sunday, according to the DPA news agency.
"The German government will discuss possible consequences of the ruling, including for the 2027 Ice Hockey World Championship in Germany, with the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) promptly."

blocks.caption: Frank Lutz is expected to meet with government officials in Berlin this weekImage: Adrian Goldberg/BEAUTIFUL SPORTS/picture alliance

blocks.text: The DEB's chief executive, Frank Lutz, is to travel to Berlin to discuss the matter with government officials this week. Speaking on broadcaster MagentaSport on the weekend, he conceded that surrendering Germany's hosting rights for the lucrative tournament was a possibility.

"I do not want to paint a black picture. I do not want to call the World Championship into question either. But of course, we at the DEB also have to consider the option of handing back this championship," he said.
Many disappointed, Russia delighted
Several other national ice hockey federations have expressed disappointment at the CAS decision, including those of Ukraine, Sweden, Finland, and Czechia.

The International Olympic Committee opened the door for Russian athletes to return to international competition when it lifted its ban of the Russian Olympic Committee in July. However, the IIHF had already decided to continue to exclude Russian teams for the 2026-27 season – over security concerns. The CAS decision – handed down after an appeal by Russia – found this reasoning was insufficiently proven.
Russian reaction to the ruling was, unsurprisingly, positive.

"Russia is returning to world hockey. This place rightfully belongs to us, and discrimination in hockey has been brought to an end," Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev told state television channel Vesti.

blocks.caption: The Russian Olympic Committee team won silver at their last tournament, the 2022 Winter Olympics in BeijingImage: Maxim Thore/Bildbyran/IMAGO

blocks.text: No return to business as usual
A boycott of the World Juniors, Men's World Championships or other tournaments by individual nations appears to be a possibility.

Latvia is prohibited by law from competing against Russian teams. Finland has said individual players would be free to opt-out of tournaments that include Russia, while Swedish Ice Hockey Association chairman Anders Larsson, who is a member of the IIHF Council, told Swedish news agency TT that "a boycott is not on the table."
However, at the same time he also noted that "our position is that Russia cannot participate in international championships in the current situation."
Further-reaching implications?
There has been the suggestion, that having won this victory at the CAS, Russia's next focus could be on football, where its national and club teams remain excluded from international competitions.
Russian FA general secretary Maxim Mitrofanov told state news agency Tass that there "should be one rule for all."

World football's governing body FIFA allowed a Russia boys' team to play under its national flag in the inaugural Under-15 World Cup and Festival in Azerbaijan, which kicked off last week and ends on Saturday.

articles.title: What we know about the alert app hack in Ukraine and Russia
articles.summary: Both Ukraine and Russia say their air raid alert apps were cyber-attacked - Joe Tidy explains what we know so far.

blocks.text: Ukraine's emergency alert app issued a nationwide air raid warning, as well as alerts for a radiological threat, a chemical attack and street fighting in Kyiv on Sunday evening - all of which turned out to false.
A few hours later, Russia said its equivalent app had also issued false alerts, with both countries claiming their systems had been hacked.
It is still unclear who is to blame for the cyber-attacks and whether the two incidents are connected - the BBC's cyber correspondent Joe Tidy explains what we know so far.

articles.title: LA communities kick out Big Oil
articles.summary: After years of advocacy from residents and legal battles with Big Oil, LA has voted to ban drilling and phase out oil extraction in the city. It's the first city in the country to kick the oil…

image.caption: LA residents fought urban oil drilling for years — it's now been banned by LA City Image: Gissela C./STAND-L.A.

blocks.text: Los Angeles has become the largest city in the US to ban oil drilling, after years of lawsuits and campaigning by residents who raised the alarm over pollution and potential health risks from nearby wells.

"Frontline communities have pushed the city for a solution for this for over a decade," said local resident Wendy Miranda, who has campaigned for years with STAND-LA, a coalition of community groups working to end neighborhood oil drilling.

The ordinance, approved by the LA City Council on October 28, puts an immediate stop to oil extraction and bans re-drilling or deepening of wells, while existing operations must be phased out within city limits over the next 20 years.
Though LA City is only part of greater Los Angeles, the move affects hundreds of active wells and thousands of inactive ones, many located in working class communities of color.

"In South LA, working-class families have had corporations drilling across the street from their homes," said council president Marqueece Harris-Dawson in a statement. "No one should have to live near an oil drilling site."

blocks.caption: Oil infrastructure is running just a stone's throw away from homes in LA neighborhoodsImage: Nils Hünerfürst/DW

blocks.text: Rock Zierman, CEO of the California Independent Petroleum Association (CIPA), told DW, "CIPA believes this ordinance constitutes an unlawful taking of private property."
LA follows much smaller Culver City, also in California, in moving against urban oil production, and begins the process of ending its long, complex relationship with fossil fuels.
Why residents campaigned to end city oil drilling

California's oil industry expanded rapidly in the early 20th century, when the state produced roughly a quarter of the world's oil. Lots of that so-called black gold was around LA and as the city grew, homes, schools and businesses were built around existing oil infrastructure.

Today, wells can be found beneath residential areas, close to playgrounds, along the coast and in some of the city's most densely populated and largely working-class neighborhoods. Some have been permanently sealed or plugged for decades, while others remain active or are idle.
Under California law, an idle well is one that has not produced oil for two years. Unlike plugged wells, they can potentially return to production.
How LA is plugging hidden oil wells

Residents living near the active and inactive wells report strong odors, headaches, nausea and breathing difficulties. Another concern is air quality. Oil wells can release toxic pollutants, including benzene and hydrogen sulfide, and research has linked proximity to oil extraction with higher rates of respiratory illness and reduced lung function.

But both active and idle wells can also leak methane — a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change — while residents say occasional accidents or breakages send oil flowing down city streets.

"Frontline communities have been experiencing or have experienced for decades living near these toxic sites and having to pay for that with their health," said Miranda, a policy director with Esperanza Community Housing, a nonprofit providing affordable housing services.
Miranda told DW she and her mother both have asthma. The council vote "definitely represents hope," she added.
Previous attempts to ban oil production

LA City Council initially approved an ordinance to phase out oil extraction back in 2022 after successful lobbying by residents like Wendy Miranda. But oil companies challenged the measure in court, with industry groups successfully arguing that the city lacked the legal authority to impose the ban.
California subsequently passed legislation giving local governments greater power to regulate and restrict oil and gas operations, putting the possibility of a phaseout back on the table.

blocks.caption: Some oil wells are hidden in plain sight, such as this building hiding an active oil-drilling operationImage: Nils Hünerfürst/DW

blocks.text: In an emailed statement to DW, CIPA CEO Rock Zierman said energy companies were prepared to challenge the new ordinance.
Zierman added that it would make Angelenos more dependent on foreign oil from countries with lower environmental standards when they are "already struggling" with high gas prices.
"It sends the jobs, investment, and revenue elsewhere, while leaving Californians to pay the bill," said Zierman.

The relationship between local oil production and prices at the pump is not straightforward and is influenced by a number of factors, according to the California Energy Commission, the state's main energy policy agency. Those include the cost of crude oil, refining, transportation, distribution and local taxes.

Even though the US is the world's largest oil producer, it exports and imports crude oil, as well as refined petroleum products. Because oil is traded globally, US residents are exposed to the same price fluctuations as people elsewhere, no matter how much of the fossil fuel is produced domestically.

California's oil industry and the amount of oil it produces have been steadily declining since the 1980s. In the LA Basin, output is 43% lower than eight years ago, with the amount of oil extracted falling more rapidly than the number of open wells.
Who will foot the bill for the cleanup?

When wells stop producing, it is up to the oil operators to remove equipment and plug them. The state agency that regulates oil and gas, CalGEM, and the LA Fire Department oversee plugging operations, and also seal wells for which no-one takes responsibility.
But many have not yet been plugged — some 80% of idle wells in LA have been inactive for more than eight years, and about a third for over a century.

The cost of plugging a well also varies widely, with estimates ranging from hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars. California law requires operators to submit plugging plans or face annual fines that increase with the amount of time the well has been idle.
But those fines aren't always paid. According to CalGEM's own data, the agency collected just $1 million out of $36 million in fines in 2025.

A report by Carbon Tracker also found that if all future profits from oil companies operating in California went to decommissioning wells, the state would still face a shortfall of $7 billion. The cost would by default fall to taxpayers, according to Carbon Tracker.

Miranda told DW that the next step for community activists is to reduce the 20-year timeline and have the oil sector "pay for this cleanup." For now, she is says both she and her mother are hopeful that future generations "can have better health and breathe cleaner air."

articles.title: Global pedestrian Karl Bushby returns home to UK after 28-year trek
articles.summary: Karl Bushby, a British man who traveled 50,000 km without transport over the past 28 years, has come home. Starting in Chile, he crossed the Americas, Russia and parts of Central Asia and Europe —…

image.caption: Karl Bushby has returned home after 28 yearsImage: Paul Ellis/AFP

blocks.text: British adventurer Karl Bushby, 57, arrived back his hometown in England on Monday after crossing four continents on foot.
He was met by a cheering crowd of some 500 people in the northeastern city of Hull at the end of his 50,000 km (31,000 mile) journey, which began in the far south of South America in 1998.
"I didn't do this alone. There was a big team, the biggest team, Earth. That's what it took to get me back," Bushby told the crowd.
On his trip, he obeyed two rules: to avoid all forms of motorized transport to advance; and not to return until he had finished what he had set out to do.
A very final leg of his journey was to take him to north Hull, where he was to reunite with his mother, Angela, his 36-year-old son, Adam, and a 12-year-old granddaughter he had never met.

blocks.caption: Bushby was welcomed by a large crowd in his hometown of HullImage: Temilade Adelaja/REUTERS

blocks.text: What did Bushby experience on his epic journey?
Bushby, a former paratrooper, began his adventure in Chile aged 29 after a marriage breakup that saw his wife return to Northern Ireland with their son.

During the trip, he crossed an iced-over Bering Strait from Alaska to Russia with French explorer Dimitri Kieffer in 2006 — nearly losing his life in the process — and, returning to Britain early last month, he swam the English Channel from northern France to Dover over four days.

He interrupted, or was forced to pause, his journey several times, including when he was refused a visa by Russia, which caused a journey originally planned to take 12 years to last more than double that time.
He also spent some jail time in Panama for entering the country without a visa.
The COVID-19 pandemic also caused delays, and he spent some time living at a base in Mexico.
But he always resumed the trek at the exact spot where he had left off.

blocks.caption: Bushby transported the necessaries largely on a handcartImage: Paul Ellis/AFP

blocks.text: The famous German filmmaker Werner Herzog is making a feature-length documentary about the journey entitled "Walk of Life."
In an interview with the AFP news agency from northern France in September, Bushby expressed apprehension about returning to a more normal life back in Britain.
"I've got to try and get established in the grown-up world again," he said.

articles.title: How Iliana Yotova won the presidential election in Bulgaria
articles.summary: Iliana Yotova won the presidential election in Bulgaria, promising to be a "president of peace." But the campaign showed how divided Bulgarians are about the war in Ukraine and drone attacks in the…

image.caption: Iliana Yotova (center) addresses the press after winning the Bulgarian presidential election runoff on Sunday, garnering 57.6% of the voteImage: BGNES

blocks.text: "We are choosing between war and peace," Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told voters ahead of Sunday's presidential election runoff between incumbent President Iliana Yotova, who opposes military aid to Ukraine and favors dialogue with Russia, and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, who is regarded as staunchly pro-European and pro-Ukrainian.
With these words, it was clear that Sunday's runoff had turned into a kind of referendum on the country's foreign policy and stance on the war in Ukraine.
Now that the official results are in and it is clear that Iliana Yotova won the election decisively by 57.6% to Gyurov's 39.5%, Radev claims that Bulgarians have chosen peace.
But is it really as simple as all that?
First-round surprise

When the presidential election campaign began in Bulgaria on September 25, there did not seem to be any doubt about the outcome: Iliana Yotova was well ahead in the polls on 44.5%. Gyurov, her main rival, trailed far behind on 26.1%.
Yotova was backed by both the prime minister and his ruling Progressive Bulgaria party, which won an absolute majority in the parliamentary election on April 19.

blocks.caption: Yotova, who succeeded Ruman Radev as president when he stepped down to run for prime minister earlier this year, is the first woman to be elected president of BulgariaImage: Nikolay Doychinov/AFP

blocks.text: But the first round turned out to be much tighter than anticipated.
While Yotova got 34.8% of the vote in the first round, Gyurov was close behind on 31.95%, which meant that a runoff between the two was necessary.
Decisive victory, clear divide
While Yotova won the runoff convincingly, both the campaign and the outcome showed that the Bulgarian electorate is divided.
This division is both generational and geographical, explains Dimitar Ganev, sociologist and political scientist at the Trend market and electoral research agency.

"Younger voters — those aged between 18 and 40 — favor Gyurov. Those over 40 tend to prefer Yotova," Ganev told DW. "It also appears that Gyurov dominates in the capital, Sofia. In smaller regional cities, other towns and villages, Yotova dominates decisively," he said.
'President of peace'
This divide was also evident during the campaign.

blocks.caption: Candidates Andrey Gyurov (left) and Iliana Yotova (right) faced each other in Sunday's presidential election runoffImage: Desislava Kulelieva/BNT

blocks.text: While Andrey Gyurov relied mainly on social media for his campaign, Yotova chose to speak mostly to supporters of Progressive Bulgaria in closed venues.
At such events, the war in Ukraine was always high on the agenda.

"As long as I am president, and if you place your trust in me, not a single Bulgarian soldier will go to Ukraine," Yotova declared at an election rally on October 6 — even though according to the Bulgarian Constitution, only parliament (not the president) has the authority to send troops abroad or declare war.
Throughout the campaign, she referred to her opponents as "warmongers" and described herself as the "president of peace."
"We won because we talked to people about income and about peace," Yotova said after the election.
Russia's war in Ukraine a major campaign issue
In this, she is similar to Prime Minister Rumen Radev.

When it comes to Ukraine, Radev regularly speaks of the need for peace and avoids calling Russia an "aggressor." Both Radev and Yotova oppose military aid to Ukraine and criticize European leaders for not making sufficient efforts to engage with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Gyurov, on the other hand, has sharply criticized Russian aggression in Ukraine.
Appointed caretaker prime minister by Yotova in February, Gyurov in March signed a security cooperation agreement with Ukraine, provoking the disapproval of both Yotova and Radev.
The impact of drone attacks in the Black Sea
In the weeks leading up to the election, several ships in the Black Sea were hit by drones off the Bulgarian coast.

blocks.caption: Bulgaria's former interim Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov is regarded as staunchly pro-European and pro-UkrainianImage: Nikolay Doychinov/AFP

blocks.text: The European Council criticized Russia for the escalation, and the European Parliament called on the EU and its member states "to consider deploying an EU naval operation" there.

Prime Minister Radev, however, was not as equivocal, going no further than summoning the Russian ambassador and stating that "logic suggests that the outcome" of the attacks in the Black Sea "is to the advantage of the Russian Federation."
Just days before the runoff, he noted that "two ships were struck and sunk in Romanian territorial waters" after Romania had held Russia responsible for the attacks in the Black Sea.

"Many people think that once the aggressor is identified, the attacks will stop," he said, downplaying the Kremlin's responsibility. His remarks drew criticism from politicians and the media in Romania.

Yotova also did not name Russia as the perpetrator, instead saying during her campaign that she did not want to see "foreign flags in Bulgaria" — a clear reference to the Ukrainian flag, which has been displayed outside several institutions in Bulgaria as a sign of solidarity with the war-torn country.
How other voters voted

Most opposition parties, including the right-wing conservative GERB led by former long-serving Prime Minister Boyko Borisov, refused to field a candidate for the presidency, which is one reason why turnout on Sunday was less than 30%.

In the first round, the pro-Russian candidate Kostadin Kostadinov from the nationalist Vazrazhdane (Revival) party came third with 12.5% of the vote. According to Dimitar Ganev, around 70% of Vazrazhdane voters backed Yotova in the runoff.
To secure their support, Yotova targeted pro-Russian voters.
How Russian aggression is shaping Bulgaria's presidential election

"Russia is by no means an enemy of Bulgaria," she said in a podcast interview just two days before the runoff, adding "Russia is part of our history, and I very much hope that it will be a key factor in the future security architecture across Europe, including for us."

In the days leading up to the vote, some of her supporters began claiming that the opposition was preparing a "Maidan," a reference to the Ukrainian revolution of 2014 that culminated in the ousting of President Viktor Yanukkovych, who had close ties to Moscow.

"All of Gyurov's lackeys are speaking openly about inevitable protests. They're using prime time to stir up a Maidan. Every single one of them," Sonya Momchilova, who was appointed to the media regulator by Radev, wrote on Facebook on Sunday.
Similar claims were made by both former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban and former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic ahead of this year's elections in their countries.
Bulgaria in the EU and NATO

"This claim that Ms. Yotova will be a president of peace is directly linked to the incitement of a fear of war," said former Defense Minister Todor Tagarev, who was part of the committee that nominated Andrey Gyurov for president. "Bulgaria will be in a much worse position within Europe and NATO under her leadership," he said during a TV interview.

Dimitar Ganev, on the other hand, sees no threat to Bulgaria's commitment to the EU and NATO. "Over two-thirds of Bulgarians do not question the country's geopolitical orientation, and around two-thirds have a positive attitude towards the EU," he told DW.

But the positions of Radev and Yotova, which many view as ambivalent, mobilized both the pro-European camp and Eurosceptic voters, who, according to Ganev, make up around a third of the country's population.
According to Prime Minister Rumen Radev and President Iliana Yotova, the Bulgarian people chose peace in the presidential election. Nevertheless, the war continues.

articles.title: Her neighbour built a garden suite. She calls it a 'watchtower' over her Toronto backyard
articles.summary: Fed up with what she calls a violation of her backyard privacy, an East York woman is going public with her campaign to have new garden suites limited to just one storey.

blocks.text: Toronto
Fed up with what she calls a violation of her backyard privacy, an East York woman is going public with her campaign to have new garden suites limited to just one storey.
East York homeowner calls for limit for garden suites to be 1 storey high
'I lost all privacy': Toronto woman speaks out over neighbour's 2-storey garden suite
An East York homeowner is going public with her campaign to change the city's rules governing garden suites after what she calls a violation of her backyard privacy.

Sandy Chambers, who lives in the Danforth-Greenwood area, says this past summer she returned from a one-week vacation to find a six-metre-high, two-storey building with a picture window, looming over her back fence.
"After you get past the shock there's a little bit of anger," she said. "I lost all privacy in my yard, I stopped using my yard."
"It fired me up."
In response, she planted trees across the back of her yard, and erected a large screen on a backyard shed, which blocks the view from the neighbours’ new picture window.
In 2022, the updated planning rules to allow homeowners to build garden suites on their properties with fewer city restrictions. (Michael Smee/CBC)

She also ordered dozens of lawn signs that read "Save Our Neighbourhoods. No 2-storey Garden Suites Without a Say." An online petition that she started also appears to be gaining traction, she says, so far garnering about 80 signatures.
CBC Toronto tried to speak with the homeowners but no one answered a knock at the door Thursday.
One of the people who is displaying one of those signs on her front lawn is Rosanna Manarin, who lives next door to the house that installed the garden suite.
She says she was shocked at how completely her light and privacy were limited by the new build.
"I understand the city’s need for density, but what is now sitting next door to me is a watchtower," she told CBC Toronto.
Rosanna Manarin, who has lived in the same house for 25 years, says the emergence of a two-storey garden suite overshadowing her yard this past summer was a shock. (Michael Smee/CBC)
“Your oasis is completely gone.”
New planning rules introduced to ease housing issues
Technically, the homeowners are within their rights under new city rules that govern the construction of garden suites.
Garden suites are self-contained, detached units often built in backyards and not connected to a public lane, according to the city of Toronto's website.

In 2022, the city updated planning rules to allow homeowners to build garden suites on their properties with fewer city restrictions. The idea, known as gentle infill housing, was first floated as a way to help ease the city’s housing crunch.

Instead of requiring a zoning change — which would have meant an opportunity for public discussion about the new build — property owners are now only required to apply for a building permit to put up structures such as garden suites and multiplexes.

items: This couple says they are paying the price of Toronto's housing push

blocks.text: The new process doesn't include an opportunity for public input, as long as the plan doesn’t require any variances — smaller setbacks, for instance.

Numbers from the city show the public has reacted enthusiastically. In 2022, the first year that garden suites were allowed without expensive and time-consuming rezoning applications, just 34 building permits were issued. By 2025, that number had risen to a total of 361.
Staff say so far, 627 have been built while another 755 are under construction.
But there have also been complaints.
Garden suites a 'turn off' for buyers: real estate broker
The city does not track criticisms for the initiative, but anecdotally, real estate experts say they’re hearing from unhappy homeowners.
Real estate broker Justin Bregman says potential buyers he’s encountered are not enthusiastic about the lack of light and privacy that some garden suites bring to a neighbourhood.
In terms of resale value, "It’s a turn off," he says.
"If all of a sudden there’s a two-storey, or a 20-foot (six-metre) high [building] that’s completely blocking your backyard, that absolutely is going to affect value."
City staff did not answer directly when asked to comment on Chambers’ drive to have garden suites limited to just one storey as-of-right — meaning without rezoning or input from neighbours.

In an email to CBC Toronto, staff wrote: "The City of Toronto recognizes that new construction can raise concerns for neighbouring property owners, including concerns related to privacy, sunlight and construction impacts," the email states.
"While these concerns are understandable…these concerns do not, on their own, provide a basis to withhold a building permit" if the project complies with the provincial building code.

items: Alberta government to force Edmonton to change infill rules

blocks.text: Toronto real estate lawyer Bob Aaron points out that backyard privacy is never guaranteed in an urban neighbourhood.
Garden suites aside, most people with a two storey house can see into a neighbour’s yard.
"Frankly there is no right to privacy from neighbouring properties looking into your property in Canadian law," he said.
"That’s the joy of urban living."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
michael.smee@cbc.ca

articles.title: Merz says next German president 'must be a woman' — report
articles.summary: German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier's second term is due to end in March next year. Meanwhile, Merz has called for 'digital sovereignty' in the era of AI. Follow DW for more
articles.byline: Natalie Muller, Matt Ford, Timothy Jones

image.caption: Germany's federal president is the country's official head of state, as opposed to the chancellor, who is the head of the government [FILE: Jul 29, 2026]Image: Markus Schreiber/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: November 2, 2026
Merz says next German president 'must be a woman'
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has spoken out in favor of having a woman succeed Frank-Walter Steinmeier as Germany's president.

"I will propose a consensus candidate to the party, a candidate from the political center," Merz said at a non-public meeting of local Christian Democratic Union (CDU) chairs in Berlin, participants told the German DPA news agency.
"I am firm in my belief that it must be a woman," he reportedly added.
Germany's federal president is the country's official head of state, as opposed to the chancellor, who is the head of the government.
Current incumbent Steinmeier, a former Social Democrat (SPD) foreign minister, became president in 2017 and his second term will end in March 2027.
Bavarian premier Markus Söder recently proposed Ilse Aigner from his Christian Social Union (CSU), the CDU's Bavarian sister party.

But the CDU itself may propose an alternative candidate from within its own ranks, with current parliamentary speaker Julia Klöckner, Families Minister Karin Prien and former CDU leader and Defense Minister Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer all having been mentioned.
The CDU's top leadership is expected to propose a candidate on November 9.
